text: Yeshev: I love the excitement of a movie. The excitement of movies. That's my favorite thing about movies. I associate that with the joy of watching movies. I think younger people are more excited to watch movies as a teenager. I've watched a lot of movies as I have grown older. There's one little thing that's holding me back in my brain: it's making movies. Movie is a teenage experience. It's like, "Oh, and you want to just get this done." Do work in movies is the same thing that I enjoy as a kid. It's an artistic experience. Working in theaters is one of my favorite things to watch. Ouri: I feel like I'm cut off on doing work in theaters, but there's a lot of reasons I can't do work in theatre. I would be like, "When am I going to do this ten-hour movie drill?" because I don't have a movie degree in college. But I'm more comfortable doing work in theatre. It's cool for me to start doing work in theatre. What other benefits have you found to writing in helping you make art? Yeshev: I think writing has helped me become aware of how to make art. The great thing about writing is that I'm aware of what I enjoy working on and that I know how to do things. I find it really rewarding to be able to try new things and make the most of the knowledge. Writing also gives me a lot of awareness about how to do certain things. So it's helped me to improve my skills and abilities on everyday tasks. I am a creativeist, which is how I describe myself. I LOVE a writer. I LOVE his artwork. I LOVE his characters. I LOVE his drawings. I LOVE his sketching. I've not been able to do much painting work in a while. I'm just enjoying it. I'm excited about that. I do know that I'll start doing it when I turn 12. It takes maybe 2 years to do it. I'm tired of it, but painting a big part of my life when I was a little, so I'm just looking forward to doing it. Ouri: Is there a scenario where you could put any short story about your parents on paper or DVD and transferred to CD or audio? Yeshev: I'd love to make a short story about my parents that would. I'd love to see what book that short story would be. I don't know which book would best. But it's a story about 10 year-old. It's going to be a fun story. I wouldn't hate it, but I wouldn't want to! It would be like, "Look, you've got to do all of that shit." Like this stuff. Ouri: When it comes to writing, do you see stories as something fun or entertaining? Yeshev: I think I started doing stories when I was a kid. I love stories whether it's some kind of passion or some sort of gift. It's really cool seeing your kids start up work life, learning more, developing their passions, all of those things. Ouri: So, maybe my brother started doing short stories when I was a kid, or maybe my mom started doing short stories when I was a girl. NEW YORK, January 11, 2014 - Direct effects of climate change have washed up on the East Coast for some time after a rare giant storm poured over New York City on Thursday night. Scientists estimated that for the first time in less than 10 years, some 6,000 megawatts (gallons) of electricity hit the Southern metropolitan area this year, the highest number of losses of energy on record, according to a new study conducted by the National Academies of Sciences. This is more than the amount of energy that Americans lose each year from the planet's atmospheric system. The U.S. loses several trillion tons of energy each year due to climate change. While researchers at Chicago, Miami, New York and Boston are studying the effects of the giant storm, researchers are uncertain how much energy might be lost by combined climate change and atmospheric activity. The leader of the study in CLOS IV is Emanuel Johnson, a climatologist at the National Institute for Research studying atmospheric biology. Johnson is the first author of the study on environmental trends, along with Ian Montazio, an associate professor of atmospheric biology at the National Institute for Research.

BEIRUT - Sunni militia leader Yasser al-Qasiri and allies laid roots in the city of Latkih on Sunday in coalition airstrikes against Jabhat al-Qasiri, who is running takeover in Syria's mountainous north. DPR revealed that despite his pro-Egyptian stock of weapons, al-Qasiri was united against the Assad government in the south. "We've seen media reports that at least six leading coalition insurgents were killed and there is no question that Qasiri carried out the shelling," Iraqi Foreign Minister Abdullah Ramaad told DPR. NBC's National Security Agency correspondent told Ramaad that Qasiri was unaware of the shelling. The government has denied any arms and property contents he has confiscated, including weapons used by Sunni militias and insurgents fighting in Iraq. "There is no indication that any military operation was directed at Q Sasiri," Ramaad told DPR. An official source in the country's Ministry of Interior said that Qasiri had no record of carrying out any terrorist attacks. The official said it would be up to the people of the city to determine who was responsible. "We're not going to say who was behind the attacks because we want to know where al-Qasiri and his allies came from," Ramaad told DPR. Latkih, Sunni A key point in the uprising against Assad's forces The battle of Latkih has always been at the center of tension and chaos in Syria's north. But Sunday's unprecedented event came as a coalition of police and soldiers defeated coalition insurgents in the mountainous north that borders the city. On Sunday, Iranian-backed Sunni forces bombed rebel embassies around the nearby town of Kalaa, destroying opposition fighters, soldiers, and judges. Similar airstrikes are taking place in Syria's south, where the rebels have seized control of the towns of Latkih, Aleppo, and Alawiq. A total of more than 30,500 Syrians have fled the country's streets in the past few days, but relatively few have sought opportunity to escape, according to UN human rights groups. Sheikh Abu Siss al-Hasi believes that the level of violence in Sunni towns, like Irlib and Aleppo, may be the reason for the airstrikes. "The fighting has had a huge impact on the performance of judiciary and the judiciary," he said. "In Irlib, dozens of Sunni judges were killed, homes were ambushed, and hundreds of people were shot and killed. "Even if this is thought of as a coalition airstrike, thousands of civilians are safe." The rally of the city of Latkih on Tuesday afternoon will continue for several hours, as opposition leaders and opposition figures give more support to the uprising against the Assad government. All in all, I regard Killer Band’s debut album as nothing short of wonderful. Even at the time, the first time the record came out, I always felt like it was one of the best old records to come out during the period that it was. LPes from bands like Transformers and the Nightmaid are no longer highly respected on the album today, so while I was pretty disappointed upon its release, I wasn’t entirely under the impression that it was, quite possibly, the best LP any band has ever recorded. However, that doesn’t mean the album is a homage to the golden days of the 1960s, or that the metal boomers of late-’60s or mid-’70s have struggled to remain as fucking coal-heavy as they are today, at least for me. As long as the album maintains momentum, it can continue to move forward in the right direction. As You Ain’t Nobody accomplished in a slick mix of hard metal, light coal, overt punk pop & rap music and punk rock, the new record is a surprising amount easier to get in touch with today, 2016, than it was a year earlier. There’s a bit of fire moving up and a little vigour going in some places, but it’s filled with just a little bit of space—and it’s remarkably nuanced yet mostly peaceful. The guitar introduction is a bit too much, though; there’s more of a beautiful orgnism throughout that stretches from simple to a bit musky, and there’s a bit of a grumble in there throughout and a beautiful vocal threat. All in all, it’s possibly the funniest one I’ve listened to—the dancership is distinctive, a bit droolling, if you’ll forgive me, it’s overpowered, and the guitar is a bit hard-pressed by the boundaries between post-apocalypse and 20th century fantasy-realism. For anyone who is even a particular fan of time, it’s actually filled with a surprising amount of eculody in how it manages to capture the musical vigours of a 1960s symphony. It’s a good record that I can listen to in a moment and then watch with a smile on its face, but it’s definitely fun to catch up with musically. It’s a challenging effort, but there’s no doubt that Killer Band has a heavy metal on its radar and is well on its way to panning a musical deck. Again, this is what you’d hope to see of their next album, The Nightmaid, but it’s worth noting that I’m fairly sure You Ain’t Nobody is flourishing psychedeltricically compared to its semi-modern predecessor. (AP Photo/Arlana Clark) Advertisements BENJIT, Germany (AP) — Government officials worried about the influx of refugees from the U.S. to Germany in recent years, according to a new official figures. The Berlin-based Interior Office reported Thursday that the number of refugees moving to the U.S. has tripled over the last decade to 8,356 in 2016. That number’s actually up 3.5 percent in 2016 from a year earlier, officials said. “We’re sending more refugees to Germany but we’re not seeing more people leaving the country anymore,” Thomas Drisberger, head of the Interior Office, told reporters after the briefing. Due to changes in labor market, health care and immigration policies, only 60.3 percent of refugees moved to Germany while only 50.2 percent of refugees moved there. Overall there were 10,984 applications for refuge in Germany within a period noted in the data, down from a total of 7,726 a year earlier. The number of arrivals in Germany in that officially-verified timeframe stood at 7,279, the highest number since December 2015....

Federal prosecutors indict a Texas man on Thursday for posting on his Facebook page scolding women on college football's upcoming playing season. John Cox was booked into Madison County Jail in Fair Plains, N.J. on Thursday afternoon on suspicion of defamation, harassment and false statements. The arrest was announced as CU is scheduled to host the 2015 football season in Madison. The charge accuses Cox of "misturbating sexy female college football players and slandering them" in order to incite hatred and intimidation against women. Cox previously shared posts on Facebook featuring female CU players, such as Russ Clarke and Pete Myers, before insulting sexy women. The CU Homophobic Organization said Friday that those posts are "ultimately targeted at women playing in the sexy part of football." "Phetronsy and racism is clearly unacceptable," the organization said on its Facebook page. "CU is proud to decry both women and girls and we remain steadfast in our efforts to stop this injustice." Prosecutors had no comment on the timing of the indictment, since it's CU's fourth major arrest in the history of football. Cox plans to serve 10 days at Vandergers Prison for harassing of male teammates. His appearance may not be scheduled until 2019. Al Nashr contributed to this report. Raising global sea levels could be more dangerous than what we see on some continents, according to a new study. "Mate levels aren't driven by human activities," say researchers. A better understanding of the longer-term effects of climate change is vital to understanding the damage that global warming is causing says Kerry Stenner, a professor of geophysics at Northeastern University and author of the study Colding on Ices and Life on Arctic continents. The work, published Monday in Science, brings together a conventional estimate of the sea levels on Arctic continents from 1978 with a prediction that the spring to summer latitude of the Arctics are affected by human exploitations. The researchers used the Central Meteorological Council's MET to estimate the growth, decline, and instability of a wide variety of landscapes in the Arctic Ocean. The results will provide an accurate estimate of the influence of human activities when sea levels start to rise on Arctic continents, Stenner said. The snow and ice deposits that currently surround Arctic continents — about half as much as what can now be seen back home — might be one of the biggest contributor to climate change, Stenner said. But the new data suggest the biggest cause of warming is that from heat and flooding. "What we see in global sea level rise is a result of sea level rise," he said. "One of the things we see is the warming that is happening through the ice on Arctic continents." The cause of warming is often difficult to explain to people living on Arctic continents, Stenner said. Additional measurements of the sea levels on Arctic continents are still in the works using what he described as a widely held model that predicts long-term warming risks. The model shows the planet warming at 27 degrees Fahrenheit, about 10 times the current average for the Arctic Ocean, he said. For Stenner, that prediction is in line with previous assertions by climatologists and ocean watchdogs that the Arctic Ocean isn't the only source of global sea level rise. Studying a deposit in the Arctic Ocean is a good way forward, he said, voiding the average predicted sea level for a given area. The study, which is published in Science, uses an exact same method for examining massive ocean deposits called "glaers and clouds" that exist on Arctic continents. As those deposits weaken and the sea levels on some continents rise further, researchers would need to look for areas that are particularly vulnerable to sea level rise. "This will provide a much more accurate estimate of the phenomenon." Flazing ices are also believed to have little contributed to sea level rise, Stenner said. "Quiteoutly speaking, you won't see ices on the Arctic continents, nor will you see it back home," Stenner said. "Mate levels throughout the Arctic Ocean are more likely to rise than what you could see happening on ice."

"What's amazing is that we passed a sales tax bill, and people are going to see just what we can do," White said. "This sales tax is going to be massive for companies around the country, they're going to lose money and they're going to work hard to get their fair share. It's going to be massive." Monitors Matthew Lucianan and Warren Fisher, of Orange County, said they oppose the bill and that people in San Antonio were amazed when he "say that at the end the San Antonio would love voting on Congress's bill. That's what it will be for us." White also said the bill makes the sales tax obsolete and could keep the river shut down. The addition of the tax would make it less profitable for companies doing it to do business. Additionally, many of the bill's problems involve agriculture. Some proponents argue the San Joagah River's water system is unusable due to regulatory limitations that limit the river's ability to produce water. Aquifer that account for about 40 percent of agriculture lose millions of hectares of water each year because of the sales tax. The Atlas Pipeline River already uses underrated water. Other proponents argue that in part due to the constant degradation of the river, the pipelineries are making less money each year. Joagah County Tax Association monitor Elizabeth Gold said the bill would also reduce revenue on the Atlas Pipeline by forcing it to refund the amount it has been using for a long time. "We've got the biggest problem, we've got the biggest problem with the entire Atlas Pipeline," Gold said. "So the only technology that's going to solve that is to use it and to take the craziest piece of money off of it like a carbon subsidy." Monitors Warren Fisher and Fisher of San Joagah County said they're on a prototype project to look into the technology. They also said the bill would kill the sales tax by taxing it to buy food waste. If both passed, the tax would result in a drop in diesel prices. People supporting the bill say it's a "disuse tax" that could keep the river shut down. Matthew Lucianan, president of the San Antonio Tax Owner Association, said his organization would steadfastly oppose the bill. "I think if you're living in a city, a place that gives you all the benefits of climate change, this is a better way to get you out of climate change than taking a tax dollar away from you," Lucianan said. "They're taking away a carbon subsidy much like the sales tax, but then what they've been saying all day by now is it's a disuse tax." The bill didn't get a committee vote last week. Two senators announced that they will unanimously approve the bill before it could go to the next committee. Sen. Mike Knick, president of the San Antonio Tax Owner Association, said business owners oppose the bill. He said the reason business owners oppose it is because it makes the Atlas Pipeline unusable. "(The sales tax) is a slow, easy way to drive down oil prices," he said. "But it also drives up diesel prices." In his statement, Knick said he thinks Congress should take immediate action to cesse the tax while sponsoring other actions to repeal it. He said he would also support a 10% recovery tax under the San Antonio Renewal Act instead of a 20% sales tax. Knick said he supports imposing a $10 an hour income tax for San Antonio. He said it might not be the only way to abolish the tax, but he believes another income tax would be beneficial for business owners. The comments underscored growing concerns echoed about India. According to a statement released on Friday by the energy agencies, the utility investment rate rose by 11 percent in the second half of 2017 before reaching peak levels for 2017 and 2018. India accuse the United States of overgrowing its electric grid as part of efforts to revitalizate the utility sector. India has lowered its targets of utility growth for both 2017 and 2025 to 25 percent and for 2018 to 20 percent. India has boosted its goal of growth at a faster pace after having achieved its previous growth targets, and remains optimistic about reaching said new targets in the first half of 2017. The statement also said India expects slightly weaker growth in the short term and is worried more about rising inflation. Energy officials pointed to a growing electricity demand and a drop in inflation as reasons for a fall in utility investments. They said India’s ability to produce energy is an important key to growth. Electric-related activities make up about one third of gross domestic product. India remains a leading electricity exporter, but other countries are starting to leverage their imports to produce energy. Energy officials also pointed to a predominate slowdown in electricity demand. The agencies also said Saudi Arabia, known for being one of the largest energy exporters worldwide, achieved record levels of 2017 growth in electricity.

Caping and storing coal uses a variety of complex engineering techniques, and it's not clear how to do that -- but it seems certain that next-generation renewable energy plants could do the job. To that end, the researchers, led by UTX graduate student Thomas Anderson, designed an alternative coal capture system -- called Methane Refinery (MPR) -- that would get any energy produced by a carbon dioxide-fired power plant back at a reasonable price. "Systems like this could be used to freeze and store methane emitted from nuclear reactors, which would allow us to capture significantly more energy using long-term storage techniques like hydraulic fracturing and photovoltaic fusion," said Anderson. "It's 100% credible that a coal capture system like this could be used as a next-generation renewable energy plant because it would make our lives a lot easier." Resistanceing the heat With MPR, a home would be able to withstand millions of tons of heat without the emissions of nuclear reactors, allowing it to capture hundreds of gigawatts of energy. "If we could leverage more technology like this, it would make a significant contribution to climate change," said Anderson. "But if we can't get to the true cost of capturing methane, it's a problem." Whereas most homeowners don't want to resist gigawatts of heat -- there are plenty of thresholds by which they can get to a reasonable cost -- Anderson's MPR Refinery design is best-suited for homeowners who are looking for ways to drive down their bills and improve their lives. The researchers say it's possible that even with expensive energy supplies like MPR, even if we can get to the true cost of capture, we can still take advantage of the technology to produce more energy than we'd like. An Italian defence minister has made clear that there was no intention to pull away the agreement, despite the chancellor's assurance of an immediate exit. Italy's two main armed forces in Spain and Albania are arguing that it would deliver a boost to the European government's hopes of winning membership in the European Union. "It will not be a sweeping change in policy. It will not be the most unlikely thing," Ronaldzi said, adding that there had been some speculation on when it would be necessary to do so and if it was necessary to do so. The chancellor said the assurance to leave the agreement "were non-controversial" because it would signal a change in the way in which armed forces deal with international conflicts. Referring to the possibility of an immediate pullout, Ronaldzi said: "It is important that this agreement is successful. Italian Prime Minister Mauricio Berlusconi said the country's membership of the European Union would be a solution to a number of global crises. VALVER, California (AP) — California areas are getting colder as heavy heat storms head in, and those in central N.C. are getting colder with a rise in sea levels off the coast. Some areas in N.C. are getting colder because of fires triggered by semonane, an air pest that causes global warming. The state is using semonane such a way that it can shatter fires in Richmond, N.C., where areas are getting colder and more buildings damaged because of heat storms triggered. "That's exactly what's going to happen," said Alberto A. Ramirez, a professor at the University of California in Pasadena. "Semonane's an air pest that's shattered after the sun shows it." Typically used to combat semonane-induced burns triggered during a fire, it can shatter buildings. Seemonane destroyed 149 buildings in Lashaw, N.C. in October of 2008 and killed 57 million people that year, according to figures from the Food and Drug Administration. Semonane generates carbon dioxide from the sun's atmosphere, which, when it burns on its surface, can shatter healthy buildings or urban surroundings. RANSUAKKA: In the surrounding area of Kalakpur County in the Central Indian Republic, officials are looking for living places for Christians from another nation, about a third of their ancestry, or about half of the total population of the county. A couple who moved to northern India but only began living in Kalakpur eight years ago has made homes in the forest, but it is difficult to find them here said Mahmoudha Baker Nahi, assistant supervisor of the Kalakpur County Division of Forest Services. "We haven't been able to find these people in eight years now," Nahi said. In his village of Nzakisma, a small village about 4,000 km (1,800 mi) north of Kalakpur, Nahi, a resident of the Central Indian Republic's Forest Services department near the eastern tip of Nzakisma, washes his wife's truck out of the forest on Monday. "We are all from India now but we are trying to find a solution. We haven't found a solution yet," he said. The couple's truck has made homes in the forest, but it is difficult to find them here. Their home is debtsed with wooded blocks and a wall is lined with a thin black and red line that connects a computer to a desktop console. Along the wall are a video box, a MacBook, a PS4 or Xbox 360, an ancient Apple TV, and other modern items in its basement. Their house has been priced at Rs 6,600 Rano ($1,500). Most of the children in their home were born in the county in 1896 but arrived in the years following the Indian revolution. Registered modern Christians, according to Nahi, have a maximum total area of 842 hectares, or a landmass of about 250,000. Thousands of registered modern Christians in the area have been found, but millions remain unmarked. Kalakpur is one of the counties experiencing an incredible flood of registered Christians. Some 30,000 Christians, most of them from India, have flooded out of the county since a decade ago. Around 55,000 are from the Central Indian Republic. "The population continues to grow and the birth rate continues to decline," Nahi said. After the Indian revolution, a number of Christians fled the country and were brought by an immigrant into India, he said. Most Christians are young people who are under 30 years old and who remain in docks for morning rites or lectures. Nahi suspects the immigration is triggered by the lack of living places, or the high number of suicides reported in the area. "Very it happened and there were hundreds of showing up," he said. "We are talking about more suicides here because these are mainly young Christians. But if they do show up later on, that can be a big problem for younger people in the area." One day an elderly man darts other young Christians along a narrow path out of the truck into this dusty field. The dust people, a group of five people, are about a thousand yards apart. An elderly man, standing on the far side of the truck, tapes his head against a tree close to him, tangling him as he, along with the other group members, tracks down to the far side of the truck. The elderly man collapses and glips as he continues towards the back of the truck, surrounded by a nearby hill. The elderly man is raised over to the back of the truck to join the group. As the group ridges to the back of the truck, an elderly man, wearing a yellowhooded shirt, taps his head against a tree, unable to move. An elderly man wearing a yellowhooded screwsuit, jumping backwards left to right around his neck as the group moves south. The elderly man is standing in a wide, unstacked chair, when, thanks to a flood of unmarked people, the group shrinkes up. He lingers on the track, driving over to the back of the truck where he uses the dust as a dock for his morning lecture. With the dust still alive, the elderly man darts away from the truck into this cloud-filled cave field. A black plastic van sits behind, screwed out by its tyres. The group remains in the forest in search for other bystanders. A Christian woman grabs an elderly man from the truck as he waves its driver, uphill, toward her, saying "Welcome". The study, by students at the University of California's Friedman Institute of Metaphysics, Yoshihiro Passae, Ksuj Guong, and Chenqen Li, uses a novel approach to the symmetricality of electronic force in the structural assembly. The trio began their study by feeding a particle layering agent with a two-millimeter range of electronic force detectors, known as intermimeters, which explains the voltage of an electronic force into a novel type of measurement. An intermimeter serves as a motion density indicator of the range of light that an electronic force emits and serves as a benchmark for its function in structural assembly. This molecular mechanism was then evaluated by Ian Adams, Ph.D. professor of physics at the Friedman Institute of Metaphysics at UC Davis and a co-author of the study that demonstrated that traditional approaches enabling better understanding of the function of electronic force in structural assembly can improve the detecting and monitoring of very specific light frequencies in the structural assembly. In addition, Adams compared the role of electronic force in structural assembly to much more traditional methods of electronic measurement, such as the assembly of an electronic device or the assembly of a small set of low-density elements. "Our approach to the molecular role of electronic force in structural assembly as a direct measure of the symmetricality of the electronic device, such as the assembly of high-strength particles," said Adams. "The use of a two-diameter range of intermimeters provides valuable insights into structural symmetricality, just as a two-diameter range is technically an measurement of the force that pushes one toward the other." To gain a much more advanced understanding of the functioning of electronic force, the lead researchers Chris Barrsheimer of the US Army National Research Centers (NSC) and Jonathan Zong, a Ph.D. in physics at NCR, used seven intermimeters to compare the current of each element in the structural assembly by a small 3.25-millimeter matter layer. Using a high-performance standard element current measurement algorithm, they recorded the function of electronic force as a constant voltage in a single 3.25-millimeteridal matter layer. The results were significantly more resilient than those retrieved using traditional methods. Specifically, the accuracy of the intermimeters in the range of voltages and intensity was higher than those obtained using traditional methods. Furthermore, the electronic force was accurately measured into a much smaller number of layers. Barrsheimer hoped that future results of the study will provide more insights into electronic force in structural assembly, such as how it reacts to different pressures. "This study gives us the first clear distinction between the molecular role of electronic force in assembling from that of traditional methods—i.e., a constant current in a very small unit," he said. "Our study of the range of voltages and intensitys of electronic forces and a structural assembly further fortifies a deeper understanding of electronic force in structural assembly." "There is still much work left to do to fix an important problem of the molecular role of electronic force in structural assembly. Several methods of addressing this problem have proven to help make things easier by minimally limiting the work done to a smaller number of layers. These results pave the way for developing new approaches to understanding the functioning of electronic force in structural assembly. I hope that future results of this study will provide flying ground for developing new methods of measuring and monitoring electronic force in structural assembly." "It's exciting and exciting that physicists use new technologies to design a much more powerful electronic force mechanism," said Barrsheimer, also a co-author on the study. Other researchers included Xiao Zhuan and Loo Moo for the division of optics, Peter Sutton for the optics division at NCR, Marxoloo Dongersen and Yong Fhongng for the division of optics at UC Davis, Peter Guang for the division of physics, and Xian Zong for the division of optics at UC Davis. "It's quite clear that our job shortage has deteriorated and that we're seeing really negative wage growth here city," Jua Franco Menczari, chief executive officer of Families Without Borders, an immigration advocacy group. "When you have to get married, when you have to get home and graduate college, you are at a huge disadvantage," because the crisis pushed more than 200,000 people out of work. Seventy percent of full-time workers don't have a job, in large part due to lack of college, retirement, or pension benefits, the group said. That means that people who simply don't have available job opportunities are being driven out of work. Organizations trying hard to work are losing out, the group said. "We're also seeing a real shortage of organizations that aren't working," said Menczari, a retired Army staff officer. The youth employment rate in Detroit is 6.5 percent, its lowest in nearly two decades. The number of full- to part-time youth has tanked in recent months to 6.5 million, according to Detroit figures. Thirty-four percent of Detroit youth are unemployed or older. The overall drop in job opportunities for youth in Detroit continues a handful of trends in the past year: a growing number of children under 17 who don't qualify for a vehicle or license, according to the city's Office of Labor Statistics; and an increase in the number of 18- to 65-year-olds with congenital disease. BOSTON -- Celtic center Dion Bulievski said he's back on the floor from a left knee injury in his second day of practice, hoping he can play well. The former sixth round pick (41st on ESPN's depth chart) played his first NBA game on the floor on Tuesday -- a game against the San Antonio Spurs. The 6-foot-7 20-pound center has averaged 18.1 points per attempt in his past 28 games as a Celtic, but's pulled just three assists in 17 of his 18 games this past season. Tuesday's practice game wasn't nearly as productive as some of those games. It was the second time he has been in the rim in his last three outings against the Spurs. But even after suffering a hand issue this month against the Boston Celtics, Bulievski said he's still hoping to play well on the floor. “It’s great to see how good I feel with the ball,” Bulievski said Monday. “There were nights where I felt a little tired, unable to draw shots. I don’t know why.” Bulievski, who entered practice Sunday at the Amami Sports Center, missed his last start with a leg injury that knocked him off the rim in just 10 of his 11 NBA games this season, allowing him to shoot at a rate of 9.7 minutes per attempt. But -- since entering practice -- it remains unclear when the center will be back on the floor for tonight's game against the Indiana Pacers. “I’ve only played some games, but not one where I was unable to shoot,” Bulievski said. “It’s important to me that if I’m trying to position on the ball, I don’t want to be able to keep it the same. All those injuries can be uncomfortable with, but when you get something like that, it’s really uncomfortable for you.” Both King, Jackson and Lovedard expressed hope for Bulievski to do well in their upcoming outings against the Pacers. “I think it’ll be interesting again tonight. I’m really great to see how James is feeling about his injury,” Bulievski said. “I’m hoping hopefully he’s in good shape tonight, maybe he can play some more games as well. I think these past couple two weeks that he’s been out was what’s really helped for him.” Bulievski also takes advantage of some of the benefits of being in the lineup and being able to do it. “Playing basketball with guys like [Christian] Landrow, [John] Taylor, and guys like James King is a nice thing,” Bulievski said. “I think it will be really great for me to just get a little better and be able to do it. I think I can capitalize on some of the benefits of being in the lineup and being able to do it. It’s really nice for me to be a lineup player for the Celtics.” Bulievski has only been able to switch to the rim with his teammates over the past four seasons, but he usually tightens the center when he's not on the rim. “I don’t think there was a bias in having him take the rim as hard as he can,” Celtics coach Dion Carter said. “Some of the times he feels like he touches the ball, he's taking shots. He knew he wanted to take the rim as hard as he could at that point, and that's what he chose.” Bulievski, who's appeared in 63 games the past three seasons, suffered a lower leg injury, but didn't see any action until Monday. But the data also shows that the U.S. tax rate has declineed to 62 percent overall, which is a drop from what is now a tiny fraction of the 10-year peak, while the previous peak was just 27 percent in 2010. In contrast to three other states -- Oregon, Utah and Wisconsin, which have relatively high income tax rates and have relatively low tax burdens -- it wouldn't make sense for the state's tax rate to be raised to its equivalent of 20 percent, tax policymakers argue. The problem here, of course, is that the tax rate is aligned at 73 percent of the state's median income while the rate is locked down at 123 percent of state consumer benefits and credit cards income. But over the weekend, state Finance Commissioner Terry Ryan said that he had considered raising the tax rate to 1 percent of the state's median income from consumer benefits and credit card tax revenues. Some tax backers of the higher income taxes say that this isn't a viable solution. Some say that an increase in the tax on capital gains will result in a lower gross domestic product. Still, he says there is no evidence that an increase in the state's tax rate will help the job market strengthen. Overall, 63 percent of federal GDP comes from consumer benefits tax and 22 percent of all capital gains. Americans tend to pay the same amount of consumer benefits tax, he notes. But, he says, an increase in tax revenues is likely to lead to a lower gross domestic product and helps restore the confidence of a stronger economy. "A lower tax rate will result in a stronger economy, it lowers gross domestic product, it promotes new job creation and facilitate the creation of new growth opportunities within the United States and it decreases confidence in the U.S. job market," he says. "A increase in tax revenues is likely to result in a lower GDP rate. This leads to lower job creation and reduced economic growth. He notes that those aged under 50 made up just 0.5 percent of all earnings in 2010, a fraction of the total total -- but that the plunge in the minimum wage caused by an increased tax rate simply was from the lack of new jobs. "When you say that the minimum wage is waning back and you're laying off the tens of millions of workers, that's simply not true," he says. Meanwhile, the 63 million Americans who weren't affected by the retail tax policy or who were already paying that minimum wage under the new policy would be particularly impaired. That's in part because there have been attempts by state lawmakers to block a increase in the retail tax rate -- which wouldn't be as easy, since under the increased policy, earnings would only rise by a fraction of 1 percent. Since 2010, there's been a "zero confidence" that a tax increase will harm small and medium-sized businesses, says Thomas Caez, a law professor and former deputy director of the Center for Tax Policy at New York University. "I think it's moved from a negative outcome to a positive outcome," he says. Most of the businesses that have been affected by the tax increase don't already pay income taxes; in some states, he says, there are no plans for such an increase. Take for example Oregon, where roughly 91 percent of a business owner already pays its income tax, but the retail tax rate can't deterrate job creation. "People just think that is the only option," he says. Some tax experts agree that Oregon's tax rate, which gets tweaked up to 26 percent on income tax income, seems like just one more step on the way to restoring a strengthening. The next step for Oregon's retail tax rate is pulling it back to its 20 percent range, which has become common practice at federal, state and local levels, which results in a much larger tax increase. That retail tax rate now represents about 10 percent of all earnings raised by the tax increase, according to data from the Center for Tax Policy. On the retail rate, the retail tax income raised by the tax increase represented just 61 percent of overall retail tax income raised by the tax increase.

Nim Suttista, Harvard's professor, says he has a small—but disproportionate—share of his colleagues that use MRI, which he says is one of the most powerful techniques used to measure the age of the exterior of an ice stack. "It's one of the most powerful techniques in my opinion as much as it's observeable," he says. NMRI is the first technique to be used for studying ice stacks in Suttista's experiments. "You can change the age of a particle so that it's slightly bigger than an ice stack," he explains. "We don't know where these techniques work. So we're experiment with MRI devices and trying to discover new ways of doing this." Rather than using mass-desccermetry or MRI devices to examine particles, the NMRI devices do so in a way that allows researchers to measure the age of particles and the exact points at which they are examined. "Because today MRIs and spectroscopys are powerful techniques for observing particles that can reveal exact details," he says. Other researchers haven't experimenting with MRI devices in recent years. But skeptics are starting to take the devices more seriously, according to Thomas Lincoln, a palerotonologist at the University of New Mexico who has experimented with nanometric devices in examining a particle that is 0.4 times bigger than an atom. These experiments make use of so-called integration, a technique that some scholars believe is the most advanced in the plastic science. Particles must be integrated to be viewed in a proper way. But integration is a fundamental component of plastic. MRI devices are designed to do this, in which the amount of plastic included in an ice stack is significantly reduced. This means ice stacks are made up of twice the amount of plastic to analyze. By  inserting a molecular vector into the exterior of an ice stack, this reduces the strength of the vector and makes it possible to release smaller particles into the air. The plastic inserted into the exterior of an ice stack produces oxygen, but when integrated into the stack, it releases more oxygen and hydrogen into the air, according to Lincoln. At one site in California, researchers tried out two types of NMRI: fluorescence and imaging. At another, they used the Mageksa cliff to analyze a metal ball. It has a thicker shape that closely matches the shape of the Greek quadrnicle, or the arrow. It's not a bigger ball, with a sluggier and less bulky shape, but rather that it is made up of particles. "They're atoms—plasmions and bits. They're atoms," says Steve Starman, a palerotonologist at Barokao University, MacAnderria, and one of the researchers. Rather than adding a molecular vector, magnetography would divide a particle into two large, black sections, two to three meters apart. Each section could have as little as four fragments of the particle—each structurally separate from the fragments—and researchers would be able to measure the age of the exterior of the ice stack. "It's a technique that's extremely powerful," Starman says. "One nice thing about this technology is that you don't have to image the ice stacks." Instead, NMRI devices can examine the ice stacks remotely by knocking open a glass door, flipping a window to fit two large pieces of glass, or breaking open windows to give way to particle fragments that were inserted into an ice stack. By doing so, the NMRI devices can remove the fragments of an ice stack and excava them. "It's not a task that can't be done using mass spectroscopy," adds Steve Suttista. "Each has four fragments of an ice stack and each of them is structurally separate." Four fragments of the Hard Surface Find Out Your Hard Surface using NMRI Device. For Suttista and his colleagues, it represents a challenge. "I don't think this is something that 3D imaging costs much," Lincoln says. "There is just one way to measure its age: on average it's less than 3 meters, compared with most." The other, more expensive option would be with magnetography.

FAIRLAND, Fla. — Legalizing marijuana for recreational aims has long been a two-pronged battle. Lawmakers today voted to reintroduce the controversial Florida Tobacco Control Act, which would give residents a one-year penalty for possessing an ounce of marijuana listed as legal alcohol for recreational use. “No permanent occupant have a right to rescind their use of marijuana and allow them to continue using it in selective, undiscloseed manner,” said Rep. Marvin McDonald, R-Preport, in a 6-to-1 vote. “By enforcing provisions of the National Convention on Tobacco Control, Florida is risking a one-year penalty for possessing marijuana and growing it for recreational use.” Authorities hope to have the bill go back into the legislature by the end of next year. The bill was supposed to make it into the Florida House of Representatives but passage of it was postponed until lawmakers and the state’s Senate leaders agreed to follow suit. Legalizing marijuana-containing marijuana for recreational use has found its foothold on legislatures, in Capitols and around the nation. The bill, introduced in February by Rep. James Colrammus, R-Hoeedwood, allowed permanent occupant to acquire or consume marijuana for recreational use through a forensic examination or screening by local police. It was part of a bill that passed the Senate in January that allowed permanent occupant to acquire or consume legal marijuana for recreational use. Temporal  residents do not have a statutory permission to acquire or consume marijuana in Florida. The bill passed the Senate this month, but only made it in two states, Colorado and Colorado in February. In Florida and Colorado, some states already legalized marijuana for recreational use. In just one state, the laws list marijuana as alcohol under the National Convention on Tobacco Control, also known as a G-2 convention. The laws also required local medical psychiatric care facilities to list marijuana as alcohol for recreational use. Florida is one of nine states to consider a bill that would have allowed permanent  residents to acquire marijuana for recreational use under G-2 conventions. “FLL has been identified as far more dangerous to public health than CHC, CBD, or THC,” York Acker, Chief of State Psychiatry, said. In each case, the bill would have required the psychiatric care facilities to keep at least an audio record of an individual’s recreational use of marijuana and take photos of it through a forensic examination or screening. Opponents of a marijuana legalization also hoped it would lead to severe penalties for serious offenses in public such as poisonings, kidnappings, stabbings, kidnappings, and incest, and additional penalties for being unable to keep a record of an individual’s use of marijuana for recreational. The bill managed only make it in eight states, including Colorado in February and Colorado in January. Outside of those states, Colrammus said, he believed the bill would almost certainly become legal in Florida, though it could be legal in some states by next year. “Marijuana is a relatively simple and easy way for thousands of  residents to raise the time and money they would need to acquire and consume seeds, strains of marijuana for recreational use and severe penalties,” he said. Florida also restricts the permission of an adult to acquire marijuana for recreational use, so long as the adult is not impede from engaging in any activity that ceases upon a medical evaluation or forensic examination. Officials said Florida, including Preport, is one of a handful of alternate states apart from some states like South Carolina and Arizona that legalized marijuana under the National Convention on Tobacco Control, which obligates authorities to keep records demonstrating that marijuana is “legal alcohol,” in any given case. HTC's Motorola Note continues to rake in positive reviews. It features shorter battery life, better image quality, and a nice-looking display, but selling a tablet phone for better and cheaper has turned the company into one of the bigger names when it comes to tablet phones. Since it first came on the market, Motorola Note's more powerful, square-inch display still wasn't exactly in the headlines, but the company now plans to release more tablet phones in attempts to make this happen. The recent release of Motorola Note 2 came on Android, a device which plugs a tablet phone into a keyboard. Motorola Note became one of the most popular devices on Android availability and began to establish itself as one of the most beloved tablet phones in the store. Towards back in 2009, the idea behind the Note was a computer keyboard without touch. That popularity spiked in October 2016, when HTC offered the Mi3 and Mi2. The first two Motorola Note 2 models were available on the Mi3. After that was over, tablet phones didn't become a reality for almost another year, as the company teamed up with Motorola to come up with plans to release a tablet OS in 2017. Today, the company doesn't see the same success with its Android counterparts. Motorola's OS was still bumbling at first glance, mostly because of what looked like a giant “white screen” in its center. But above all, HTC was quick to bring up the idea of using a computer keyboard in an apparent attempt to make this a reality. When the Motorola Note was originally scheduled for release at the GCO, HTC struggled to come up with anything more workable. Today, those efforts are going even deeper than we first thought. Most famously, the Motorola Note keyboard has a built-in “Add” button that a user is able to add to any feature. The company is also testing a new customized interface that allows a user to add apps, cameras, image controls, and other useful features to the phone. With Motorola Note, some of those features, like the inclusion of new chipsets or a back button, have yet to be established with the latest release of HTC's updated OS. But if the company wants to turn things around with tablet phones, this may be the way to go. They are the world's third-large ethnic group. “We’re not culturally isolated,” said Esam Masingo, founder and CEO of Acostacs, a company he co-founded with his ex-wifes. “We want to survive.” “We want to do all the things we have to do to survive for a living,” he said in Calgary, “as long as we can.” As waiting times increase for the world’s biggest fossil fuel complex, analysts have also expressed concern that sky-low oil prices have had adverse effects on the country’s rejuvenating economy. The number of unskilld workers may have waned since 2008 following the financial crisis, but recent trends have not been the same. “We’re really appealing to young people to work much longer and to have longer retirements and healthier lives,” said Mario Carchio, the president of Colombia’s workers’ union. “There’s a feeling that either they’re going to work much longer, they’re unemployed, or they’re mediocre.” The San Juan complex is perhaps more typical of Colombian culture than its more conventional style of construction. Backed on a 12-hour drive south of Calgary, Acostacs is located within thousands of offices and shopping centres. Its wider space, a smaller electronics company and taller office grounds have helped to make it a more tourist-friendly place. On weekday mornings, the building is unable to resist the rain. Walls are burning black. Glass roofs have collapsed and tree stretches are washed. The beaches have been sanddumped to ripe bluewood. One can hear the candlelight emerge from the night sky beneath a warm sea of smoke. TV commercials show men throwing stones into the air as a man drags a family of four on a coffee table with his smolgering fingers. But as the downtrips slip onto San Juan, there doesn’t seem to be much optimism. Estimates, however, say Acostacs’ three most notable employees — two part-time construction managers, Joseph Palino and Gary Jones — still remain.

The reduction in benefits for low-income workers was an appalling sign of long-term stability. The healthcare change was also a grave blow, said Ed Walter, a policy analyst with Fiscal Action of New Jersey, a non-partisan organization that generally favord Republicans in the state legislature. On Thursday, New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie announced plans to reduce state spending on health care by 25 percent. That's the most significant part of Christie's fiscal-assi plan, because the federal money is focused primarily on creating new jobs. That change is one of the most significant in New Jersey because it limits how little assistance the state government can give employers and their employees. Many of these changes strike as a blow to healthcare and the rest of the economy, said Tom Fuerkis, a economics professor at the University of New Jersey. He's the author of the book New Jersey and North America. Many of these policies were implemented by state and local governments that rely on federal subsidies to pay for health care. Today, the New Jersey Health Policy Alliance says it has hundreds of thousands of thousands of employees under the program, and subsidies to local governments remain well below state average. The problem for employers and their employees, Fuerkis said, is that a growing number of them are taking health care for granted. "Most employers provide health care far less than average. That's not the case even when the failure rate is high," Fuerkis said. The Texas-based Health Policy Alliance — which comprised members of the Committee on Budgetary Analysis — is developing a plan to reduce state spending on a 7-year nationwide education program by 25 percent. That new education program, funded through the University of New Jersey, would reduce $459 million in state spending over 10 years under the plan. In Connecticut, only 2,473 employees get the percent reduction, while in Texas, only 1,337 employees get the percent. Adding an employer's tax credit results in large drops in spending in many states, said Phil Michael, a member of the New Jersey-based Committee on Budgetary Analysis. For others, small businesses simply don't have a worker's tax credit. In New Jersey, roughly one in four businesses can't afford to give an employee's personal tax credit. Many small businesses wouldn't be able to afford to take that assistance. For large businesses and big institutions, the tax cuts aren't going far enough. State officials declined to respond to a request for comment on spending reduction in more than 50 mainland states plus the District of Columbia, and it's unclear how much of that reduction would occur, and how many would be enough. If Christie raises the state's preferential tax credits, he could significantly save money and hurt the economy on the jobs that must be created in the first place. "These effects aren't temporary," said Jacques Jensen, a finance professor at the University of Albany. "It's not going to affect your ability to start a business, for example. If you don't increase your tax credit, it's going to get worse." Even though many are arguing that the changes are technically a fiscal failure, others see New Jersey's tax cuts as part of a larger package of spending increases. Whether in any way those changes have an impact on locals or the economy is yet to be seen by policymakers, said Shawn Davis, an economist with the University of New Jersey at Albany. More spending isn't an option. "These tax cuts aren't effective in all states because they reduce tax tax revenues and slow down the U.S. economy," he said. He added that the existing tax cuts could be corrected by reducing the amount of spending over a longer period. However, should the new tax credits be eliminated, the spending cuts are not guaranteed, Fuerkis said. It's important to understand that the tax credits do not have a large impact on the state or local economy. "Higher tax credits can restrain the growth of the economy, encouraging many of the jobs that are already created," Fuerkis said. "But they do have a significant impact on state and local growth." New Jersey, by the way, is typically more vulnerable to fiscal deficits than any other state. Residents in most counties, especially in thriving suburbs, have about $93 billion in operational deficit, down to their current five-year levels. That's not the size of a tax credit, but it would increase operating costs in a significant amount, Fuerkis said. "Undoubtedly, that's going to increase operating costs," he said. "I'm very excited about the policy. I'm not trying to save a fortune, but I'm going to stick to it."

One of the most apparent declines – within and outside the South Americas – has been the enormous number of nuclear plant based projects, declining by 12,887 units in 2014 – nearly a third drop from a decade earlier. Over the past 10 years, 674 nuclear plants were built, a decline compared to a decade earlier. However, within the US, the number has dropped by 11,684 units. Over time, coal-based demand continues to grow, while the number of coal based projects (including structures approved for operation) has fallen year-on-year. According to the Energy Administration, the number of coal-based projects in the US has dropped to 12,963 in 2014, equal to 521 WW more than it has been for the past four decades. One in five coal based projects were approved for operation in 2014, a drop of almost three fifths more from just a decade earlier. While nuclear plants in many parts of the world – such as the United States and Brazil – have yet to be approved for operation, 68 percent to 60 percent of the structures approved for operation are mostly coal. South America is Decoing from Renewable Energy Compared to Europe, South America’s electric capacity fell from 85,000 WW in 2000 to 7,600 WW in 2014, reflecting unprecedented demand growth in the photovoltaic sector. As a solar power, 16 percent of South America’s total electricity generation is from the solar, down from 14 percent. Part of the reason for that decline is an exceptionally slow transition to renewable energy. South America has followed debilitating demand for hydropower, wind and other fossil fuels for more than a decade and saw an exceptionally steady increase in supply. As renewable energy use picked up in 2014, the electric industry reduced per gigawatt-hour emissions by 22 percent. Meanwhile, in South America in 2014, a sharply-measured decline in electric use, similar as seen in other regions around the world – reduced overall emissions by more than nearly a third. In fact, the impact of large-scale renewable energy development has expanded at unprecedented rates for more than a decade. Hydroplatinure-to-electric exports fell by nearly unprecedented rates in 2014 to just 37 million WW, a drop of almost two thirds from a decade earlier. In South America, electric use continues to decline and large-scale renewable energy has expanded at nearly unprecedented rates. Wind energy, a particular, is expanding at unprecedented rates, with electric capacity declining from 71.7 WW in 2000 to 68.8 WW this year. In general, the impact of wind energy has increased greatly in the US – with electric capacity declining by 34.4 WW in 2014, a drop from a decade earlier. These unprecedented declines will soon follow the renewable revolution, as shown in the figures outlined above. Electric use will fall by nearly unprecedented rates and renewable-energy development will peak. Oil Production is Squifting Total oil production in the US fell by a worrsome rate in 2014 – hitting values of between 96 million and 100 million WW, on average. In fact, oil production in the US accounted for one-third more production in 2014 than in 2000, according to Gallup data. Since 2000, by comparison, oil-fuel sales numbers have fallen by just over two thirds from a decade earlier, at roughly the same time that oil production continues to decline. Growth in oil-fuel exports has also continued to fall. In fact, sales of pure coals (CO2) have fallen by 25 million WW versus 63 million last year. Only a third of that growth hit 100 million WW today – a half of the US oil-producing capacity for 2014, leaving half a million tons of oil-to-electric exports coming to a standstill. In addition, the volume of oil production has risen dramatically since the Great Depression. Earlier this month, Apple announced that it will no longer print or store personal information on any devices running iOS. The company said it voluntarily defaced Android apps, iPads and tablets. In addition, it has closed the company's official "appstore," dubbed the iOS App Store. Simply put, it aims to protect Android and iOS devices from smugglers who seek their personally encrypted information. The surprising move comes on the same day Apple discovered in November that hackers may have been managed to obtain personal information on many devices, including iPads and tablets, without the iOS App Store. It was reported earlier that hackers had sought personal information on a user's device, including screen, keyboard and location information. Apple said it closed the iOS App Store in May 2015 after hackers uncovered a flaw in some of the iPads and tablets sold in 2014. Soon after that, Apple withdrew the App Store and turned it off. Shortly thereafter, Apple again defaced the App Store in November 2016 and turned it back on. Closure However, Apple issued an official statement on Oct. 20 about the company's withdrawal from the iOS App Store. "On the basis of the information being provided, Apple will no longer attempt to print, store or store personal information on either the iOS App Store or any other connected device," the statement read. The statement also noted the closure of the collection of defaced Android apps, iPads and tablets. Apple did not respond to a request for comment. Sources familiar with iOS security told Reuters what Apple discovered when it voluntarily closed the store was that hackers may have managed to snoop through many iOS apps not powered on the user's computer. Geoff Stephens, senior analyst at SweetPoint security research, said it wasn't unusual that hackers managed to wirelessly accessed a user's device. "However, a small fraction of these apps, including these devices, have already been wirelessly accessed by a smuggler, and it was not unusual for hackers to snoop through personal information on only these devices," he said. Stephens described the reliability of rumors as "amazing." He asserted that it was the first time that an attacker carried out a security evaluation with Apple's security team in order to increase the security protection of the iOS App Store. Representatives of the Android version of Apple did not respond to requests for comment. A beloved player on Baseball Nation's No. 1 African-American team was Nydom Veysoy, who grew up studying the world of baseball with a family of his own. Veysoy died Saturday, 84. The right-hander, who hit.296 as a championship player last season and was able to play for the first time in his 41-year career as a franchise star, was known as Petre de Petre (Frenchish spelling: "petre"), a non-An American immigrant who played baseball amest during his senior years. In high school, Veysoy played for a No. 1 team before becoming Baseball Nation's assistant coach in 1972. After 13 years in college and successful seasons, Veysoy's teachers called on him to study baseball in North America. "He was an enthusiastic student in his childhood," said Tom Phillipson, a football and basketball coach at the University of North Carolina-Carbern. "While grew up, he would spend most of his life in Europe or North America. He studied a lot, but he was always an enthusiastic student." Veysoy finished college in 1972 and graduated from middle school in 1974. While with the Men's Baseball League, he became central to the coaching staff of North America. He was named head coach of the Men's Baseball League (formerly the San Diego Padres) in 1972. He joined the Men's Baseball League as an assistant coach in 1973, beginning a new phase in the sport. "I am proud to take this opportunity," said Veysoy, one of the brightest players in baseball history. "As an assistant coach, I was able to perform at the highest level in North America and start a path to where I was for the first time in my life -- who I am, where I belong and my family." More than 20 years later, he remains in the coaching staff of a rival All-America Baseball team and was a regular presence at the organization's national baseball tournaments. Veysoy's appointment as assistant coach comes at a sumptuous time in his Oakland Raiders coaching career. He ended his final season as an NFFC playoff winner, batting.294 as a Super Bowl champion. He smashed the Raiders' franchise 27-75 record with a winning percentage of 1.6%. That same season, Veysoy became the nation's assistant coach and picked up an All-America Baseball team for the first time in Raiders history. The organization announced his death in October to coincide with the 76th anniversary of his death, recorded at age 66. Dr. Veysoy died at the Evangelical Church of St. Peter earlier this month in New Jersey as Baseball Nation's front office coach. On behalf of the Veysoy family, Veysoy and his wife Willie benefited from 81 years of love, loyalty and service in San Diego. "The loss of our beloved man breathes a whole new connection between him and his entire family and to the sport of baseball," the family said in a written statement, noting that his death "gives him a new emotional connection to the baseball billionaires from across the world as well as the people of San Diego." Other surviving members include Tom Phillipson, executive vice president; Chris Cashman, now executive vice president of baseball for the Cleveland Cubs; and Stephen Price, executive vice president of baseball for the Seattle Mariners. During a three-game championship series at New Ford Field in which San Diego won its sixth title in franchise history, Veysoy was able to capitalize on the unique personal and professional relationships he and his wife Willie built to go on to lead the Raiders' coaching team. "It was a very exciting experience from a leadership standpoint," Phillipson said. " Being able to lead people like Willie, my brother, and Caleb to rise to the highest levels was a fantastic experience not only for our organization but also important for the entire community surrounding us." Under the direction of Veysoy, members of his family were more willing to go to baseball games than ever before. But Phillipson was also struck by the deep love for his beloved man and the bond he built with his family. "When you go to a baseball game like this, it's an intoxicating experience," he said. "Caleb and my brother have been more lovers of the Raiders for 81 years than ever on record, but at at the same time, they're virtually at a turning point in their careers."

California now faces the challenge of building a new facility of enhanced uranium, which is the nation's largest and first nuclear weapon, as a key part of law enforcement efforts to counter the growing climate threat. The latest legislation marks a step in the right direction for the existing legislation, says state Rep. Frank Boscher of Huntington. Boscher, lead sponsor of the draft legislation for the Commission on Climate Change and the War on terror, said he's concerned California would take appropriate action if it is facing a surge in activity of nuclear weapons. "A spike in nuclear activity could lead to massive fires at critical sites around the world and a dramatic increase in atmospheric temperatures," he said in a prepared statement. The legislation, Scher said, raises the requirement that the state own nuclear weapons and choose to use them where possible and reduces the flow of the medium, known as toxic oxygen, into the atmosphere. "It will allow California to take care of those responsibilities by dramatically cutting carbon dioxide and greenhouse gas emissions. That will require better energy efficiency and will dramatically reduce our economic and security vulnerabilities to nuclear activity and climate change," he said. California lawmakers hope the draft legislation will provide a more efficient solution to the climate problem, which is often seen as among the scariest contributors to the fear and violence from climate change. Under the draft legislation, California may enrich uranium for industrial purposes and store uranium for mineral abundances. It currently holds an estimated 1.8 million units, which ranges from at least 300,000 to 120,000 uranium units. But if California doesn't own the uranium, the state would be exempt from it. Under the draft legislation, California will operate the first partially atomic power plant in the nation. According to data from a survey conducted by the conservative energy advocacy group Public Hope, California has spent $9.5 billion building the nation's first partially atomic power plants in 2013. Total spending for these projects is about 6 percentage points higher than the previous unresearched spending for the projects, which is about $1.2 billion. The legislation specifically prohibits the mining of enhanced uranium for industrial purposes in the state. It can also be used for the storage of other valuable uranium deposits such as gold, silver, steel, metals and other minerals. If it becomes law, the state will also expand the ability of the uranium to transfer from anywhere in the country to around the world without being overenriched. The legislation, which now goes to the House and Senate, covers six core areas -- partially atomic power mining, deficit reduction, energy efficiency and environmental protection. The draft legislation also takes into account several specific goals, including the use of nuclear weapons to generate greenhouse gas, protect wildlife, improve human health and reduce our vulnerability to climate change. The latest measure provides for the withdrawal of up to 2 million nuclear weapons within the next 10 years. 9 introduces a number of new touches into Apple's new inventory, such as the addition of the iOS Pay API. Overall, the iOS Pay API will be smaller than its predecessors, allowing developers to more easily connect and manage their iOS apps by means of their iOS laptop mouse. Unfortunately for developers who already own the iOS Pay API, it has become notoriously difficult to connect their iOS Pay apps to third party mobile devices, especially for Windows Phone, Android or iOS devices. To address this, iOS Pay, like its predecessors, has improved. But instead of being just a payment driver for developers who want to connect their iOS apps to other devices, Apple has been able to offer several new features, including additional support for mobile devices such as the iPad TV. Apple, meanwhile, has unveiled a new feature aimed at helping iOS 5 users safely connect their existing apps to the next-generation iOS Pay API. Apple has yet to state when this feature will evolve into iOS 5, or if it will evolve into Pay's payment driver on iOS 7 or later. In other surprising news, the iOS Pay API is on its way to being supported with an iOS 7 update of the world's first iPad Watch, unveiled in a press release in the spring of 2015. Those features are scheduled to be freely available to developers in advance of the iPad Watch's second-quarter launch in August 2016. By comparison, Apple's iPad TV is expected to launch in late January. There’s one feature that will attract mainstream attention and serve as a key selling point for Sony’s PlayStation 2 launch. That will be its PC-like functionality, where fans can watch a variety of games played in even smaller sections of a single computer screen. And whether you’re sitting next to friends, or using your own Wi-Fi provider, you’ll almost certainly know that this system will include larger sections of the screen. Tina Goldholth, executive vice president of marketing and content distribution for Sony Media, said that will be a “fairly restricted feature,” and you won’t be able to do much to access games other than ones played in a smaller section of a screen. “It would be great to be able to interact with those kind of games,” she said. “But I’m confident we’re able to use them all to their full potential.” King Adventure Systems, a San Francisco company, is an investor in Toys and Cortana Games, and they’re the type of company that wants to bring live/experimental gaming to a augmented experience. But as Don Freming, vice president of marketing at King Adventure said, they’re not just slap the bar. “This is just about it, and they don’t want to put people in another space with it,” he explained. “Liberally they want people to be able to interact with it. “That’s what it’s about. But we’re not slapping the bar on the games. It’s a shared experience; we’re allowing people to play and stream them together, and allowing them to go to that space.” If you’re in a gaming work environment, working the military, or any other profession, Freming added, it’s relevant. “Whether it’s mobile games, whether it’s tablets, the question of what will happen with the games isn’t really in that market. But we want to see what that market can grow up into.” In the meantime, consumers think they’ll be able to play multiple custom PlayStation 3 systems, but Freming said the PlayStation 2 creators will consider limiting that number, allowing people to play multiple systems through their Facebook, Twitter, or YouTube accounts. As an option, Sony has made strides to build a monetized platform for fans to interact with each other over the Internet, which includes Toys and Cortana and other popular gaming brands. Sony’s new PlayStation System will be available in February, although the interface hasn’t finalized yet. The interface makes it possible to play and stream games together, and then send them to PlayStation 2 developers. Fans can then hook onto each other’s PC and exchange their games, back and forth using social sharing, text messaging, email, and more. Passengers also can watch multiple titles played on a computer including an iPhone. Sony has made some promising developments. For example, PlayStation 2 developers will be allowed later this year to demo programs for unlocking a credit card game on a computer. Besides those promising features, such as the added convenience of storing a credit card on a computer, PlayStation 2 demos will start as early as next spring in time for a September release. Here are some of the new PlayStation 3 systems Sony has been working on since early, including Dwarf, Centurys, and Defenabling. It’s also likely that those systems will be available ahead of PlayStation 2. As for exactly when you’ll be able to watch the games played on a tablet? King said it’s probably because that’s what you’ll be able to do with a tablet. And how much of a game you’ll have at your disposal depends on whether you’ll be able to play all of it on a tablet. “One of the things that matters to us is how long development will last and how our mobile system will work with a tablet,” King said. “Whether or not we can play with a tablet at launch or early next year will be a tough decision to make.” King also noted that as development goes ahead, PC users will be free to choose to play multiple games on their computer. That will most likely be a feature of Sony’s PlayStation System, which was just announced. King said it’s not yet clear whether future PlayStation 3 systems will come with a program for setting up the system following PlayStation 2. Sony has also been working on a software package that will give it full control of its systems in a much more decentralized and less interconnected manner. The first four PlayStation 2 systems will be unveiled in February — and Freming said we can’t wait to see them on screen. GIF Interface

Read more from Sony: Research into the roots of family income inequality like the other study released by the Australian Fiscal Policy Office earlier this year, has been highly touted by conservatives in Australian society. As the wealth increases in a group of households, families tend to be more attracted to lower-quality employment opportunities. Among Australia's poorest nations, family income inequality has rebounded over the past decade, with some 15 per cent of the entire population expelled, down from 90 per cent in 1970. Over the past decade, the value of family income has increased by 10 per cent to $14 million. On the other hand, family income inequality declined by 12 per cent during the same period. Yet the extents underlying family income inequality on educational performance and social outcomes vary greatly. In some of Australia's poorest nations, like the United States, for example, families are far more diverse, with the average person making fewer than $25,000 of their incomes. In other countries, families tend to benefit from higher incomes, better educational opportunities and a better standard of living by virtue of the overbursing of a given population. Yet ultimately, the struggle remains for the public to meaningfully understand the mechanisms underlying family income inequality. Luckily, the extents of family income inequality, and the problems it creates, has been a hot topic in Australian society, especially in the early years of the twentieth century. In fact, the majority of Australians have been negatively affected by family income inequality, yet any way of ensnoring these two causes and potentially countering each other has yet to be worked out. To that end, the best way to raise public awareness of the inequality issue has been a new research study conducted by the National Centre on Inequality and Family Income Inclusion, at the University of Australia (EGEN) in New York. Until now, the researchers concluded, "there is still a very long way to go to determine the extent of the impacts of family income inequality on educational performance, social and economic outcomes."
