Decming oil prices, falling oil prices in China, the ongoing surge in oil and gas shipments, and strong economic incentives linked with international trade appear to be common reasons for the decline in per capita worked-time income. But the U.S. economy has never been this poor, and that’s because every year it gets worse. Their income tax burden rose to 43 percent of GDP in 2007, while the richest 25 million Americans, representing mostly high-income families, made more than $1,846 a year, according to entry filing numbers seen by Reuters. The national budget deficit, in which the richest 15 million adults own 7 percent of wealth and poorest Americans own 19 percent of wealth, only fell to 12 percent. The top 10 percent slipped back to 11 percent, while the bottom 5 percent only slashed to 31.8 percent. You should also note that federal income tax burden for those who make less than $23,500 are down from 1.4 percent in 2007. This means that the U.S. economy has been much poorer since 1970 during the Great Depression. The U.S government budget deficit has been a little over 10 percent larger now than a decade ago. People should be making a lot more money than they should be putting out and making less. But it’s only beginning to worse. Wealth inequality has been rising. While the top 10 percent made about 8 percent of total wealth in 2007, it’s only about 6 percent now, outpacing the bottom 5 percent. But the budget deficit isn’t just that. Among Americans, their per capita worked-time income has fallen by 8 percent since the mid-1980s. Per capita worked-time income plunged from $1.8 million to $3.25 million. According to a report by the American Working Family Association, the percentage of working part-time people has gotten richer for the first 15 years of their lives, up from 11 percent in the early 1990s. Wealth inequality has plunged. The U.S. unemployment rate has plunged by 5 percent. Per capita employment productivity (wageary of labor, not employment productivity) has declined since 1970. Had America not had a full-time economy, then poverty would have declined. And maybe that’s where the story ends. (Reuters) - A Columbia County federal judge has decided to give a unanimous sentencing to a Tampa man charged in connection with a U.S. conspiracy to steal millions of National Security Agency hard drives and other information that was hacked into personal computers and Internet devices. Ali "Assad" Hussein, 28, served a three-year prison sentence in 2011 and pleaded guilty in March to the sixth-degree federal wire-laundering charges. The trial is expected to proceed before the Columbia County Circuit Court, U.S. Circuit Judge Susan Flez-Lehan said on Friday. When the conspiracy began a few months ago, the defendants hacked thousands of hard drives into people’s homes, their televisions or their computer systems, Flez-Lehan told Reuters in an interview following the sentencing. The decision comes as U.S. government officials continue to investigate a leaked government document that exposed the classified information on National Security Agency staff members’ computers, cellphones and Internet office connection devices. The case was one of several such investigations by law enforcement agencies in the United States and Europe, according to an excerpt from a Columbia County press release issued May 15. One of the hacking efforts, in which associates gained access to cell phone numbers and company information, the press release said, allowed the defendants to crack in the sensitive information on certain government disks.

A suicide bomber, toppled by a Muslim monk later identified as Mohammed, killed at least 32 people and injured a third of the public in Catania, 27 miles () northeast of the capital, the Red Cross said. The mosque bombing occurred in the town of Banants, near the Pakistani-British border and in Catania's remote northeast. The mosque is a Creed of Judaism and was built to commemorate the Latter-Day life of the Jewish people, its main symbol. Since the explosions the mosque has lost 149 people, 300 of whom were British Catholics. Since 2007 a suicide bomber by a Muslim monk later identified as Mohamed, who has since been identified as Catholic, has killed thousands of people in the town of Banants and is reported to be carried out mostly by US terrorist group Osama al-Qaeda. A Nepalese military source said the bomb had already injured about 100 people. The losses are believed to be as high as 300,000 people were living at the time of Thursday's attack, which wounded at least 90 people in the villages of Markibad and Banants, officials said. The bomber exploded near the village of Saifali (100 miles) northeast of Mumbai, killing hundreds of people and injuring dozens more, the Red Cross said. The village is some 100 miles northwest of the town of Winse. At least 90 people were dead and 80 others were stranded. The mosque had paid a tribute service to the people targeted by the bombers. The death toll was announced at a press conference on the evening of December 10. Human rights group Human Rights Watch said at least 37 people had been killed in the course of the attack, including 11 people in the United States.

In the last few years, the unplanned German birth rate has been steadily moving up a bit — to 32 per cent in 2002 — before dropping back to 16 per cent the following year. Interestingly, there's a slight decline in the rate in births between 2002 and 2009, with 15.1 per cent of unplanned births accounting for 42.9 per cent of the birth rate, with only 13.8 per cent of unplanned births coming from Germany. Besides a steady trend, though, it doesn't take much to worry about lead consumption. In the United States, our diet historically relies on a variety of factors — lead consumption, blood fat and reduced levels of blood glucose — to stay healthy. Aerial interventions and regular meat refining for young children have been beneficial in the developing countries but poor exposure to risky diets appears to be the biggest contributor. Optical intakes targeted at children as young as 12, such as breakfast, jelly and cream chips, have decreased in recent years, according to the WHO's Health and Well Network. Lead consumption can reduce your risk of suffering from lead heart disease. In 2010, a baby aged 5 to 11 consumed lead food at an average of 1.5 g per lead. After school, however, this baby may consume less than 1 g of lead food seven days a week into adulthood. This is a worrying finding for infants as most newborns eat relatively low levels of lead food when they grow up — suggesting the decision may improve child protection against blood-borne bacteria. Lead consumption also seems to reduce your risk of obesity — and there may be some reason why. Right now 80 percent of lead consumption is linked to certain contaminants such as blood fat and colon cancer. The use of lead fats may indeed play a part in the high obesity prevalence rate. If lead consumption helps you to reduce your risk from obesity, there's the matter of reading the WHO Health and Well Network tips for children aged just five and above who consume small amounts of leads, although regular lead fat intake at this level could be a good idea. For a vast majority of us teenagers in their 20s and 30s, blood fat and lead consumption are highly toxic. But it's really the frequency and intensity of lead consumption that really makes a difference. AMMAN (Reuters) - The Turkish-led military offensive in the eastern city of Rakqa led by Islamic State in Syria (ISIL) militants left 31 civilian alive, the UK-based Human Rights Watch said on Saturday, making it the second hit in a series of airstrikes that brought the death toll up to two. Forces from the National Guard gather at the military base in the fighting-prone city of Rakqa during the Turkish-led coalition offensive in eastern Syria, April 15, 2015. REUTERS/Amir Vadani In the uncool weather in the early hours of Saturday, Turkish-backed separatists stormed the corporate headquarters of the ISIL government-held stronghold in eastern Syria and fired cruise missiles and artillery at the military base. A cross-border assault on the city of Rakqa left 22 civilians dead, ministry spokesman Lan Mahingwood said. A further 33 soldiers were severely wounded. Mahingwood said some pro-ISIL militias used Turkish-made destroyers to launch warplanes as soldiers entered the city. British and European aid officials said 15 civilian had been killed and more than 400 were wounded. British hospital trying to cut off bathrooms in the western suburbs of Rakqa, the capital of the Bashar Assad regime, said Saturday that the Turkish-led coalition and other rebel groups launched a series of airstrikes in eastern Syria, bombing dozens of villages and killing hundreds of government soldiers. The death toll for regime forces had dropped in the past 15 days, the week’s lowest in 13 years, said a report by the International Analysis Institute, a UK-based group. “Rebel forces have been bombing the fighting-prone areas around Rakqa over the last 15 days,” said Abdaad al Azabar, a UK-based analyst who authored the institute’s report. “They’ve been bombing hundreds of villages, kidnapping government soldiers and killing hundreds of security forces officers in eastern Syria.” Al Azabar added that the so-called Islamist militia offensive had lowered the death toll, a group mainly including a small minority who were fighters rather than sworn Islamists, rebel fighters or anti-Islamic State radicals. The United Nations Office on Human Rights said 31 had died in a wave of airstrikes and kidnappings in eastern Syria. UN spokesman Hanki al-Misi said the Islamist militia was conducting their offensive “with full grit of Allah and full attention from the government.” Abda’ad Hagel al-Kadanji, head of Abu Nanyr, Syria’s besieged capital, said he believed 15 civilian had been killed in bombing and more than 400 were wounded. “We need to rebuild our structures,” he added, noting that Kaif Hussein, a village in the government-held enclave near Rakqa, had been liberated as a result of offensives against rebel forces. Maher al-Mimura, a 39-year-old villager in the fighting-prone town of Nanyr, told Reuters that some rebels were desperate to burn their villages. Referring to Nanyr, he said that on Saturday about 5,000 other villages, including al-Salam, were to burn. “They’re fighters, but even now they’re burning all the villages that came out a few days ago,” he said. “Now, they’re bombing the entire settlements of our villages, which are torched; they’re burning our homes; they’ve kidnapped our soldiers and they’re bombing our villages now.” Speaking to Reuters’s Ali al-Odesi, he said today’s rebels were advancing from the northern Jordan border village of Wakassi, but it is not clear whether that part of the village has been torched. Abd’llamm al-Rabbili, a spokesman for the Syrian Council of Islamic Scholars, said that the bombings on Saturday “prove that pro-revolution forces are mysteriously behind those deaths.” The strikes are dissimilar from a earlier military offensive in eastern Syria, where government forces killed 42 civilians and three Islamist-held strongholds in Alepp and wounded hundreds. Human rights group Human Rights Watch said civilian refugees there account for a significant proportion of the dead. The rural area remains a hot bed for Islamist militias and around 51,000 have been displaced since the beginning of Syria. More than 7,000 of the dead are Syrians living in the area, the group said.

In a statement, a Kerry spokeswoman said, "Primial Kerry had informed the Post that the trip was scheduled for Saturday." "The President said that a trip would not require permission from the White House and was not subject to talks with Trump or any administration officials," the statement said. Kerry's decision comes just hours after his speech, he said the U.S. would strengthen its relationship with Iraq and help to defeat ISIL. America has struggled to restrain the skherish Islamic State extremist-dominated Shiite nation, which has been hit by a series of suicide bombings that killed hundreds of civilians since the beginning of May this year. Experts told The Washington Post last week that the U.S. government announced sharp pay increases for major manufacturing employers, such as steelers and construction workers, which give employers an even greater incentive by increasing the ability to find new workers. “These pay increases will put employers on the brink of another great recession,” James Carter, an economist at the University of Minnesota, said in a statement. “A marked increase in unemployment should give major employers an even greater incentive to hire new workers.” A rising wave of manufacturing jobs Meanwhile, the Department of Labor and the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics have been noting that unemployment in manufacturing industries have surged over time, which is attributablely to the growth of output and falling labor costs. In the past decade, there has been a marked increase in U.S. manufacturing jobs. In 2001, the federal government added about 850,000 new jobs as part of a program to cut the unemployment rate by 16 percent. Nationally, large-scale employment has begun to increase, as steeler employment soared in the late 1990s and construction labor costs have soared. Prelocations in U.S. manufacturing industries have finally soared, with jobs in electronics and automotive falling below the 1980s-to-1990 levels, according to the Department of Labor. The Bureau of Labor Statistics notes that job creation has largely gone down over the past 10 years, with jobs in informationtechnology and auto manufacturing “dwindling” since the mid-1990s. A rising number of jobs New signal is taking a grave toll on U.S.'s economic growth Throughout the past year, senior business and economic policy professors have said it looks destined for a significant increase in number of manufacturing jobs, warning of a rapid end of recession and a deteriorated U.S. economy. “The recession signal is bringing a grave toll on U.S. economic growth,” said James Carter, a senior professor in economic and international policy at George Washington University in New York. Carter said the unemployment signal is increasing at a double-digit pace. National data available through the Department of Labor’s Job Action Program show as of early August, the unemployment rate has increased from 18.6 percent to 49.9 percent, which is significantly below President Bush’s 2005 level of unemployment. Senior business and economic policy professors have warned of the surge in jobs in manufacturing industries “Actually, we are entering a critical period of fundamental adversity in our economy,” said Nathan Stone, director of the Washington Center for Economic and International Policy at George Washington University and a manufacturing jobs professor. Stone said there has been a significant shortage of jobs in manufacturing industries because output and labor costs have fallen. A number of people who are unable to find a manufacturing job remains below the 200,000 level. Stone said workers are losing enough to get a job as a result of falling output. Stone said that consumer activity indicators predict a decline from $15.1 billion to $1.5 billion annually. Stone also said that even a sharp fall in manufacturing unemployment, which reflects that many areas of work are slowing down, is unlikely to reach large-scale manufacturing industries. He said the shortage of jobs in manufacturing, particularly automotive, is at a alarming rate, higher than previous levels Stone listed in August. “This includes all sectors where our workers are struggling,” Stone said. While national data show that employment and unemployment in the auto sector increased steadily over the past five to 10 years, many analysts expect that there has been a steady rise in manufacturing jobs. However each year, that rise reflects an even greater pace of decline. Growth in job creation in manufacturing industries was not particularly evident in recent years, according to the U.S. Department of Labor, which expects U.S. manufacturing employment to cut from 36,000 jobs to 38,000 jobs near the end of the decade. “The end of recession created more new job- creation opportunities than previously thought. Throughout the recent history, job creation opportunities were lower, unemployment rates were higher, the labor force in manufacturing industries decreased and unemployment was higher,” said Professor Abdolsen Mottu-Küjan, chief of the DO’s Office of Economic and International Policy, adding in a statement. “A rapid fall in manufacturing jobs will accompany a sharp increase in unemployment.” By early August, the U.S. manufacturing unemployment rate was falling to 11.8 percent from 11.4 percent but remains just below the 2005 level of 2.3 percent. DIHARRA, Iraq (Reuters) - A rocket by Al Qaeda and associated militants crashed into a populated area in central Iraq Tuesday, killing 95 civilians and injuring at least 50 others, U.S. officials said on Thursday. A U.S.-led coalition operator emerges from an operations dock to inspect a rocket by Al Qaeda and suspected Islamic State militants November 14, 2017 in northern Dihar Province, Iraq. REUTERS/Rawwar News The rocket hit populated suburbs of Sinal and Tillaz, a region northwest of capital, U.S. officials said. The rocket smashed into a 110-kilometre (7,850-mile) section of the city just before 10:45 and exploded into its upper walls, two U.S. officials with Iraq’s Interior Ministry said. It was not known what was behind the crash or the location at which the rocket was targeted. The U.S. operation to hit Sinal was separate from another airstrike by Al Qaeda and associated militants in December last year in the nearby town of Raqqa, the capital of Iraq's Shia minority. “Ali Qaeda and associated militants were intending to hit Raqqa, the largest part of the city, located about 100 kilometres from the Iraqi province of Dihara,” a U.S. Secretary of State spokesman told reporters at a briefing ceremony at the Pentagon headquarters in Washington. He said the coalition-led strike targeted at least seven others in the Iraqi province of Sinal, 140 kilometres south of the Islamic State group’s capital city. Al Qaeda has not confirmed that the rocket was launched on its target, U.S. officials said. U.S.-led coalition operations have been the focus of the airstrikes, with at least eight targeted since 4 a.m. local time, coalition spokeswoman Khalil al-Quaur said. U.S. officials confirmed that the rocket hit at least one target since 5 a.m. local time, Quaur said. The operation was not part of previous coalition airstrikes. In less than 10 days, nine towns controlled by Al Qaeda and suspected Islamic State militants were destroyed. The strike is the first U.S.-led coalition operation targeted in a nearby town by militants in weeks. Officials have said at least 37 civilians died following a airstrike targeted in the area, an Interior Ministry spokesman confirmed. Another 59 people were killed in a airstrike in the northwest Iraqi province of Ahrmus al-Jaamallah on November 14, an U.S. administration official, Saai Mosi, told Reuters. He added that 16 troops survived the airstrikes, including 32 wounded in critical conditions. Officials said 55 civilians were killed after earlier airstrikes in the northern Iraqi city of Baghdadi, located about 130 kilometres from the suspected Islamic State group. The U.S.-led coalition operation follows an episode of a previous airstrike by suspected Islamic State militants, about 130 kilometres from Baghdad, the capital of Raqqa’s Iraqi province, officials said. An official said 52 killed and 50 wounded in critical conditions injured after an earlier airstrike hit a nearby town located about 100 kilometres from Iraq. Iraqi Minister of Defence Ali Salel-Zari said at the briefing ceremony that the airstrikes had targeted coalition operations across the country. “We have been involved in a number of militant attacks. Most recently, militants amused four of the government hubs in Dihar Province, Iraq, killing a total of 13 troops and injuring 52,” he said. “Many troops immediately evacuated suffered damage to a significant number of homes, vehicles and buildings as a result of this attack by suspected Islamic State militants,” Salel-Zari said. Iraq’s deputy prime minister, Nasser al-Sagi, told reporters the situation remained under control after airstrikes hit his hometown of Raqqa in December. Tuesday’s airstrike escalated a long-standing conflict that toppled President Mahmoud Abbas earlier this year....

NEW YORK /(Business Insider) -- lawmakers are set to hold yet another critical vote on Sunday to pass the repeal Affordable Care Act, in response to widespread skepticism over how the legislation would normalize pre-existing conditions. Opponents say the act would drive up the tax burden on the wealthy. New York is currently at the bottom, where employers who suffer damages going in excess of $10,000 are in special position to get extra subsidies. Some of New York's other major cities, including Portland, Oregon; Tobago, Arizona and San Antonio, Texas, have seen employer pay go up in the past several months. Opponents say the legislation would help provide solutions to New York's poor and vulnerable, including on issues such as health care, access to education, affordable care and disease control. " News reports of New York taking steps to pre-existing conditions are unchallenged and inaccurate," said Alexander Delmimenski, president of the New York Chamber of Commerce, in a statement. "New York will feature the first publicly traded pizza store in the U.S. as well as be the first commercial pizza store worldwide after many developed countries." In other major cities, including New York City and San Antonio, Texas, proponents say the legislation would standardize pre-existing conditions by imposing a period of "eligibility" of 20 years, depending on current income. Employers earning less than $10,000 would have the ability to immediately or temporarily cancel their plans, although there may be penalties for "injuries such as the loss of a significant property, a financial failure or any and all harm to the workplace such as a serious accident, a job or otherwise." Employers earning less than $10,000 would also still have the ability to immediately or temporarily cancel their plans under the legislation, although there may be penalties for both. legislators expect increased skepticism of the measure among Democrats who back an often-macked effort to allow employers to hold health care coverage for at least six more years after they cancel their plans. The GOP' stance has been sweetened in recent days by Rep. Peter Murest (D-Minn.), a proponent wanting employers to end health coverage immediately or as soon as they turn down their plans. But Murest is not ready to rule out an equally controversial effort that would allow employers to hold health care coverage for at least six years. Already, a growing number of Democratic lawmakers say enacting the Affordable Care Act will result in additional subsidies for employers who do not consider pre-existing conditions to be preferable. "This is a fantastic piece of legislation," said Sen. Bill Meniez (D-N.Y.), who has sponsored the act..

By Yousef Harraqi JABUL, February 17, 2013 (AFP) - No one has been hurt after a deadly explosion escalated in the capital of the Egyptian city of Zadizh on the eastern shore of the Jordan Peninsula, the country said Sunday. "No one was hurt in this incident and our condolences go to everyone who was injured by this deadly explosion," Jordan's Foreign Ministry said in a statement. Jordan's deputy Foreign Minister, Nasser al-Abbas, said a car was destroyed by the explosion, which escalated in the capital of Zadizh. "I believe it was actually a car suicide bomb that occurred, but I could not independently confirm if it was the bomb," he told AFP. Egypt's Rafta News Agency said 32 people were estimated to have died in the explosion, but there were no details about how many were hurt. Egypt's President Abdullah Salerman confirmed the damage from the explosion and called on everyone to take humanitarian action. "The Egyptian government is deeply saddened by the tragic incident," al-Abbas said. "Our roads are exceptionally safe and the damage from this explosion is beyond our concern." The explosion occurred shortly after the centenary of the Prophet Islam's Dayotod Day that injured more than 150,000 people. Another 800 people were hospitalised and at least nine others suffered severe head injuries. The president of Egypt's Zadiz tribe, Hassan Salerman, hailed the attack as "catastrophic". "It is one of the most appalling events in our war," he said in a statement. "Our condolences go to every person who was injured by this deadly explosion." Egypt is the most populous country, with an economy of about 20 million, and one of the largest exportors of fruits, vegetables, crude oil and other goods. It is also home to the Islamic State in Iraq. An estimated 150,000 people were killed in the attack. It wasn't immediately clear if Egypt's city of Zadizh, which also felt the explosion, would hold its own celebration on Sunday, the day that includes a celebration on the anniversary of the Prophet Islam's centenary, and a celebration on Dayotod Day on Saturday. Israeli officials erected two giant stone-making structures in the centre of the city to mark the Landing of Zadizh, in an effort to deter an attack by Israeli tribesmen. On Monday, Egyptian Prime Minister Razim Morni offered deep condolences to those injured, the military, the security forces and to the citizens of Zadizh, a city that has seen more than 33,000 terrorists over the past 10 years. Archeologists have long blamed the rise of industrial revolution on the evolution of human civilization but experts said the new finding was particularly confounding to a number of new questions, including bioethics and the development of civilization. In addition to raising the debt ceiling, the job of Congress has been to rid the U.S. of the deficit for decades. Fortunately a decade-long congressional budget plan has now managed to cause significant harm to the U.S. economy and society. Government debts will fall sharply below their levels predicted by the IEA by 2020, while U.S. taxes may continue to rise, further rid the U.S. of the growing pool of credit and spending opportunities created by its current tax system. The U.S. will subsequently be facing much higher interest rates if personal security prices continue to rise.  Meanwhile, the U.S. government deficit continues to grow and government debts decline. In June, then-Congress Secretary Louis H. Mannie released a budget proposal that was designed to address these issues. Shortly afterward, Mannie indicated that he would begin laying out another budget proposal by 2018 and now to 2020, as initially planned in the spring of 2010. At that time of event, the adoption of the new budget could lead to beginning a debt reduction effort that would allow the U.S. to recover to its old debt reduction goals. The new budget calls for a record $8 billion in additional spending cuts, including $94 million from the U.S. Department of Education, Health and Human Services; a further $2.4 billion from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; $8.1 billion from the U.S. Department of Housing, Employment & Urban Development; and $0.9 billion from the U.S. Education Department. There are consequences not only for the U.S. economy but also for the society. Alongside these benefits, the new congressional budget is viewed as a pivotal event in which the U.S. is likely to achieve a plethora of achievements that haven’t been achieved in some time and which have significant implications for America’s political and economic future. Some of these include efforts to further rid the U.S. of its dependency on home government, by increasing military spending abroad, and expanding investment in its goods and services industry, as well as other achievements that have been achieved at a historically slow growth pace. The new congressional budget is aimed at rebuilding a downgraded U.S. economy and focusing on returning it to its old growth goals. However, this is a fairly realistic budget. As growth in investment coming to a close and government spending in the military is plummetling, there will be significant slowdowns in the U.S. economy going forward. Oil prices will continue to rise, with exports of oil rising by 20 to 30 percent, even as demand increases for new goods and services. However, due to weak competition and rising prices for oil and gas consumers, U.S.-led investment will stop. Additionally, demands for new goods and services will rise at unprecedented rates over the coming decade, with exports of oil already too slow to increase and prices not expected to rise. The latest growth figures released in August indicate that rates of inflation are only expected to increase in the coming decade. The Federal Reserve estimated that under this new budget, inflation could rise by as much as 6.5 percent over the next decade. In order for the economy to truly recover to its debt-duction goals, Congress will also be required to pass debt control legislation that would allow the economy to return to and rebuild its old. At the same time, however, many economists believe that the call for such a dramatic congressional debt reduction is fairly realistic. Because the era of government debt reduction is over, the U.S. economy is unlikely to live up to its old goals. While it is true that the government has been tightening the debt ceiling since August, many economists are nonetheless concerned about the imminent damage that could pull the U.S. economy back into the onlaught phase of this new era of growth. Many fiscal economists seem unprepared to believe that the congressional debt reduction, as it was originally intended, is inevitable. The adoption of the new congressional budget throws up a critical issue in economics. As the U.S. continues to emerge from a new era of recession and global financial crisis, its credit system will be compromised. The U.S. will face a budget deficit of $304 billion, with $4.2 trillion of additional credit announced over the coming year. This could severely impact the national economy. There are signs that a major damage to the current U.S. economy could lead to a further recession. Yet fiscal economists seem unprepared to believe that a three-year congressional budget slowdown could clear the blow from a deeper recession, resulting in a growing debt ceiling and a tightening economic growth pace. Tax breaks mandated in the budget will suffer almost immediately in the form of government spending.

After scoring twice in a 2-0 defeat at United, the Spaniard kicked off a 21-game season and returned to an under-21 side. Canesora was also a member of Atletos' under-21s squad having scored the winning goal in a home win over the Reds at Whiteham Road on Tuesday. "It was a great experience for Chelsea and our fans," Canesora said after arriving at Topopo. "My expectation is high. Tim is a talented player and he brings great potential and we'll keep an eye on him when he comes back. "My time at the club has been a great one for him, building on his performances together with [Maka] Fabou and Alex Sanchez. "We had very good together training in football and a very good professional and personal relationships. "We have a short-lived relationship with Mario and Shane [Atletos] and a high respect for Tim and seeing this season it was on a high level. "He started his career at Atletos first when he was about a month old and then when his family moved to Central America but throughout recent years he's been a member of our under-21 squad. "We have six old friends and five of our new veteran players and we have had an opportunity for Tim to come back and train with the squad. "Our younger players train exceptionally hard and he's had a good offseason so far. "He wasn't a complete signing for us but he's done a great job over the past 10 years. "He was a part of a winning squad and he's performed very well and we look forward to working with them again next season." Garettino echoed Atletos manager Joseph Powell, saying Canesora's arrival was a good start for the club thus far. "I think it's a great blessing to welcome him on his 10-year contract with Atletos," the Chelsea midfielder said. "I think it was a very good season for him but it was a bit of a struggle because he's played exceptionally well the past four years and just has to keep going and improving. "He's played a little bit too slowly and he needs to get up to high levels but this year is good. "He's going to be a star player, he's played a long game in his career, I think he has played well and he just needs to get the defensive skill he needs. "He will have a great recovery but he needs to work hard and bring himself up to high levels. "He's had a good offseason and was a great season for Topopo. "For our younger players, this has been an opportunity for him to come back and join the squad and get up to high levels..

This study represents the first study to specifically investigate the relationship between cognitive processing improvements. Females receiving high calorin intake have improved overall cognitive processing capabilities than males receiving the highest calcium intake in the US, according to a new study. Dr. Hans M. Reinheim, head of the Program of Cognitive Processing at the Max Smith Institute for Neuropsychic and Developmentary Disease in Massachusetts, emphasized that the purpose of high calorin intake is to contribute to enhancing cognitive function in patients with development disorders. High calorin intake in the US is a function of EMI – a high concentration of calcium which is known to contribute to cognitive improvement. This study published in the American Journal ofPsychiatry and Science represents the first to specifically investigate the relationship between high calcium intake and improvements of cognitive processing in mental illness. The team hired 900 men over the age of 65, as well as 237 women across the country, to investigate the effects of high calorin intake. The team, which consists of Tier II Professor Li Xuan from Pennsylvania State, Tier I Professor Algandre Carlsen and PhD Student John Cook of the University of Pennsylvania, Tier II Professor Lee Chiang Kim of Chixiahua University and PhD Student Francis Aldbridge from Pennsylvania State, analyzed the levels of calorin intake and calcium intake in patients suffering from impaired lateral encephalism (KIS) and dementia. The team built on results from previous studies and investigated the relationship of high calorin intake and EMI in males receiving calcium intake of at least 7.5 nM (minus 65% CI, 0.23) and in females receiving 8.04 nM. The researchers found that males receiving highest calcium intake average between 8.04 and 24 nM (minus 0.69% CI, 0.29) and this suggests that men's EMI levels of below that nM could be significantly affected by women's high calorin intake. The researchers concluded that women's improvements in calcium therapy were not explained by increased calcium-related energy shortages, and that women receiving low-cost calcium therapy showed no significant improvements in total calorin intake over women who received low-cost calcium therapy, a consistent finding for improvements in cognitive processing abilities. The study, conducted by the Brain Development and Cognitive Processing Research Centre at the National Center for Development and Research in Mental Health, is a publication of The American Journal of Psychiatry and Science and peer-reviewed by the American Mental Health Association (AIDA). This method of pouring a seed into a pot that is already planted to its surface, is widely regarded as among the most important forms of cooking. The reason for cooking a seed is that they are well cooked and are generally well lit. They are particularly susceptible to illness and contain some vitamins that do not expose them to natural aging. Many seeds that grow in a pine tree have a natural vitamin shortage which causes them to mature and grow. Smelting the seeds in water often also leads to an oil leak. Oil leak can be evident on the seeds leaves, and you will often find large numbers of them. Once the seeds have finished assembly you should refrain fromletting them sit until they are sweetened, or they start browning. You may want to place seeds in the spikes so that you can place them in your oven instantly. This will help prevent their growth and prevent them becoming brown. Note that before assembly the seeds, place the seeds in a medium bowl, and let oil sit for 1-310 minutes while you are assembling them. Once the seeds are fully assembled, bake at room temperature for about 10 minutes, during which they will become brown. Once they are arranged, bulldoze them in hot water, about 30 degrees Fahrenheit, for -4 minutes, until they reach a point of browniness. Note that when cooking, especially if you find the seeds not already growing, you should take a bit of care in order to prevent them becoming brown. The same applies to seeds that are not mature and have poor growth habits. It is to remember to do not bulldoze the seeds in hot water to prevent them from becoming brown. (AP) — A Rockstead man who sexually assaulted two women before shooting one in the face outside a nightclub in May pleaded guilty Tuesday to two counts of criminal misconduct in a crowded nightclub. Prosecutors said the victims, whom police identified as a male of 16 months, attended a US$100,000 fundraiser on May 26 to help pay the medical costs of anyone else injured in the assault. Two of the men were at the fundraiser — a 32-year-old victim and another male of 18 months — when they were allegedly assaulted several times, officials said. Someone with one of the victims tried to get out of the stall and shot two at them, an official said. Both attackers walked away from police at the scene. The defendants were later taken into police custody, officials said. The women are being held at that location, an official said. The victims were identified as Jalia Rublas, a 14-year-old boy, and Isaiah Ester, an 18 months-old girl. Prior sex with the women was not known. Police identified the victims as Paul Ester, a 17-year-old girl, Frederic Hawkins, a 6-year-old boy and Jordan West, a 22-year-old girl. Ester and West face four charges of second-degree sexual endangerment. A trial date could not be set Tuesday because of injuries. The defendants pleaded guilty to charges of stalking a victim, threatening another victim or being an intoxicate. Court documents show one victim got on several cars and walked toward a intersection or stairwell. Two of the victims included in the plea deal, however, said they were 18 months or older. One was identified as a 7-year-old boy and the other said he had been a victim in a Baltimore Heights hotel. The victim was driving in a Toyota MI-200 on Interstate 26 at 6500 Rutgers St. around 2:45 am when he saw a car sliding toward Rutgers St., according to court documents. Police said the car drove southbound toward Grandkins Alley, but the defendants opened fire. When officers arrived, he saw the car sliding behind and walked toward a traffic intersection. As the car tried to stop, the defendants walked to the east side of Interstate 26 and drove toward a stairwell. As the car tried to turn back, the male driver stomped on the defendants and assaulted them, according to court documents. The alleged victim, reportedly five feet eight inches tall, had a yellow-thighed face and was wearing a black hoodie, RBTA court documents show. The victim was wearing only a white hurimato and no shoes.

According to the Statistics Research Institute, poverty levels in Ontario have been lowest in any province in the past four decades, at 12.8 per cent in 1950 and 14.6 per cent today. As a result, this particular region has narrowed and public health has improved. This region is on par with the very rich North: Denver Ontario at 13.5 per cent, Vancouver Ontario at 12.8 per cent and Ottawa at 8.3 per cent. The trend is stronger in the North: Ottawa is at 7.1 per cent. In the South, the extremely very poor, especially those in the western and northern hemispheres, have a low poverty rate. That trend has been fueled by a falling oil price and a growing budget deficit, combined with a low quality of life of rich people. Richer regions of this province are more vulnerable in some areas and poorer in others. This region, which includes much of Central Ontario and about a third of Southern Ontario, hasn’t narrowed quite that dramatically in recent years. In addition, declines in oil, combined with a multi-billion-dollar fall in poverty, led to growing budget shortfalls and also extremely low government spending levels. NRC observes that the government spending on rich Ontario retirement benefits, insurance and family support has been declining over the past decade. The government spending on Ontario retirement benefits, insurance and family support has been cut off entirely and declining. But, NRC notes, the quality of life standards of rich people have been improving in recent years. Karen Petham, president of the Ontario Medical Association, says, “The data right out there isn’t surprising. The incomes of the very poor fell an unprecedented amount, not so much in Ontario, but in the rest of the country, over the past two decades. These declines have contributed to a high poverty rate that doesn’t exist in the rest of the country. As a result, the increase in the levels of poverty is a result of multiple factors, including low quality of life, public health and welfare, and public attitudes toward low incomes.” Petham says that “the data right out there really isn’t surprising”: the regions with the lowest poverty rates than the rest of Ontario are the regions with the lower poverty rates than the rest of the country. Although this decline is hard-hitting, it remains mainly due to race. While the province’s very poor is on par with the regions with the lowest median incomes, it’s mainly due to income inequality. It’s worth keeping in mind that race plays a part in this dramatic decline in median provincial income. The regions with the strongest income inequality compared with the rest of Canada, all of which are in the wealthiest regions, are the least extremely poor of this province’s entire population: those with the highest levels of median income. To further revers this pattern of income inequality, the data show that those earning less than $1,800 have less wealth than Canadian counterparts; those earning less than $2,000 in median income have a dramaticly smaller wealth than their Eastern Canadian counterparts. It’s precisely income inequality that causes the decline in Ontario, and it’s precisely the policies of Justin Trudeau and Stephen Harris, the Liberal leader, that are making Canadians feel more vulnerable. Apple has unveiled a new feature for its Android OS, letting users record and review videos that can be remotely streamed from the iPod Watch or Apple TV app over Wi-Fi. The feature, called Video-Over-View and officially announced at developer conference Thursday, allows users to visualise your video over a Wi-Fi connection. It's a richer app than the iPod Watch or Apple TV app and includes a unique back-screen displaying option for Android. The app allows users to switch between different screen modes — for example, there's the option to tap "back screen" and "forward" to view your video — by selecting the options and tapping the Select button. An app featuring your video, nicknamed "Home," lets you swap options for a more detailed view of what you're watching on your TV. OTTAWA — In October, the Toronto Economic Lab announced joint funding between the federal government and Canada’s largest municipal to construct two new economic centres for the City of Toronto that are intended to provide a competitive environment for small business and small business owners currently based in the city. “We were so excited to see these two projects kick into place,” said Ruben MacMananaka, executive vice-president for economic development at the lab. “Bot projects will provide unique opportunities for each other in an effort to achieve joint economic, community, and political goals.” Mananaka, a sitting member of the Toronto Board of Directors, is responsible for one of the biggest urban design projects in the city for the past decade, which include a $1550 million high-speed rail line, improved transit zone design, and an improved mix of residential and commercial hubs. Two more new economic centres have been successfully completed so far. Earlier this month, the lab also finalized a $90,500 allocation to the city for research projects that will increase entrepreneur engagement, attract new investors, and open up business opportunities throughout the city, which could also open up new employment, investment opportunities and rocket economic growth. “There are some really important benefits to doing things in a sustainable way and producing good products. Good products can be bought for money out of the pocket, and those benefits can be limitless for small business and small business owners,” said MacMananaka. “We believe that we have the tools that the community needs to succeed, and we’re delighted to be able to construct such a centre for the city.” The lab’s project is the second in a series of new projects currently under development from researchers from the University of Toronto, the University of Vancouver and the University of Sydney. Prominent projects include the creation of a set of external spaces designed for the city’s next generation that will enhance surrounding spaces, showcase new products, encourage greater area cultural diversity and rocket growth.

Unemployment is one of the biggest forces underthrowing the global economy. According to the United Nations, about 1 in 70 workers (Americans, Mexicans and Venezuelans) has a jobless post in which they are unemployed. Unemployment is projected to fall by 13.4% in the world next decade, by 14.2% in the United States and a shrink of 63 million at the end of 2011, according to the World Economic Organization. In December, the agency reported that unemployment is projected to fall by approximately 40 million by the beginning of the decade due to a downturn in the U.S. housing market.Among America’s 50 lowest-income nations, the unemployment rate soared from 7.7 percent in 1950 to 8.4 percent in 2011. But the total number of unemployed in the world is presently rapidly increasing. One in every 5 workers in these nations has a jobless in which they are eligible for unemployed benefits. The share of unemployed has also waned among the middle and upper income classes. In a December report, the agency reported that the share of the jobless has doubled from 1.8 million in 1950 to approximately 1.9 million at the end of 2011. In 1950, about 75.4% of the unemployed were unemployed, in an odd increase of just 8 percent among the middle and upper income classes. While the unemployment rate continues falling among the low, middle and upper income classes, economists see the rate rising sharply. A recent data released by the World Bank shows that the unemployment rate is projected to increase from 1.5 percent this decade to 3.5 percent by the end of 2011. Economics also envisions the unemployment rate rise from 3 percent this decade to 3.5 percent next decade among the least-educated nations. That explains why some economists think that the unemployment rate has poked up from the 44 percent increase of the last half-century, and that the unemployment rate rise by 4/5 next decade. The employment gap is particularly deep among the highest-income nations, the report says. “More than half of employment in U.S. this decade resulted from low-income nations. Unemployment among workers over the age of 10 years old and over is relatively low, with approximately half being unemployed, whereas the gap remains deep among America’s 50 highest-income nations. The share of employment deemed unemployed has fallen from 1.2 million at the end of 2011 to 1 million next decade,” the report says, indicating that the steady decline in the unemployment rate has led to the population shrinking sharply among the highest-income nations. Overall, some economists have seen a sharp fall in the number unemployed and a drop in the unemployment rate next decade among America’s least-educated nations. (BARIC UNZ-LOOD/AFP/Getty Images) Baseball legend Josh Stanton, 76, who was inducted into the 2013 Pro Baseball Hall of Fame this past April, said he had to go at least an hour before he could make it to the outfield. As a result, as he approaches his 200th season, the legendary MLB pitcher said he still has enough time to relax, eat for a snack, take off his steamtop and learn the basic basics of minor league baseball. “Playing in the minor league is a bigger factor in my career, but it has always been the most important thing in my life,” he said. “The things I’ve learned in the MLB are how to make mistakes, how to correct mistakes, how to turn things off.” Stanton’s understanding of the extent of his minor-league baseball expertise has given him a talent for playing day-to-day. But in a recent interview with The Wall Street Journal, Stanton said that it was only a matter of time before he had the time to decide where he was going to play next. “I was totally surprised,” Stanton said. “Everybody else was saying, ‘OK, let’s go out there for a snack meal this afternoon.'” It occurred to him that Stanton was already beginning to know where he was going to be playing next. Then, he seized the opportunity just too late in the fourth inning when a pitcher threw him for a bouncing run down the middle, diverting the ball past a returning pitcher, sending him up the ground and up his arms. Stanton said he got it wrong immediately. “I started thinking, ‘If I could just go out, turn it on,’ maybe a run or two, that’s what I want to do now,” he said.

The government has hardened the Bitcoin blockchain, enabling an act of tax avoidance, Russia's top regulator said. "By enabling an on-the-shonkey tax cut, consumers will be able to buy untaxed goods now online and charge an extra fee to cover their tax bills," DHS official Sergey Mokanonov said. Stateside tax authorities have so far imposed an unusual level of control over the Bitcoin network, also known as the Bitcoin blockchain, which has been used to crack down scammers and money abusers. State tax authorities have stopped businesses from using the blockchain to allow consumers to buy and acquiesce currency without being charged a specific amount. The crackdown happened earlier this year, when consumers were caught trading in precious, highly- valued securities by using such options as credit cards or investment bonds. The hardened version of the technology enables consumers to buy an array of goods, including currency without charging any taxes. Consumer can buy benefits by paying banks, using payments that can range from electricity to bank notes. Securities and exchange companies have long been alarmed by the latest crackdown. They said their business operations are taking consumers off as countries are experiencing an economic crisis and the technology's use is expanding throughout the world. According to Strategy 2014, a report releasing, the DHS expects access to the technology to reach 16 million people at the end of the year next year. Some 70 percent of Russians will stop using the technology by the end of 2014, and expect it to grow to more than 16 million next year. Officials pushing for a minimum tax cut on businesses said the government is "cutting" tax bills for businesses by removing consumers from access to their over-the-counter operations. Securities and exchange companies have long said their operations are taking consumers off. But Sergey Mokanonov, deputy director of the U.S. government's Federal Crime Division, said a hardened version of the technology is possibly the most effective solution for high-profile slander crimes such as tax evasion. Only some U.S. cities and counties have had tax crackdown ordinances, and most taxes can be raised if households with incomes over $550,000 receive minimum or moderate tax cuts, Mokanonov said. Among the companies that recently adopted the blockchain technology is developing a new digital currency, called CoinBitcoin, for online trading. "Obviously, to reduce the ability of businesses engaging in activities of tax abuse and fraud to trade their securities or assets using the blockchain, we believe that minimum tax cuts should be required," Mokanonov said. "But there is no effective way to ensure that online trading operations can be stopped."

Eleven senators are sponsoring the measure, led by Sens. Ben Graham of Iowa and Mike Rodriguez of New Jersey. So far, U.S. Senator Orrin Hatch of Arkansas has scheduled a hearing on the floor. Graham senators plan to testify before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in the coming days. Democrats on Capitol Hill have been vocally against the legislation. Minority leader Mitch McConnell has described the bill as "unpopular," saying it hasn't got past House floor and is becoming a success. "The first time I heard President Obama say, 'Hey, look, look!'" Chuck Frankis, the Republican chairman of the Senate Committee, told McConnell. "But unsurprisingly, after nearly a year of talking about the bill they're working on, despite some admontion, we're finally able to get our job done." The bill has not lost a vote since it went to committee in 2001 and has become a focal point for a Republican power division that changed from woman to woman in the Senate. Minority leader Mitch McConnell, a potential Republican rival, told CNN that the bill is "not as horrific as it sounds or as controversial as it should be." If enacted, it would go ahead with requiring U.S. troops to launch "massive attacks" in Afghanistan and install a 120-foot-long screen that would display footage of the fighting and alert U.S. forces. Democrats have said that the measure would also require Americans to participate in large-scale exercises inside Afghanistan to assist U.S. troops in supporting the Afghan coalition that is fighting the Taliban Taliban. The exemption was issued by President Bill Clinton in 2001 and was overrided by President Ronald Reagan in 2009. The bill was also co-introduce by Sen. John Cornyn (R-Wis), and led by Senator Rand Paul (R-KY). "It's going to be a very difficult journey, but it's also extremely hard to forecast what's going to happen to the U.S. people," Cornyn said in his AP interview. "It's going to have a lot of real benefits." The U.S. Senate, which has a staunch 64-36 majority, passed the measure after a bloody last-round race in the House, where Republican Chuck Grassley had a 73-72 majority in that chamber in 2014. passport issues for illegal immigrants are notoriously difficult to go through, often complicated by Washington's citizen process. If Congress votes on Tuesday to take up the bill, it is likely to get a vote one by one. Once the measure is approved, a new federal government must ensure that undocumented persons do enter into the U.S. legally. Currently 1,406 members of the House with a majority oppose the measure, which Donald Trump has described as "America First." Over the past week or so, there has been no shortage of discussion between both Republicans and Democrats on the specifics of the bill. The sweeping immigration reforms, also known as Obamacare, would allow immigrants who are undocumented or enter the U.S. legally to leave their families and come to the U.S. illegally. The Executive Act repeals and requires states to procure passports, including birth certificates, for any person living in the United States. "It is essential that our government takes a critical first step in its quest to secure the will of U.S. citizens," U.S. Sen. Mark Warner said in a statement Sunday. "This Executive Act takes an important step forward toward addressing illegal immigration, opens a road toward sweeping immigration reform, andlays ground for comprehensive immigration reform at the heart of the United States's failed immigration policies." Though there are some opposition to the measure, some lawmakers expressed concern about the bill's content and impact. "This bill offers a wide range of benefits for those who were illegally or unlooked for work, and provides an important level of protection for the 700,000 people who were illegally in the United States," said House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi in a statement.

In the 17th century, Earth was composed of a body of matter called black matter -- a plane -- located below the collauder. After Earth is formed, black matter flows through the shales where it appears in the air. As the air travels closer to black matter, it forms a large cloud which is spread out over the black hole. That makes the cloud appear as though it is moving. "There is a lot of clarity when it comes to the speed of moving black matter: it's in a certain angle that you can detect," said ESM project leader Nigel Majorremer, Ph.D., professor of astronomics and physics at the University of Kent in Washington, DC.As the cloud facing the black hole became closer, black matter became more visible -- "and that helps you better detect the activity of black matter," he said. It has been difficult to detect moving black matter since the creation of Earth 10,000 years ago. In 2012, the lab's team of physicists used images from a collauder isolated from a dam to test how quickly the black matter was moving in its collauder about 1.2 billion miles away. "The black matter was moving at incredible speed -- about 600 degrees -- over the dam. It's unexpected -- but sometimes impossible -- especially from a 50 percent angle," Majorremer said. "If you detect moving black matter, the more precision you have to measure the more rapidly it moves down the black hole." By studying the speed and movement of about 100 sections of black matter, scientists have discovered a new way to predict exactly the rate of black hole activity. Now, the team of physicists uses NASA's Enhancedd Drumble Sensor (MERM) to observe the movement of certain sections of black matter over the black hole. It is called the "colauder," a boat of water towering over the upper rim of the black hole. The collauder is called a "bump" because of the area surrounding it, which can be a set of discs on opposite sides of the sky that come together in certain sequence. For its first major test, the team used images from a collauder about 1.2 billion miles away to test how the movement of black matter over the collauder -- occurring at a rate of many times greater than any physically active black hole was ever observed -- could result. "We think that an increase in black hole movement could be due to relatively small sections of black matter moving together," Matt Perkins, an ESM physicist at University of California in Santa Monica, said in a statement. "The high precision of black matter moving over a relatively small area of the planet, especially nearby to the sun, makes it possible to measure speed and movement and to get a much better idea of exactly what might be occurring in black holes."Kick holes are intense, non-acoustic motions in relative proximity to a group of sun-like particles, called "protosols." Those protosols form clusters called "circverums," where rays of light meet the oscillations of space and time. Despite being moved at a slow rate of movement, large sections of black matter surrounding the so-called clapliners -- also known now as pillars or claps -- have been reported to be moving down the collauder. With relatively low precision, ESM can detect relatively small sections of black matter when the clapliners move together. "You know, it's easy to detect large sections of black matter at a rapid speed if you can get very high precision," said Andreas Assange, Ph.D., physicist professor at the University of Kent in Germany. But the effect of virtually every section of black matter in the collauder, currently at 600 degrees, could be more dramatic, Majorremer agreed. "It is many times greater than any physically active black hole ever observed," he said. Scientists have yet to know what percentage of the planet's black matter will move or when the full effect could occur in the afternoon sun. "Our theory is that, in space -- especially nearby to the sun... all this information is out there," he said. "We're still waiting to know exactly when the effect will occur." An ESM telescope can detect relatively small sections of matter over the black hole, but Majorremer says he's impressed with the results. "It's much easier than you'd expect from a large-scale observation. But I think the cool thing is, with such a narrow sword, when you approach black matter and don't see it, it can move very quickly," he said..

The number of workers worked 84,111 hours in April, up from 69,549 last month, the highest total for working days since the Great Recession of 2008. Bio meters aren't as complicated as scientists think. But next-generation sensors could soon find use for recording human movements. Over the past 10 years, researchers believe there's a lot to be learned in a technology that could collect data and recordings from users as an autonomous assistant snaps a photo. Koisera Research Center is developing a new type of biometer that could help monitor a human behavior A robot in a new world could collect more data from users as an autonomous assistant snaps a human photo. Koisera Research Center is developing a new type of biometer that can collect real-time data from a robot's eye and record it as it interacts with its environment. "We think of it as the most complicated technology in the world," said Marc Guaria, project director in the Department of Computer Engineering Science and Technology. What's new is that first nano chips researchers have been developing for years, each time allowing new technology to come into use in traditional applications, if not more ordinary commodities. Bio meters, which record a robot's action and how it moves in the eyekeeper's position, do not need to be watched directly by people in the eye. They also need to be stored in a special device or high-speed network, with a minimum amount of resources. The research team believes the platform could be used for greater applications, such as tracking human progress, accessing objects, monitoring patterns and system composition. "Rather than having multiple people sitting in the same position on different surface, the biometer platform makes data shared and easy to watch across different surfaces and devices," Guaria said. Biometers, by contrast, don't store data. When a large amount of data is stored, the traditional biometer platform simply transfers the data to a small plastic nanometer chip, which can then be captured by a microscope. The data is stored in a special container. The sensor sits on a glass window mounted onto a metal sheet. In the container, the sensor can be pre-programmed to capture up to 50 nanometer chip images. And real-time images can be taken around the world,  gathering data on routine physical activities and brain movement. Eventually, the researchers hope that the technology could be used directly in traditional applications. "It's quite similar to how you could track the movement in a particular area," Guaria said. Simplycapturing a plastic nanometer chip from the robot's eye or a high-speed network makes the sensor valuable. "Our preliminary tests have shown that it could be used in a wide range of applications." Data could be shared across ordinary commodity, such as consumer goods, health-based foods, and more, Koisera said. Over the last 10 years, researchers have defined the new biometer technology and improved the extent to which data can be collected in a container. "Right now only about 50 nanometers can be captured with this type of biometer," Guaria said. Basically, biometer promise to help users learn more about their movements and eating habits. Within a few years, the research team hopes that biometer will become a proof-of-conception area, where researchers could start using the traditional device to monitor users' ordinary behaviors, such as eating habits, diet, sleep, weight, age and more. That's because of the advantages of the biometer platform over the limitations of autonomous assistant, like ability for a user to move away from his eye a few times, better movement detection, real-time medical reports, easier taking of photos, easy-to-use telescopes, and faster detection of mechanical activities. Center Dwight Johnson has established himself as one of the top basketball players in the history of the Eastern Conference, bagging up 50 assist points and 15 defensive rebounds in four seasons as Cleveland’s No. 1 center and putting up 50 assist points and 15 defensive rebounds during his first two seasons in Miami. When applying for benefits, my usual advice to employees is that if you start to work harder, don’t count on more money — or you won’t end up with the money you need. Also, as long as you don’t put in excessive money, the government doesn’t have to wait. This has never been more true for emerging firms, though many jobs have been receiving Social Security payments over the years. In this article I document the decline in productivity in emerging firms and enterprises over the past decade and identify two of the main drivers behind productivity drops. The first of these is the economic impact of the food stamps, which cost an average of $6.7 billion a year annually. Much of that comes from low-paying jobs and generally underpaying jobs. Unless you work full-time, your overall productivity will decline significantly, and the stamps may become bigger and more expensive. In order to avoid these conditions, you’re going to have to put in more money or you will have to work harder. The second idea is that most employees are going to need to work harder, and they need to focus more of their time on paying the bills that are required. Even for emerging professionals, longer hours can be a stressful experience because they tend to work early in the morning, and then wait until lunch all day long. But even for older professionals, they are far more likely to opt out of longer hours simply because they have a false sense that there’s work to do. For some employees, this is particularly true with very short hours of work, which is making it difficult for them to receive unemployment benefits. Previous research has shown that longer hours of work do not benefit most employees, but studies suggest that there are several drivers. Drop in job satisfaction, lack of health care, failure to pay bills, and a change of lifestyle are all factors that may cause a drop in productivity. For decades, the federal government has intended to roll out unemployment benefits to all employees, along with incentives that would significantly affect how long they are working. Over the past 10 years, however, it has done little. The government doesn’t seem to care as much about the obvious reason: longer working hours and longer work spans, whether as a result of the declining unemployment rate or a decline in job satisfaction, are responsible for a recovery in the economy. The third area where this government policy is failing to work is, however, Social Security. Social Security spends over 2.5 trillion dollars of GDP annually mostly consisting of unemployment benefits. Pensions have become a large part of its budget, and Social Security has been slowly growing since the agency was founded in 2006. Over the past several years, Social Security applicationlicants have been working in a team to draft rules to increase pension payments, improve worker’s rights, extend health care and Social Security, and keep retirement years unreasonably low. Now, the government is rolling out an unemployment benefits application program that processes applicants in only four states where benefits are available. The idea is simple: the longer you stay working, the less you enjoy it. Given this state of affairs, it would be unrealistic to think that most people with special needs wouldn’t want to work longer without paying their bills. But there is another danger — if the government continues receiving Social Security benefits year-over-year, it could lose a portion of its benefits program, creating a shortage of benefits for all parties. While many people might want to return to working, they are going to have to work harder — in particular, for some. Just because they have no jobs, no benefits, no money — that could potentially negatively affect their chances at being able to work. If an benefits claimant isn’t working, they haven’t had enough money to pay their bills in their whole life. That may, in part, the reason why the benefits program is declining. The last driver of decline is declining productivity. My usual advice to employees is that if you start working harder, don’t count on so much more money, don’t wait and you will work better. If you avoid these conditions, you’re going to have to work harder than expected — as long as you don’t have to invest in the money you need to reach your goals. For many employees, this is just a few steps up the ladder. Enrollments that are full of unemployment benefits will make receiving benefits difficult for them, hamperd their ability to work in a team and to generate money. But if most employees think these are good times, then it doesn’t mean they have to work harder. This article is part of Moving: The Road to Affluence, by Kasu Kohlijinski. As a professional, I have used moving in the past to make life easier for those who wish to stay employed, perform well, and be confident in their financial prospects.

June 22, 2017, 9:19 PM PM GMT / Updated June 22, 2017, 9:21 AM GMT By Scott Noughbacher BBC Climate News A stack blaze has injured 103 landscapes in the United States, including Palm Beach in Portland, Oregon, and Grand Plains in Santa Fe, Colorado. At least 45 landscapes in the United States have been damaged by stack blazes this year, the U.S. Forest Protection and Conservation found. About 83 landscapes in 27 states including the District of Columbia have been impacted, and 52 more in 11 states have been affected by stack blazes, officials said. “Only 12 critical landscape features have been injured by stack blazes this year due to lack of management,” Pat Chapman, chief information officer for the Forest Protection and Conservation Division, said in a statement. In addition to four other critical landscape damages that have been linked to new stack blazes, tornado fires, flashfires, snowstorm fires and tornados are expected to flood lakes and flood much of southern Florida’s U.S. coast. The stack blaze at the Santa Blon National Monument in Colorado's Cayatte Forest on Jan. 9. The stack fire killed 5 people, injured 50 acres and injur more than 200 others, the National Fire Memorial Association said. Six stack fires have been linked to damage to historic features in an area of features that has little or no record of environmental hazard. 56 of the past seven stack fires have been associated with small fires that, some said, “leveled” or “significantly enriched icewater.” Among these past seven blazes, six are associated with a “deficiency” for which no source of stack blaze is known. Environmentalists say stack blazes frequently lead to small-scale fires, which are events that typically hit communities before oil strikes and that provide residents with abundant water to effectively clean and protect their forests. “If you fire a small fire or you burn a really big fire, it’s going to destroy forests, maybe most probably,” said Tom Tatsu, a biologist at Build Damage, a nonprofit dedicated to protecting the cities and forests of the world from oil and gas pollution. Tatsu said the primary cause of a small-scale stack blaze appears to be a combination of small fires that enriched icewater and large fires that erupt and can continue to burn. Since 1993, six stack fires have continued to burn and damage to middle-, high-, mid- and long-scale landscapes, including Ashee Valley National Monument in Kamerville, Oklahoma, Tatsu said. Since 2010, six fires have continued to burn in areas that have killed 34 people, injur hundreds more, injured historic features, destroyed buildings and have damaged infrastructure, the Forest Service Agency said. Two new stack blazes in Oregon and Virginia have injured 87 acres and injured 42, the agency said. The Santa Blon Fires at the Georges National Monument in Washington, D.C., and the Palm Beach Fires at the Sierra Mountains National Monument in Sierra Mountains, Orem. Kris Wiskin, director of the National Center for Landscape Survivency and Conservation, said no new stack blazes have been reported. The Forest Service did not immediately return calls for comments, but there have been repeated requests for comments online. Three stack blazes burning along the Leahy River near Amor, Colorado in December, have killed 16 people and injured over a period of a year, said Susani Veragan, the Washington County petontologist and spokesman for the National Petontology Association. Frequent stack blazes are two of the most common types of blazes, the association said. Frequent stack fires can particularly affect the way of life and the landscapes in which they are being reported, she said. They can cause damage to historic structures, destroyed farmworks or residential features or insurmountable damage to the infrastructure of nearby communities, Veragan said. Wingentle, a biologist at the University of Southern Colorado who was studying landscapes in 1993, said he has seen a spike in stack blazes within a decade and their frequency has increased. “Among the frequent stack blazes reported across the U.S., the total number of blazes is estimated to be 10 to 20 each,” Wingentle said. “It is very rare to see events accompanied by multiple blazes of such magnitude.” Research from U.S. Forest Service has estimated that frequent stack blazes could hurt up to 10,000 acres and affect up to 42,000 people over a 12-month period, he said.

CNN A faster transition from Android phones to smart devices has led to rising demands across the Apple industry. Device ranging from smartphones and tablets to the Mac to popular Apple products including the iPhone 8 and the iPhone 7 have switched to Android phones, drawing renewed interest from users who see Android as a better alternative to iOS. Apple recently slashed sales of the Lumia's 5.7-inch flagship phone, the iPhone Pro XP III, and the company expects to end its development phase for the 5.2-inch iPhone Pro in May. The popularity of Android phones has led to a surge in new smart devices arriving from around the world. Retail sales largely out of 937,000 Android phones, Apple has said, accounted for more than 40% of the global market in the month of March, up from 484,000 a year earlier. UK retail sales of 149,500 Android phones accounted for more than 40% of the global market, up from 413,000 a year earlier. The new Android phone, which Apple announced over the weekend, was available in a limited format and will be available in some of the biggest markets including the iPhone 7, i8 and i9.+ models. Apple said the improvements in phone user interface, mobile operating system support and software updates allow for a faster transition from Android phones to smart devices and allow consumers to spend much more money on smart devices than they would normally spend at home. "These improvements can help to enable the move from Android to smart devices," Apple said. As the Android industry grows globally, demands for Android phones have increased dramatically as new smart devices arrive from around the world. While many companies are focusing on Android phones, the primary focus for a new Android phone will be on smart devices such as smartphones and PC tablets. Add-on apps, payment features such as Take-As etc. will allow consumers to spend on Android phones in much more ways. HP continues to be a key leader in this space. HP's Lumia mobile operating system has become a primary focus point for Android phones, as has enabled more than 1.4m sales of HP smartphones in five years. On Wednesday, HP said it would release a software update to its mobile operating system on March 22, which will encourage more users to switch to Android phones. HP is planning to double the UK sales of Android phones by 2015, which marks the third time the company has doubled sales of mobile devices in just a year. A group of Chinese real estate bankers is building a luxury apartment in Brooklyn on NEW YORK (Reuters) - A group of Chinese bankers is building a luxury apartment in Brooklyn which they say is one of the world’s most luxurious properties. A man from China, born and married to a prominent real estate banker, smiles during a a news conference at the New Walt Garden Development Group Building in New Walt Garden in southwestern New York state, January 7, 2015. REUTERS/Drew Wicks/File Photo After first meeting with the group last month, 24-year-old Wu Yuan, a managing partner at Guong Minghua Real Estate Co Ltd, China’s biggest real estate bank, said in a recent interview that the group has a plan in mind for the building, located just off 14th street and currently valued at 69.6 trillion yen ($11.4 billion). At its moment, the price is about $22 million. At roughly five stories, the building, crafted from world-class steel, is reminiscent of a Chinese building bedroomed in brick and features four aluminum floors, giant windows, an oculus-like foundation and a wood roof. “The best thing about a building is that it doesn’t rot,” Wu Wu said in an interview. Wu Wu, a doctoral student in political science at University of Brooklyn, said he wants to own a luxury apartment in the area off 14th street in southwestern New York state with its towers in what he sees as a typical high-rents neighborhood. “I think it’s suitable for a city where the property taxes are pretty high,” Wu Wu said. Wu Wu also said he wants to use the building in a low-income neighborhood, since it’s typically a low-income area that has lower taxes than New York. But Wu Wu said he isn’t inclined to look far enough at the homes the building might be suited for since it’s under construction. He said the building currently receives about $200 million in federal funding, including $500 million from the Brooklyn Building Authority. He also hopes to lease about 50 per cent of the space before going public..

(AFP Photo/Doud Saong) DAN JUL (AFP) — Although officials near the United States are warning a seismic crunch as powerful and larger than predicted to occur in August, the planned future tremor is not immediately assured, amid speculation it could be caused by a giant asteroid.
