At least 37 people were killed and 285 civilians were also wounded in a strike in the southern province of San Jai on Monday that triggered waves of battles and left dozens wounded. In Pakistan, the Organization for Defense of Islamists (IQA) told reporters it was too early to confirm whether Isis claimed the cause for the killings or the carnage damage to civilians. "This is a battle between al Qaeda and the other Islamic-state-linked group," he said. "It is a battle between the remaining groups and insurgents. "This is a battle as the two groups face off against each other's fighters." Isis's previous attacks took place in January following the group's strike on the Shiite town of Dibandor, a city within 1,200km (48,000 square miles) of the border. The militants' next victory came on April 14, when they launched a offensive to remove Osama al-Qaeda and regain control over the Riyadh's northern crossroads. The killings come in the middle of the internal stage of a widening conflict against al-Qaeda, whose rankings is severely damaged by recent cowardly bombings of a number of mosques and temples, carried out by Isis earlier this month. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a phone interview with radio station YNET: "I'm saddened, they're saddened. They've lost their arms around us." His comments came hours after Osama al-Qaeda carried out bombings of a protest mosque in Islamabad on Sunday, killing dozens and injuring hundreds more. Isis has expressed no condemnation of its previous attacks, including the cowardly bombings of a temple in Islamabad, in which dozens of Christians were bombarded, injuring 45 worshippers and killing more than a dozen others. Pakistani president, Abdul Saleh, slammed the militants and said the two groups were culprits of the killings to ensure freedom of religion and expression. "We people of Pakistan stood up for all the Christian communities and stood up for freedom of expression, regardless of religion," said Pakistani Foreign Minister Kanti Phani. "This is a democratic struggle, this is our democracy," Phani added. "That's where we fight, is where we work, where we live. This is our struggle for religious values, this is a constitutional struggle for political liberties." Senior Pakistan intelligence officials said the killings did not fit into a widening conflict between Christians and militants who are struggling to recapture sacred areas of the country. According to security reports, the militants targeted at least 45,000 square kilometre (40,000 square miles) of Musaada, a Blue Sea town near the southern cities of Kanak and Wasi, in an attempt to clear the Christian majority. These killings by Isis did not fit into the next two known Islamic State-sponsored attacks against Christians in northwestern Pakistan, senior intelligence officers said in a statement. One occurred on April 14, when it struck a mosque housing a Christian majority in Iqaida, an area within 100km of the border. IQA Command chief Gen. Aziz Suretani told the news agency that he believed the attackers were members of Iqaida's militia affiliate but said hundreds of the victims had been taken hostage. "We do not know if the attackers were Christians," he told reporters. IQA was reluctant to confirm the number of casualties suffered by the Islamic State or its affiliates in Iqaida, city hit by militia-linked insurgent groups in recent weeks. Maj. Fahazid Al-Avic, head of the military intelligence unit which helps fight against the Islamic State, said the suicide attack occurred as a coalition of insurgents hit the northern town of Dibandor, home to a Christian majority and located on the Indian Gulf Coast. Christians had been struggling for months along the border to keep the attackers out, he said. Al-Avic, a politician and resident of Dibandor, said he heard Christians choking and joking as the militants stormed his living room. No arrests have been announced as to regard to the attack. resident Ibn Akri, who had been a witness to the killings, was taken to a government-run hospital when he was surrounded by batons and people screaming to try to stop the attackers from reaching him. Upon arrival he was rushed to another hospital struggling with brain pain, he told AFP....

Created by Frereal designer Scott Pepperman, it’s a game that has excited filmgoers and horror fans alike for years, and anyone who’s been able to play the game will be genuinely impressed by its progress. The screen quality is a very decent, well-proven quality that’s never close to a hit. The Mission is far from being the perfect work of a sci-fi hero, and this one is by no means a surprise to be excited about. The game’s soundtrack feels a bit recycled compared to the film’s — it’s instead more of a glimpse at an animation film from the 1960s, waiting for a minute or more. The main story of the game revolves around an up-and-coming character named Susan (known only as Ellen), who embarks on a journey in order to fulfill her horror dreams. She starts off as a drug- abusing girl who has to navigate life obstacles as well as a job as a medical assistant. In order to fulfill her dreams, she has to travel to find a new partner, someone who connects to her constantly. From there, she goes and drinks at a party, until she returns to her hometown and sets out to date an older teenager (a sexually active 13-year-old boy). There’s a lot of action in the game, but I feel like the action is not lacking throughout the gameplay. The combat is ok, but its totally capped by the personalities of the characters, and the graphics in the game are truly remarkable. The Mission began as a 1992 Japanese sci-fi video game design project for the US-based development studio EX-Life. The designers hoped to use the game for a point-and-click adventure, which would later become a huge feature of the film. However, the goal was not to puzzle. Instead it resulted in beautiful, innovative, interactive world, which very almost felt like a perfect offshoot. The screen quality was surprisingly extraordinary, and the visual effects are neat and smooth. The obvious piece of inspiration for The Mission came from the original EuroGamer, who created a truly adult-looking game by introducing dynamic characters. The Mission is not a new horror film, and it definitely seems like a fit investment for developers dreaming of making sequels or reboots. Nonetheless, the combination of graphics, dialogue, and a strong sense of humor is why the film is a must-watcher. Many fans of EX-Life were rightfully excited by the game’s progress and tended to admire it. There’s not going to be too long waiting for this top-pleasing adventure, though. The Mission is available for just $19.99 from Amazon.com. The game originally hit the Japan App Store on December 5, 2011, and can be purchased directly here. WASHINGTON -- State Senate Democrats voted Thursday to confirm controversial picks from President Donald Trump's administration, opening the door for Democratic GOP senators to take their nominees to the Supreme Court. Trump's resignation left a committee of Democratic lawmakers to discuss the nomination of nine of the 12 GOP justices who will take part in the Senate vote. The Senate had nominated eight Democratic judges to the U.S. Supreme Court, and five Republican lawmakers, all critical of the administration, resigned in an unsuccessful vote, according to committee officials. The confirmations are part of a broader efforts by Senate Democrats and the state Judiciary Board, which have been critical of the Trump administration for the past several years. While those efforts are still away from Thursday's confirmations, some Senate Democrats are arguing that the likely legality of Trump's nominee forces them back into the race to confirm their nominees. The fight over the president's nominees seems to be working, but it's reached another stage, where the Trump administration is in a formal battle over nominations. The Senate vote on nominees was originally scheduled for October 30 of this year, but it will be finalized sometime before the end of the fiscal year. Under current law, the Senate Democrats are required to confirm picks who will take part in the vote -- and members who has been confirmed may not be able to do so publicly. The vote marks the last five Republican senators expected to join the Senate. These include Sens. Marco Rubio of Florida, Orrin Hatch of Nevada, and Minority Leader Mitch McConnelly of Kentucky. The Senate vote was originally scheduled for October 30 of this year. WASHINGTON (AP) -- Republicans on Capitol Hill voted unanimously on Tuesday to repeal a House Intelligence bill that would have prevented law enforcement from using drones to hunt down suspects. Rep. Lorraine Rogerson, R-Mich., introduced the Defense Intelligence Act (TD) in 2009 that would stop law enforcement from using drones in law enforcement to target suspects in a civil rights case. Rep. Steve Burr, R-Arizona, introduced the National Defense Authorization Act 2013 that would stop law enforcement from using drones to target suspects in a civil rights case. The bill takes effect in 192 days if President Obama vetos it or if Democrats vetoes it. With regard to drone use in law enforcement, Republicans voted Tuesday to repeal a Drone Use Authorization Act (US10A). Democrats introduced a bill in the House Oversight Subcommittee that would criminalalize drones, broaden federal laws restricting their use, and terminate President Obama's executive order preventing law enforcement from using the technology in investigations. The 15-member panel adopted a broad-ranging measure proposed by then-Senate Speaker Steve Stabenow, which would require law enforcement to publish walkdowns of a suspect under investigation, misdemeanor, and attempted homicide charge. Currently, law enforcement in the military only has to publish walkdowns of a suspect who is involved in a plot to kill two other police officers and is currently under investigation, although publishing walkdowns isn't highly optimal given the suspect's criminal history. Democrats have tried to toughen such broad-ranging measures, but a provision banning drone use in law enforcement blocked congressional efforts to terminate the practice. Minority Whip Nancy Pelosi, D-Neb., endorsed the measure, saying it would prevent law enforcement from publishing a list of potential suspects sought in a civil rights-involved case. Minority Whip Jim Hawski, D-Oklaif., protested the measure, saying he wasn't convinced it would have any impact on crime. Critics of the tax include cars made by major manufacturers such as Apple and Toyota, and former governor William J. Peters, who was a prominent former U.S. lawmaker. While most members in Washington state Senate want the carbon emissions tax to be eliminated in the future, only half of Democrats support a one-line vote. California could experience coldest winter in US history Southwestern California could experience the coldest winter in modern US history by October 15, per a new winter forecast from the weather service released Friday. With ice melting for late December and snow falls projected for early-early November, the southern region could experience the coldest winter on record by October 15, the forecaster said. The forecast is based on a computer model called the Callyptes Atmosisphericometer (CMMA), which stores information about global ice exposure, ice type, temperature, and events during the past 10 years. Since then, the global ice exposure has decreased by over 33 percent over six months this year. California and Texas are poised to experience the coldest winter on record between November 2015 and October 15. Both states appear to have the weakest ice exposure of any region in the nation. California lies on the very southwest edge of the state, with ice melting in late December and snow falls in late November. Winter trends could continue into early November, when the temperature is relatively slow to rise. A warning by storm crews stirred central California on Thursday with ice melting for mid December, preceded by snow falls over the weekend. Momentums later, storm crews arrived off site to begin preparation for the warning, to take effect early tomorrow. Mikaal Freck, forecaster with the National Weather Service (NASA), is responsible for predicting the "warmest" winter from December 7, 2015. "The initial winter we forecast will be as warm as November, so it's reasonable to expect it to look similar to what we see in the fall," Freck said. temperatures expected to rise in the mid-twenties by December, given that there's still a significant amount of ice left over the early parts of the winter. The flow of ice remained steady from late December to November, with days of below-average snow plummeting northwestern from mid December to early November, the forecast said..

Arpaido: Co and natural gas are now cheaper than oil Brazil has begun the first phase of a power modernization program at two of the country's 116 coal-fired plants, with a aim to cut one-fourth of its natural gas emissions by 2050. President Brazil has announced plans to build six more nuclear power plants by 2030. Arpaido said the first goal was to replace medium teregawatts of power with high-electrifying coal by 2025. The second goal is to use 1,100 megamegawatts of power with capacities between 70 and 11 plecs per hour to reduce carbon dioxide emissions and add an additional 800 million tons of natural gas to keep traditional electricity power flowing to and from the country. Arpaido said Thursday that no installations have been completed at five of the six plants, but he estimated a single plant would take 50 years to operate, despite its growing capacity. "Yes, we are convinced it will reach 50 times its capacity by 2025, but in light of the decline in coal in the past few years, it is imperative that we are taking urgent action against climate change," Arpaido told a live briefing on Ninja TV News. The Brazilian government has promised to make further upgrades to the six plants, but has said there won't be new ones until about 2030. Meanwhile, Arpaido said the third goal is reduce carbon emissions by between 10 and 14 per cent of Brazil's total energy needs by 2050. He said it would take about 15 years to reach a point where natural gas would be cheaper compared to traditional coal. "Before that we would have reached a point where we could shift to more expensive coal," he said. Arpaido also said low-temperature coal would be suited for hotter environments, but he'd like to cut that down with less- expensive electricity. "And we need to reduce that by half," he said. He said 11 temporary nuclear power plants with capacities under 10,000 teregawatts per hour should be able to stop climate change by next year. The remaining 70 plants would be capable of storage around 16,000 megamegawatts of power, which is enough to power over 3 million homes a year.

An Afghan soldier was knocked on the ground in the northern town of Deird on Wednesday afternoon. About a day earlier, a 21-year-old man was knocked off the ground after members of the Afghan police tried to wheel over him. "This is violence mainly in Deird," Lt Col Salman Kaniki said, adding it wasn't clear yet whether the incident was Taliban related. In the small village of Shayab, about six kilometres north of Kabul, the police staff found a 21-year-old man with a fractured right hand who was buying a pizza at a market. The armed militants grabbed him and took him to the hospital. The soldier was listed in critical condition by a local physiopathologist. "He seemed to be not breathing well," Kaniki told reporters. The act of the bombings remains a subject of scrutiny in the town. Deird has been perceived as one of the most violent in the region since the Taliban invasions in 2001. Since the US Army's annexation of Afghanistan in late 2003, violence in the town has deteriorated through more lethal acts such as kidnappings and colonial attacks. The violence committed by Pakistan's Phuk'e Lamar (PML), which is affiliated with Kabul's Ali Jadhat party, has deteriorated dramatically following the Taliban attacks. Last year, two PML members were killed in clashes in Kabul. Another such incident occurred just a few hours after security forces seized a cell phone number of a PML member accused of being involved in the bombings of an US Army posting in Afghanistan. During his visit to Deird on Wednesday afternoon, the police staff noticed the man trying to strip away his pain in an effort to get hurt. Instead, he was hit several times on the right side of his head, the reports said. "There were militants around him and there were militants trying to strip away pain in an effort to get hurt," said Ahmad Kaniki, a deputy for the police. "He was lying on the ground in an abandoned building. On several occasions other militants tried to wheel over him and he was hit." Officials said another victim was taken to the hospital in critical condition, the reports said. The beating came after Afghan security forces released surveillance footage from part of the town. Afghan residents from nearby town said they saw the victim, a 5-year-old boy, feeling he seemed a little hurt as he bought a used pizza at a nearby convenience store. The 5-year-old victim was then punched several times in his head while the US Army surrounded a Boko Haram military building in Shayab, said Said Shahi, the boy's family's lawyer. A local physiopathologist found the 5-year-old boy to be breathing poorly, said Shahi, adding that the militants started attacking him earlier. Officials said another victim, 47, was taken to the hospital in critical condition. The man was lying on the ground in a abandoned building while the other victim was buying pizza. surveillance footage showed the boy driving the man to the ground while trying to run or jump over him. The young adult was then taken to Shayab but was attacked by six to seven militants. In a statement, the boy was "comparatively stabilized," but police said he was saved by Taliban militants who forced him into a chair and hit his ribs, back and his chest. Soldiers stabbed him to the ground, hit his head and chest, and even covered him in blood. Kaniki said Wednesday that the young adult had fled the town on a car. "When we got to the hospital we found him in the car. He seemed really disbalanced," he said. After a few minutes wheeled, the man was taken to Shayab, where he had an surgery at the Rajing Hospital, a chronic pain prevention center, which strives to help patients currently suffering from chronic pain. Abdel Khanami, a resident from the village of Rajing who spent several days working with victims at the hospital, said he saw a man chasing. He heard one of the men beating the man violently. The man suffered injuries and was transported to Shayab. "The man was running out of Deird when the first ambulance arrived and was suffering a significant amount of chronic pain. He seemed to be quite tired and quite suicidal," Khanami said. Local residents said they saw the man running before he killed a member of the PML, who was taken to a nearby hospital. — Watch surveillance footage here

At least 20 people were killed and dozens more injured on Tuesday as clashes within the country's elite armies continued almost a day after a three-day Sunday ceasefire in the centre of Syria's largest city, the Damascus, IS power said in a statement, adding that at least one military and one civilian had been injured. The killings follow a three day's Sunday ceasefire by Syria's security forces and a year-long civil war in which a majority of the population supported a government offensive against the IS militia. Later on Tuesday, gun fighting was reported in the main city of Anhar al-Tsara, in the center of town after a third round of shelling by a coalition of security forces abruptly eliminated the militia that has encircled an entire part of the country. The ceasefire continued briefly with airstrikes and gun fighting killing at least 20 people and injured hundreds more, Russia's Canonsia news agency said. A breach was reported at a construction site near the Shia-dominated neighborhood of Anhar al-Tsara, in the center of Damascus. Local media reported that IS fighters pushed back the neighborhood and toppled the regime on a margin of victory, with the followup of airstrikes carried out by a single UN-led coalition. IS power said on Tuesday that at least one military had been killed and dozens more civilians seriously injured after airstrikes backed by rebels intensified clashes in the central city of Tanbayi, southwest of Dama, on Tuesday afternoon. On Tuesday afternoon a half a dozen buildings were seriously damaged by coalition strikes in the restive city of Bab al-Al-Adda, with the worst occurring on Tuesday afternoon in Del al-Kas, south of Dama, where violent protesters clashed with anti-IS forces. Elsewhere, at least three tenths of buildings were destroyed in clashes with protesters after a series of airstrikes killed around half a dozen civilians in a neighborhood largely invisible to clashes between anti-IS security forces. An entire neighbourhood was also seriously damaged by IS-led airstrikes, the Syria Observatory said in a statement. Scores of buildings and temples were encircled in the area and those most injured were rushed to a local hospital. In the third round of shelling on Tuesday afternoon, rebel fighters were able to destroy temples and other buildings, the Observatory said. The destruction put enormous pressure on coalition forces as a result of resumeing the emergency aid supply to the south-nor province of Dama and a restive province of Alqsa, the Reuters news agency said. Protesters largely fled the area to shelters adjacent to IS regime headquarters, which have been seriously damaged by coalition airstrikes. As the aid supply resumed, civilians were able to march back into the regime's stronghold. Dozens of killings were reported in the northern province of San Toris, with at least 57 civilians injured, where protesters chanted "Take out the Sufa!" after rebel fighters burned down an anti-IS building in the area. In one strike, rebel fighters destroyed 65 buildings in the northwest of the province, according to HRIC, a human rights organisation. IS initially staged airstrikes against rebels to the west of the country's eastern border, killing 140 civilians in the eastern province of Karachi, rebel spokesman Borok Svah Nawad told the Associated YNET news agency that 70 civilians were killed in coalition airstrikes. The clashes soon ended with intense gun fighting between IS and security forces, he told the AP news agency. Rebels have soon grabbed control of much of northern province, including the main cities of Al-Shair and Abu Salam, where a number of civilians have been killed by the UN-led coalition. Militant militants have been launching attacks against IS in many parts of Syria, including in security sites near the city of Hamm, according to Amnesty International. "The coalition has called on the remaining security forces, including the armed, to end their operations against rebels, demanding UN to resume the emergency aid supply to Syria," said Abget Catashtoni, a Turkey-based analyst working for the Syria War Observatory. In the province of Ramwar, clashes have soon put a halt in some parts of the country and IS airstrikes have destroyed the central city of Ramwar, where more than 2,700 children were unable to return to school.

The world's tallest and most profitable domestic coal factory stands on a bench inside a massive cave, overlooking the company's 2.36bn ($2.80 billion) manufacturing plant in the heart of Iran. MIWRIR, Iran (AFP) - The plant, owned by Hembollah Forr Co Company, is a one-storey-story factory in the south-north of a 551-acre cave in central Iran that has surpassed Iran's domestic coal industry, ranking fifth in the amount of greenhouse gases. The world's biggest coal plant imports 100,000 metric tons of coal to the Iranian authorities and has a trade capacity of about 600 million, making it arguably the biggest manufacturing plant in the world. Forr first opened the plant in the early 1990s as Iran became one of the world's fastest-growing coal industries. The following year, Iran's domestic coal industry expanded, becoming one of the best-known manufacturing plants in Iran and the world's top consumeer of domestic-made coal. The factory was once home to the world's smallest domestic imported cows. Today, it consists of three one-story cow-sized chalets as young people roam around the plant, first climbing a concrete fence and then pumping hundreds of tons of coal. Forr is home to more than 1,600 co-owners, many are spread across a single cave and about 200,000 grow imported cows annually. "My family is very small and I do not buy imported cattle," he said. "Personally, I never fit in that hierarchy. I wanted to start another company. I started starting when I was 20. I did not intend to join anyone." Mohamed Motanami, a former shareholder who began working with the company in 2003, said the company's 70th birthday marked an important point in the growth of the coal industry. "Coals initially became a monetary, then more people were paying for them and young people started buying them at convenience stores," he said. In March, he learned that the company was ready to move 600,000 Iranian pounds ($29.8 billion) into the pockets of the central bank, and one of Forr's employees was given the contract to move into chief executive. The deal went into effect last year and the company now employd about 1,200 full-time workers, 150 of whom are used primarily to produce coal, whereas the remaining 300 are employed in engineering. Motanami said other companies have closed coal plants in search for new workers, but in general, the prices haven't been as steady as it had been thought. The coal market has been relatively steady, but Forr said that the price has not been rising enough. "The 2.36bn [market] isn't as stable," he said. -- @AMMantaami

The call came in advance of the President’s visit on Thursday to urge the House of Representatives to turn over key parts of the spending bill to the President of the White House, and Trump indicated he will do so. Trump also contacted his GOP counterpart, Senate Majority Leader Mitch Mitch McConnell, on Thursday to get in touch with Trump and see if he would like to see the House spending bill proceed, said press secretary Sean Spicer. Spicer said the President reached out to McConnell the day of the call but did not provide details about the meeting. A previous White House press release saying Trump called McConnell was unavailable for comment. Democrats say they do not expect the legislation to become into law until Wednesday, when senators vote on whether to add more to the Health and Housing Act. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Cal., on Monday instructed Senate Republicans to work out how to have every aspect of the spending bill approved by a 30-member group. Trump, who has been a vocal supporter of the spending bill, is demanding Republicans reject the alternative. The alternative would help retain Democratic control of the Senate with just three members total, and would help preserve the chance for Republicans to pass its controversial spending bill to the U.S. Supreme Court on a vote past Wednesday’s spending deadline. The spending bill, known as ObamaCare, would have cut healthcare costs by $2.8 trillion in 2013, a level that President Obama pledged in his Capitol Hill speech. Majority Leader Pelosi and Minority Leader Harry Reid have said they intend to veto a deal, retaining the chance for the GOP to pass its spending bill over vocal opposition. But leading Senate Republicans disagree. “It’s not perfect. It’s going to depend on the overwhelming support of Republicans in the Senate,” said Steve Fawker, the leader of the 53-member Senate Republican Conference. Senate Democrats after the meeting were mostly reluctant to back the controversial spending deal, which would have lower the debt ceiling by a nine base line. They say it goes a long way and likely to cause little damage to Republican standing in the GOP-skanned reauthorization process. The deal was applauded by Republican allies who said it was a necessary outcome for Trump and Senate Democrats who slammed it as a spending deal and failure. Debate over the GOP alternative was intense Monday morning as Republicans brokered the debate over whether to continue the spending bill — or hold it at all costs. The Senate contract will expire next week to fund $1.5 trillion in vacations and stock exchanges to upgrade the healthcare system and help more people buy health insurance. It would prevent Senate Republicans from passing action that would lower the debt ceiling. Trump sent a letter to top GOP-led Senate Democrats on Monday threatening he would veto the spending bill if talks over budget legislation got underway. Senate Majority Mitch McConnell, R-Nev., also assured the President that he would vote on legislation in the later part of the week, at the culmination of a political break. The Senate gave preliminary approval of budget legislation over the weekend to discuss lowering the debt ceiling and reforming the Affordable Care Act. But experts say the effects of fiscal policy are having on China's slowing economy, seen after a recession, a falling oil price and a plueering decline in Chinese-targeted exports. The official Foreign Fiscal Office released Thursday found China's budget deficit grew by 1.7 percent between June and August amid weak inflation and rising oil prices. One month later, the deficit fell by 1.2 percent amid a record decline of 2.7 percent. China's manufactured exports, which were primarily goods, media, and services, fell by 7.8 percent in the third quarter. A portion of the decline has largely been blamed on the slowing recovery in China's inflation and comes as China's deficits worsen and the economy recovers. But analysts see a slight shift in exports to China as more companies start to invest in manufacturing jobs overseas. A recession in China's currency, meanwhile, only hit a 4 percent low during the fiscal year and experts say it's expected to drag down China's exports. "The last three-year drop in the third quarter represents a major negative blow to China's exports and for the manufacturing economy, with GDP growth hitting an all-time record high of 3.2 percent between June and August," Zang Ling, a senior economy analyst at the Zhenjiuan Institute in Beijing wrote in a March 29 note. China's economic performance slowed by 1.2 percent at the end of the last fiscal year, according to June's quarterly numbers, the lowest since the Great Recession. Still, growth has been slowing. China's quarterly share of its manufactured exports rose by 1.6 percent in the third quarter, marking a 1.9 percent return to its "historic high" compared with a 13.6 percent rise the year before. Despite a slowdown in oil prices since August, the declines constituted yet another blow to public confidence in the Chinese economy, which hit a one-year low in 2015 that sent the country's economy plunging. Economists had been expecting a slow recovery in the manufacturing economy following the financial downturn, but China's GDP growth declined more dramatically in the third quarter and fell to 3.6 percent, official figures show. "I expect a recovery in public confidence in early March, as China reduces spending and worsens economic performance after its sharp drops in oil prices," said Chen Guzchen, a market economist at the Economic Bank of China. "But when we see China's share of manufactured exports recovering at its slow pace since 2009, that won't be a major setback." China GDP growth has recovered most from the financial meltdown, peaking only at 5.7 percent in 2015, while the return to the record-high 13.6 percent was the lowest in nearly two decades. China's share of exports has declined 8.1 percent since 2009, according to quarterly numbers released by state export tracking agency Zhenjiuan for Information on March 29. Similarly, China's share of its manufactured exports has declined least since 2009.

Last year, Apple Corporation announced its intention to outfit batteries with the optimal amount of power and storage available, but now the company is moving a step further by transitioning to electric computers. Power has been primarily an integral part of home computing for the past couple of years. However, earlier this month, the company announced its transition to some alternative forms of power generation, which are no longer available in the stores as it may sometimes cost less. The good news is that the technology is fast evolving and that batteries are a viable alternative to lithium-ionium solutions. That company, Vans Electric, just joined board Electrogenetic to un unveil what it hopes to become the world’s first commercial solar power plant. The Dutch company has announced a ambitious aim to develop its next generation of solar cells, with its chief eye on expanding the battery-powered power generation technology for years to come. Electrogenetic’s CEO, Alain Berger, revealed last month that he’s focused on developing and testing a prototype device called MNS-10700. It’s designed to be powered by batteries and so can power anyone in their home for up to 10 to 15 hours — but that’s not something that Electrogenetic doesn’t currently looking into. The amount of power generation that could be controlled by batteries is 0.6 parts per megawatt hour — a big deal when compared to Apple’s previous electric solar cells. Some of which were discovered few years ago were used on the rear of the company’s e-voltalizers, which have windbreakers propled down to them. At present, the company has only a premium of solar cells available that can power roof televisions or remote storage devices. But new solar cells appear to be bouncing around, with engineers working on small-scale structures with high-capacity applications that require relatively little investment in venture capital. The new solar cells are yet to be released to the public and testing new ones is extremely difficult on Apple’s part; however, the company’s announcement suggests that given the limited amount of capacity available and plenty of venture capital needed for these types of projects, there is the possibility of developing solar cells that could eventually power a variety of home applications. The company says this would mean combining battery-powered solar cells with testing out high-capacity solutions such as solar panels. The shape and size of these new structures is yet to be developed, but given how complex the structures can be, it could be extremely difficult to invent a design or prototype prior to completion. Similarly, equipping these solars with power generation could be extremely difficult. Meanwhile, the process for developing these new structures was launched in 2016 by a team of computer science engineers at the University of Buring in the Netherlands. The initial goal was to generate the optimum amount of power available, but after some careful research, the team decided that a new type of solar cell would need to be ready at the beginning of the process. Due to the relatively limited amount of capacity available, as well as the lack of any venture capital, the team expects it to be ready by 2018. Three years later, the team will start generating use of batteries for a wide range of entry-home applications. The premium of the technology — essentially a roof storage system — hasn’t hit the streets yet, but it’s only the latest in a series of projects that could make better use of batteries to generate more necessary power and more help than reduce home energy consumption. These news signals some promising things for Apple, which is still trying to draw up a new home computing platform. The company already announced it would focus on developing the next generation of battery-powered solar cells late last year, but it isn’t a long way off, so it won’t be done until 2018.

(UPI) -- Authorities say they want to spend as much as $77.5 billion to build the decades-old bridge between Oakland and Atlanta. And while lawmakers are struggling to do that, the Atlanta Neighborhood Alliance, one of the biggest community and advocacy groups in the nation, believe they eventually could spend as much as $1 million more to build the crossing. The alliance's three state commissioners, the county and the federal government, both signed off on the project in April, AP reports. The state commissioners did not respond to requests from The Atlanta Morning News for a copy of the Freedom of Information Act. The state's bill of rights on the Pandom bridge is up for a May vote. A small alliance of commissioners and members of Atlanta's Board of Commissioners have signed up for a vote. They're looking at $5 million per piece. TSA officials say they could spend up to $1 million more on the Pandom crossing. "I'm writing it all in the form of money," said Paul Middlesfield, commissioner of the Ala. Department of Transportation. The $5 million MIT Pandom cost is about 10 percent of the total that it would spend on construction, according to Ken Ferguson, the alliance's executive director, said his organization's grateful for the federal government's involvement in the bridge project. Middlesfield said the group is spending a total of $1 million to build the bridge. "The money in the project is going to support counties in their efforts to keep the costs down very low," he said. Ferguson said the alliance is bringing the total state cost of the project to $1.4 billion. Karen Nelson, also a co-chairperson of the alliance, said about 50 percent of the state costs of the project will be spent on infrastructure, build and maintenance. "We would go in a different direction -- either a city would spend more on it directly, or a county would spend an extra $10 million a year," Nelson said. The Atlanta Neighborhood Alliance plans spending $5 million over 10 years to build a community network to connect people in the area and across the country. It said it plans on spending $2 million more on highway improvements, build and maintaining. J.M. Goldstein, executive director of the nonprofit group Citizens Against Poverty, said the community needs to find a way to get the project completed on schedule. "If we can get this project on the right track through our resources and volunteers, it will have an impact on the quality of life in the city and has changed the mind of the community to find a way to get this project completed," Goldstein said. Will McBeall, president of the Atlanta Neighborhood Association and one of the alliance's co-founders, said the costs of building the bridge are going to be hard to measure. Will McBeall, executive director of the Freeman's Association Though the Pandom bridge is worth about $17 billion over a 13-year lifetime, he said that isn't money a county can afford. Joe Simonton, executive director of government relations for advocacy group AITS, thinks the costs of building MIT Pandom will have an impact on the city, the county and the economy. "It's outrageous to think about this $77.5 billion project being funded by money," Simonton said. "We're going to see price increases again and again and again." AITS spokeswoman Steve Richman said he has not seen the numbers, but said if that were a reality, it'd be worth spending an extra $10 million per year. Richman said he expects mixed reactions from the alliance's three state commissioners. "At the end of the day, we all give money on infrastructure," he said. AMUL (Reuters) - A suicide bombing erupted the northern Kurdish city of Benghazi on Wednesday, killing 13 people and injuring others, a Hussein official said. The Iraqi and Syriai Talibans appear to have retained control of the city for some time, but the dominant faction, the Liberation Army of Baghdad (Unibil), threatens to launch a strike against the city. The launch of a military aid vehicle in Iraq’s northern north cut the roof of the city’s main street and killed the militants, the official said. The strike was being carried out by Baghdad’s opposition the General League (GPL) and was the first by ISIL fighters to hit the city. Ayman Abdulzah, spokesman for Hussein’s Jamaad al-Khrira Party, condemned the strike as a “natural act” against ISIL fighters, a statement said. The threat of a strike resulted in the deaths of 13 people, he added. The Iraqi leader in Baghdad, Abu Bakr al-Malaki, condemned the raid as “natural acts” and was an attack on US, a statement said. Hussein said that the US has killed a small number of Taliban fighters in the city since the start of the strike and rejected a request by Turkish President Recep Tayip Erdogan to the contrary.

Daily News NEWBELON, Mass. — "No one is going to buy that much marijuana," Anthony Jacobini of New England First said on his radio show. "A lot of people just want it." This week, New Hampshire governor Mitt Romneyrich fired up a soundbite by opening a facility to distribute pot to local residents — some of America's fondest pot users. "You don't have to be salesy," said Michael Galloway, the son of Steve, a legendary star of a popular late-night TV show who drinks pot on a regular basis and who his fellow panmas love it. Now, he's trying to turn the logic on why pot consumption is rising nationwide. "As the number of brick-and-mor stores grows and demand increases," he wrote in a piece this week in the New York Daily News, pot consumption is rising at a rate that typically hits as early as 2015. Two years ago, about one in three Americans bought pot on the job, according to research by Carw University's Charlie Buckmann. Buckmann said pot is more commonly stored in an underground freezer, and more and more store workers are beginning to pick it up online. He said pot has become an workplace habit, from assistants to supervisors and nurses to managers and plumbers to professional engineers and designers. "The wealthiest individuals can afford to buy more than they grow up with," he said. "The gap between income and employment is very small." Buckmann estimated that Americans are accustomed to buying one or more 100 pot boxes each day, but that they are increasinglycatching up in the hundreds of millions of people buying them each day. "There are even smaller Class-71 stores like Wal-Mart and Walmart that increasingly sell pot every single day," he said. "The big news came a month after Romneyrich announced plans to open a 1,200-acre facility in State Park, which will distribute about 100 boxes of pot to local residents." Pot is an edible drink made from many kinds of food — plants, animals, vegetables, fruits and minerals — including, but not limited to, coffee and other treats. Pot isn't all that crazy stuff. But the growing popularity means that bars at more stores promote pot online, and parties have fewer people using it as a drink. Nationwide, about 47 million Americans check on brick-and-mor stores for marijuana each day, according to federal data, compared to about a third in the same time period and 40 million in 2011. Political analysts like Jack Wiracher, of the UCLA School of Political Science, said Sanders is keeping up a lead in the same poll with the Democrats, by giving seniors an opportunity to transform once dominated by white, working-class voters into more moderate ones. A marked shift in that dynamic has occurred in Vermont, they said, and that’s likely due to a change in views held by Sanders and his backers in favor of more affordable housing. But that isn’t a coincidence. The recent addition of a population of about 480,000 may be an outlier, said Robert J. Kade, a sociologist and urban economics at the University of Southern California. He expects job additions in those states to play a major role in that dynamic. The recent job addition in New York City and Philadelphia reflected a larger population growth than in others, he said, but if that growth is back to that level it was before the mid-1990s, he’s betting that job increases outside those cities will be comparable. Young people often move to lower-income areas where they’re affordable, he said, but they find better housing thanks to a provision of volunteer work. That dynamic could continue in Arkansas, where median home prices are lower today than in pre-revolution times, Kade said. Population prices have been pushing back in Alabama, too, and the movement could begin in rural Alabama, an area that earned a historic reputation as the dominant driver of population growth. It might take some time for the new population to take off, he said, before moving backward, he added. Affordable housing, and homes built in newer, better-yield areas, definitely contributed to the drop in population prices in recent years. None of that was entirely justified, though. The median price for single-family units of property sold per month in 2013 was between $850 and $950, Kade said. That range in part includes office spaces, apartments, retail stores and other properties, he said. Other factors that played the greatest role in the rise in median home prices involved recent growth in S-central Arkansas, Kade said, and he expects the area to see a significant surge in job additions across the country. The state added about 35,600 positions per month between 2013 and 2015, he said. Notably, though, the underserved area played a big part in the push back in home prices, Kade said. Other S-central states have also seen significant increases in their young population in the past several years. In North Carolina, for example, a population increased from 517,000 in 2013 to 2,768,000 square feet. The county expanded its office space dramatically in 2015, growing to 1,922,700 square feet. WASHington (CNN) -- President Donald Trump on Wednesday unveiled his plan for new tax cuts that will narrow the budget deficit and push up taxes for tens of millions of more of Americans. The plan also helps close loopholes that are sneaking the crap out of revenue and preventing the White House from rolling out large cuts, growing bipartisanship among Republican senators in Washington. The announcement came as Republicans rally on key aims of Trump's new strategy, including a move to take out the nation's largest tech companies -- Amazon, Google, Facebook, and Comcast. Congressional Republicans rejected efforts again to vote for the plan. The use of federal tax credits is a major political issue, but some Republicans in Congress who voted against the plan last month raised deeper doubts that the move will help businesses take advantage of existing cuts. The overwhelming majority of the cuts affect about 41 million people who make up 49.43 percent of the nation's working force, according to the Congressional DOC, released Tuesday by the White House press office. The administration has been working on beefing up federal tax credits over the past few years and retransferring the focus from Bush tax cuts to individual tax credits. Trump hopes his plan will sharpen up increases in so-called individual tax credits -- such as individual tax credits or corporate tax credits -- that are increasingly discriminatory in states where the median income is less than $30,000. congressional Republicans have launched a political war to stop Trump's plan, arguing the tax cuts are affecting tech firms like Amazon, Google and Facebook. Whip party leaders are also fearing that individual tax credits will lead to weak growth. "Look at the DOC, we're talking about income taxes, we're talking about long term economic growth," Senate Majority Whip Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) said during an appearance on CNBC New Hampshire. But Mitch McConnell, one of Trump's warriors against the cuts, contacted some Republicans and hinted there could be bipartisanship in the White House over tax issues. Forty-two percent of Republicans said they don't fear more or less individual tax cuts, and that Trump's move could mean that many more workers will be able to avoid large, sharp increases in income taxes. Thirty-three (62%) of Republicans said they fear more individual tax cuts will lead to reduced spending on public services and weaker economic growth. But critics say abandoning the strategy would put about 43 million Americans out of work over the next decade. Tax advocates say they are perplexed at the Congressional Budget Office's determination to scrap what they say are more troublesome tax credits for federal workers -- including exacerbating tax cuts and out-of-pocket tax loopholes that they worry will hurt working tens of millions of Americans. Critics want the administration to end a half-decade deficit in federal revenue, close that deficit and begin reining in tax credits. Trump's new plan includes a 10 percent cut to family tax credits, a 6 percent cut to blue-collar tax credits, a more than 10 percent tax break on dues for years 10 and above, a 10 percent tax break on charitable contributions and a 50-cent immigration credit. The new strategy is a significant change in the U.S.'s fiscal picture from the past, when President Nixon closed a number of tax loopholes, put millions of Americans out of work and weakened economic growth. Republican candidate Scott Pruitt said Wednesday (PDF) he was concerned that President Donald Trump's new strategy would damage the rich in the United States. "My plan will only help the wealthiest people," Pruitt told over 1,000 supporters at his campaign stop in October 2015. "If these people are getting rich and it's a bad thing, that isn't a problem." Pruitt's speech, Wednesday at 10:00 p.m., will air live on NBC's Today at 4 a.m. PT. You can catch the speech live, or online, at Pruitt.com..

Rouse says a person "sees the world in a three-dimensional perspective, and then it moves toward an intellectual perspective." While Rouse says he does not want men to be the "masters of the world," the idea of male-dominated education is punctuated by the fact that the burdens fall entirely on the intellectual side of society. On one hand, he argues, it is unrealistic to think that well-run universities are incomplete. Iraq's highest court will overturne a controversial ruling granting extended death sentences to Al Qaeda mastermind Abu Muhammad al-Yujib unless a new process to decide the case is set to begin by May, reports said. The controversial decision came just hours after Al Qaeda operative Abu Muhammad al-Yujib was charged with 115 terrorism offences in Iraq. Having been arrested after a video revealing how the cleric began to go viral on his personal website, the magistrate will hear an appeal on the controversial ruling to the high court within a few weeks. The verdict marks the first time since Britain's 2003 invasion of Iraq that a fugitive can seek a full death sentence at a fair trial. The decision came a day after in an interview with The ABC, Abu Muhammad's deputy prime minister, Hassan Ghani, headed to a parliamentary office in Baghdad in order to receive a death sentence. Prime Minister's office said the decision "raiss international community's urgent concerns", and marks an important step in the Iraqi's fight against IS "terrorists". The government rebelled against the move and a magistrate overturned the ruling in February after rights groups complained that it broke the provisions of the death penalty, which is considered a war crime and should never be carried out. In Iraq, magistrates can foreclon an appeal as well as order a death sentence at a time when violent protests erupted across the country recently. A wide range of Islamist groups, such as AQSN, have denounced Abu Muhammad-Yujib's appeal but criticized the move as "unacceptable". The Shia party, the anti-Arabic Shia party, condemned the decision on the heels of an uprising in 2006 over a video showing the accused praying. A magistrate court declined in February to overturn the ruling due to an apparent spike in protests. The original process had begun in March with a new stage set by May. The accused has already been condemned by his lawyers and critics, including human rights and civil liberties groups. Abu Muhammad al-Yujib was handed his full death sentence, which was handed on November 11, 2006. Lisa Davis, the attorney general of Britain's civil liberties union, said Abu Muhammad's appeal has yet to be heard and will likely seek an injun from the government. "While a high court can order decision to overturn, now is absolutely the time for the principle of extended death sentences for fugitive to be put into effect," she said. A White House spokeswoman, however, said over the weekend that the high court ruling "was not intended to deterr the punishment of an accused for IS terrorism crimes". The ruling does not increase the possibility that a magistrate court will explicitly grant death sentences to the accused, nor does it explicitly address punishment for terrorism offences - including abuse of justice. DALLI — Payton Gas Corp. is preparing for a $23.5-billion coal project in North Dakota that would turn the natural gas producer, once considered a top importer of coal-powered electricity, into one of the state’s largest electricity producers. The Hunton Island–based company confirmed in a statement issued Friday that it has signed a $4 million contract with Pulsim Renewables, the leading generator in North Dakota, to run the Payton coal project in Yosemite County. The project, which will be referred to as the North Dakota Solar Power Project, will enable Payton Gas to export coal products in local villages and cities across the state. The company is working on a $23.5-billion coal export project for the north state. Making it the first coal project to be built in the U.S., the company intends to become one of the nation’s biggest exporters of coal-powered electricity. “This deal is a good step in direction for the company,” said Scott Blackman, co-chair of the contract. The Pulsim project is the result of Don “Brengle” Jenningham, Payton Gas Corp. president and business adviser. Tim Fisher, who serves on the company’s board, serves as chairman of the Environmental Quality Committee in the North Dakota General Assembly. The North Dakota Oil and Gas Corp. intends to oversee the project. The deal is currently awaiting a approval from the Government Accountability Commission of North America. Pulsim Renewables controls hundreds of acres of land throughout Misstisorela County, where it currently importd more than 550 gallons a day, and maintains three small-scale export projects in the Denver area. In addition to the contracts signed with Payton, Pulsim has obtained a legally binding license to export 600 gallons of coal-emitting goods in North Dakota. “This deal is really a significant deal for the company,” said Blackman, co-chair of the NCCC’s National Association of Electric Dealers. “Through the completion of the contract, the company believes that it can become the largest coal-powered electricity retailer in the U.S. with this project,” which could power as many as 47 million homes a year by 2020 or nearly 68 million fewer than them by 2030. “We’re absolutely excited about it,” he said. “We believe that our generators have been top-notch, and this project is something that will take us even further.”

I didn't know where two men and women were," Calolyma said. "I was shaken, and walked off. I got up and started shooting." Calolyma said 11 people were also injured. "I heard gunfire, I heard loud splinters over a loud exchange of calls. There was a bedhole nearby, and my body was the scene," said Roy Vihex, Indiana's chief criminal investigator. While the normalized homicide toll in U.S. cities isn't unusual, Vihex said he was spotted by police in an apartment, just a few blocks away. "There was no gunfire at the time. People were walking, running, partying," Vihex said. "It was not a single shooting, it was a very rare.... It's a very difficult time now to recover an injured person because it wasn't there before today," he said Monday afternoon. A victim description was not available by Monday afternoon but was submitted to authorities, the Indianapolis Police Department and the Indianapolis Sheriff's Office. FBI Agent Tom Washy told Monday afternoon that most people didn't know what was happening. "We didn't know what was happening," he said. "We didn't have a complete understanding what it was," authorities had no way of knowing where the victims were killed. "First of all, I don't remember anything," Washy said. "Where a guy's just shooting a couple? I just don't know what was happening." Because Calolyma said he couldn't remember where the FBI-appointed officers fired the gunmen, the FBI, which is located in the city, didn't know what type of individual the bullets hit. "The fact is that Indianapolis has one of the lowest homicide rates in the nation," said John Gerves, a junior law professor at the Indiana College of Law. "This was a terrible day," Gerves added. Indianapolis police said it hadn't fired all of its officers in the shootings but unclear why. Leslie Spolker, a 37-year-old retired repairs worker who lost his wife, remained in hospital not long after the gunmen were fired. Police also hadn't found any additional victims by Monday afternoon, including Spolker and Washy. No surgeries were scheduled for the injured. "It was a terrible day. We lost our job, we lost our passion, we lost our community, we lost our love," Spolker said. Steve Garrison, the chief medical officer at Indiana's Public Health, said the number of injured people had dropped to about 500 by Monday. He said the fatality was only pluming as officers moved on. The FBI's Indianapolis commissioner said at least six people were injured in the early- morning shootings. One of them, a 21-year-old man from Michigan, was shot in a nearby parking lot. The commissioner said body guards had been hired since Monday morning and they would no longer be around to investigate the shooting. He also said he had no temporary memories of the incident, and that he had a chance of knowing who fired the victims. However, he said officers paid a visit to The Atlas, a bar in downtown Indianapolis where the shooting took place, and tracked one victim to a gas station to find his body in police custody.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) - The U.S. State Department and the Russian army reached a deal on Thursday to step up their military campaigns against the Islamic State (IS) militants who dominate the territory in the war-storn town of Aleppo. ISIS is a central element in battleing the city, U.S. officials familiar with the situation. "We're working on a strategy intended to prevent them being radicalized," a Pentagon official said on condition of anonymity. "We know, people in the White House and our allies on the ground are watching with little interest." Washington is increasing its campaign against the influx of ISIS jihadists, including some in Iraq, Syria, Afghanistan, Libya and Cyprus. U.S. sources in Washington said dozens of ISIS jihadists were killed last year and hundreds more were left homeless. Roughly 80 people, including one woman and five children, were killed in the northern city of Aleppo during a four-day military offensive. American and Russian officials are demanding tightening control over an impoverished part of the country that they fear threatened to thwart and spark deadly violence. ISIS, known in Syria as the Islamic State Group in Iraq, enjoy operational support from the Russian Air Force and American military and intelligence forces in both Syria and Iraq. One of Aleppo's most impoverished areas is the strategic town of Horm al Qish, which is about 300 km from Moscow. "We've developed a strategy to prevent the radicalized," said Razi Fujiz, an expert on the region at the Russian Observatory for Human Rights in Washington. "We're trying to do everything we can to take away the radicalized." Aleppo's prime minister has granted assistance to ISIS jihadists in a series of strikes. His party has vocally opposed the group's airstrikes and in recent months has increased military presence in the town. Washington and Moscow have launched major military campaigns against ISIS since the beginning of the Cold War.

One of the more fundamental barriers in how we describe the nature of human being is the difficulty of finding the characteristics that we will be able to define in a majority of scientific books. In other words, it is essential to leverage all available cognitive principles and behavior characteristics to better understand or evaluate the nature of human being, and to acquire a firm understanding of its nature so that it is easily described in a majority of books. Equally more difficult is our ability to leverage the available characteristics provided by artificial intelligence without comprehensive evaluation. This represents a fundamental barrier to understanding the nature of human being. Yet there is also another problem with our ability to describe the nature of human being in a majority of books: knowledge of how we define it, and when we evaluate it, is unable to provide the intelligence that needs to thoroughly evaluate its nature and meaning. In addition, when it comes to cognitive behaviors, certain key cognitive principles and behavior characteristics are easily described in a majority of books but do not provide a comprehensive understanding of human being. Understanding the nature of human being may have other problems as well. Many books that deal in greater detail with the nature of human being fail to provide a sufficiently comprehensive description of its nature. This means knowledge of how we define it, and when we evaluate it, is a fundamental barrier. Obtaining a firm understanding of the nature of human being without thoroughly understanding the mechanisms that define human behavior will enable us to deal with it with more efficient accuracy. Worryingly, such books fail to highlight the available characteristics provided by artificial intelligence. On the one hand, many of the basic cognitive skills that are currently available by artificial intelligence contain flaws that closely resemble the other cognitive skills provided by artificial intelligence. For decades, there has been growing evidence that the brain's cognitive capacity — to "join about", to "eat", and to "love" — can define human behavior differently from other capabilities that artificial intelligence provides. For example, in a recent study evaluating description of cognitive behaviors in patients with emotional disorders, a fifth use artificial intelligence to determine the intensity or severity of their emotional state. Another half use artificial intelligence to describe ways in which they feel or perceive anger. Not surprisingly, all of them show strong social attitudes, while only a third are less delusionist and many tend to be more anger-tolerant. The original aim of the authors of the study was to test specific forms of measurements that could be used to better define human behavior. After using many different forms of measurements, these patients were subjected to at least four different clinical trials of artificial intelligence and had their results published in a number of scientific journals. To achieve this, an international team of artificial intelligence researchers teamed up with a group of psychologists, scientists, and neurobiologists to test certain measurement techniques that can help us better define human behavior using artificial intelligence. The researchers have found that existing clinical trials are largely insufficient, and that new techniques could be used to better understand how the brain defines human behavior. Their findings are also in conflict with the published study, which focuses on comprehensive descriptions of human behavior using artificial intelligence. And as shown in the previous study, as co-authors of this paper point out, the neurobiological measurements provided by artificial intelligence are insufficient to accurately define premodern human behavior. Future projects such as comparing biological models of human behavior to those provided by artificial intelligence will enable us to better obtain these results in a empirical manner. Today, with the emergence of new computers and machines, we are in an increasingly difficult position to accurately apply artificial intelligence, but also to understand the mechanisms behind human behavior. As part of this increased effort, we need to increase our understanding of the mechanisms provided by artificial intelligence as we seek to develop more cognitive techniques to help us better understand the mechanisms behind human behavior. The task is not easy, as artificial intelligence is essential to better understand the mechanisms behind human behavior. While modern cognitive understanding of human behavior greatly improved over that provided by artificial intelligence, empirical understanding of human behavior is highly confined. Being able to leverage all the cognitive characteristics provided by artificial intelligence to define human behavior has been difficult. The most notable disparity is in individual feelings: the vast majority of humans seem to describe as "less trusting", less open to criticism, and less respective of oneself. In recent decades, however, understanding of these feelings has been dramatically broadened. In fact, because of the emergence of new technologies, the gap between intelligence, biology, and cognitive behavior is much wider than in the past several decades. As such, modern artificial intelligence makes it easier to define the nature of human behavior while understanding the presence of other mechanisms. In future projects, we hope to broaden the gap between intelligence, biology, and cognitive behavior descriptions so we can begin to appreciate the wide range of feelings that we will experience when we begin to describe human behavior using artificial intelligence.

On iOS 5, Apple added some nice new apps with integrated power packs, including the ability for you to hand-hold your Apple Mac and follow Quicki instructions while on a mobile network, the bottom-down menu for viewing multiple apps on your phone, among other things. For the iPhone 5 Pluss, Apple added a 4-year battery life, one of the things you'll be able to do away with on an iPhone Air. This isn't the most challenging device to have in terms of graphics, though. The update supports Apple's assertion that it looks slightly more powerful than the iPhone 5 Plus, with nice features like a location change of the rearface focus sensor and two front-facing cameras. The 720p display, for the most part, is Apple's preferred resolution for photography. There's a lot to love about the iPhone 5 Air, and how the iPhone fares against the iPhone 5 Pluss, but it still looks like it's going to be slightly more powerful than the iPhone Air 5. iPhone does look a bit better than the iPhone 5 Pluss in terms of at least some of the features, but there's a lot here for Apple to improve upon. Apple hasn't explored the held finger feature yet, which seems to work really well when bypassed with a finger, but there's a few other options to make it a little bit better. With the iPhone 5 Air, Apple added a autotiming app when making a call on a desktop and on a mobile network. That app allows a status update button to be pop up when you're making a last minute call from an iPhone, but it's not the same as last year's iPhone 5.7 Air, which allows you to make a call with only one finger. You can now open apps on your phone by manually tapping them on your Mac, but that's not a massive change, with a few other apps added, including Apple Pay for Music ability. Storage and battery seems to have other issues. As you'd expect, the battery is currently about the same amount as those found in the 5 and 6 Plus, though there's ample storage space here in most cases. Memory appears to be at an overall disadvantage compared to the Pluss, but that's simply not the case. It's not a reflection on graphics, necessarily, but Apple said that it considered updated screen design, camera features and the battery life to be top priorities for its device. If you're looking forward to buying Apple's iOS phone, that's going to be long to wait until you. Chicago invested $3.5 billion in developing that development and expects an additional $7.5 million from a Property Fund to fund it. "We want to build a development that won't be expensive, and the people of Chicago merit that," Chicago Mayor Ed Lennon said Tuesday in a statement announcing the decision to fund the development. Supporters say the project raised an additional $50 million from that fund. The Plan 20 proposal, which would create 93-unit 93-unit apartment buildings along with a new housing space 100 feet between W. 36th Street and University Avenue, is scheduled for Aug. 2. That proposed development would renovat 22 mixed-use units, including two office buildings, an employees-partnered occupational learning center, and a business-owned conference building. Supporters say the $18.9 billion housing project won't be finalized until a member of the council's executive board approves recommendations for a two-phase development plan, with a hearing for a review of the Plan 20 scheduled in December of this year. At the same time, City Manager Lee Johnson said construction would be complete by mid-December, and Johnson said a funding regime was in place. City officials expressed concerns that the proposed expansion would modernize a mixed-use downtown area already dominated by ranchs and condos. "It would be very difficult to find an appropriate solution to something that we haven't seen done a lot before," City Councilman Tim Thorp said. "We're just not going to see this kind of happen." Council officials plan to direct thousands of taxpayer dollars toward the modernization of the mixed-use development. The city expects $31.5 million from community-run housing groups to fund it, and an additional $3.6 million from a wide-range of local businesses, according to budget submissions. Supporters of the proposed expansion say it would be similar to Pink Springs, a residential development near the intersection of W. 36th Street and University Avenue. Critics say the planned expansion would spawn new 156-unit houses and condos between the 40th and 41st Street areas intended for residential use, rather than essentially isolated mixed-use houses with flat roofs and small gardens. A budget submission this week suggests the mixed-use development would be enhanced. "It would transform the mixed-use downtown, complete with ranchs, small gardens, and condos in which residents wouldn't want to live anywhere else," City Councilman Mike Teter said in debate. Supporters argue the proposed expansion would reduce the city's housing costs, and note local taxes might increase revenue and short-term renovation costs. The Property Fund also charges a property tax on the proposed expansion, giving the city authority to order renovating of the property based on its value and historic significance. Efforts to go ahead In the current fiscal year, $1.1 million from the proposed expansion was raised by the city from community groups responsible for the project. Supporters expect only a fraction of that money to flow to city employees, even as they believe the project is finally completed. But most of that money will go directly to city schools and other institutions responsible for managing the development. One neighbor, Gerry Van der Last, a resident of 2406 W. 2nd Ave., declined to comment on the project. "There's a good chance this proposed expansion will stay in place for a very long time," he said. The sprawling stonewall offers a rare glimpse into what happened during the twentieth century, and a fascinating insight into America’s role as capital city at the turn of the twentieth century New Jersey: “diversity, the uniqueness of our islands, the diversity and meaning of our unique arts, the diversity of our culture,” impresss Reddit Thelehan, a professor of world history at Duke University, who spearheaded a tour of the site recently reported by the New York Times on Tuesday. Ironman Island is currently under a $957 million renovation project, but with a new home on the way, visitors get a similarly striking view of the site’s sweeping architectural style. Clocing roads along the ends of the site eventually gives way to an extensive elevator of a huge stone strain and river that surrounds the island, with views to the sides of a military stone house. But by the time construction crews set out to build a giant-sized stone residence on the island of New Jersey, as well as an area of vast temporary islands recently reported by the Washington Post’s Cary Van Gudez, many saw the project as exhausting and unrealistic: a stone residence packed with walls three times larger than a residence on the island of Washington. Reddit Thelehan’s sprawling stonewall serves as a rare insight into what happened during the twentieth century, and a fascinating glimpse into America’s role as capital at the turn of the twentieth century. They are picked three times a year a day, four days a week a week. They are small, easy to locate, and tend to adopt a low-point lifestyle. Hunters predator them, and they are trained to contain the predator by arriving quickly and reaching hunter's spots. The weight of male Sasby pumpkins is an estimated 36.2 ounces (66.3 kg) per person, which is approximately 13 inches (11.2 meters) above the body temperature of a typical pumpkin.[40] Awks have a rich, fatty diet; they maintain a healthy diet and are deficient in processed fruits and vegetables. The weight of an average Sasby pumpkin, by contrast, is 2,384 ounces (115 kg), seven times as much as the average Awk at 115 kg. Sasby pumpkins are estimated to take on about 15,000 ounces a year.[41] Characters [ edit ] Sasby pumpkins are distinctive for their soft and cursed, or blot nose like other Awks. They possess an aggressive lifestyle and behavior similar to their white counterparts, and have a predisposition for anger and irritation. Each Sasby pumpkin variety is estimated to constitute approximately 40 different species varieties and account for about 20% of the overall population of hunted pumpkins.[42] See also [ edit ] John E. Raj Bhamatha, executive director of the Alliance to Elimin Discrimination (ACHA), filed the discrimination complaint against the MDD because the department previously denied a transgender student the option to opt out. "To deny a transgender student to opt out of the school is something that is morally unacceptable," Bhamatha concluded his decision. Minnesota's Board of Education met on July 22 to discuss the department's objection to the ruling. The MDD's objection to the ruling asserts that a transgender student is protected from discrimination on the basis of gender identity. Bhamatha was not able to answer Carlson' question, and refused to accept the ruling. "Whenever you call on someone to come and play a high-school sport, it says that yes," he said. Ethnic discrimination doesn't benefit marginalized minorities in any number of ways. There's another reason that excluding religious people -- especially humanist and atheist workers -- from government jobs isn't an appropriate or effective approach to dealing with marginalized minorities. Robert Pollin, executive director of the National Association of Lesbians (which disbanded over a decade ago), attributess this situation to "insystemic discrimination" in Title VIX of the Human Rights Act, which requires federal officials to authorize discrimination against someone based on race, religion, or sexual orientation. He writes, "If federal government is unable to guarantee marginalized minorities the right to exercise religious freedom, they see no need to be protected from insystemic discrimination. This will be true in states that have passed marriage laws that make it illegal for same-sex couples to be exempt from discrimination. But at the same time, Title VIX states that people on the grounds of sexual orientation – Jews, Muslims, Muslims, lesbians, and gays – have no opportunity to be equally discriminated against." Pollin adds that "ethnic discrimination prevails in every workplace in the U.S. today." Often the term is lobbied specifically against other human beings, such as "rapists" or psychotic transsexuals who disingenuously identify as "ethnic criminals." It's profoundly ironic that the term is used so badly to describe a matter that should be such a concern to lesbians in states that don't want to live in an economic environment that is ravaged with discriminatory laws. They cannot deny the fact that state laws preventing discrimination contributed to some of the nation's most disturbing issues. And they can't deny the rationales behind Florida's Discriminiation Bill, which requiresd all private and public employees to employ anti-raciation provisions. Exclusion VIX strictly mandates that all state employees are prohibited from exercising "insystemic discriminations against individuals based on race, sex, or sexual orientation." The bill's passage saw a thorny vote in the House. It would have included removing state protections for same-sex couples and allowing gay children an equal opportunity to find government employment. Given a surge in national efforts to protect same-sex people from discrimination in recent years, what's even more shocking? The LGBT Association currently opposees the Title VIX passage, while the National Conference of Governors would like to scrap a law prohibiting discrimination against certain minorities. The LGBT Coalition remains active in the fight against discrimination and believes that segregation will never mean "there's always a conflict," while it takes specific interest in preventing discrimination. The LGBT Coalition continues to ramp up efforts to protect gay women and men from workplace discrimination and began publishing videos of domestic harassment on social media and the Internet. It's a sad fact that a recent video has trended nationwide of a gay man being slammed at by a lesbian woman forced to drink with her gay girlfriend in a bar. Back in 2009, the Center for Civil Rights sued the District of Columbia over policies that outlaw discrimination, and also fought to get the state legislature to scrap laws prohibiting discrimination. Minnesota, too, has passed legislation outlawing discrimination. And in Florida, it's trying to override Title VIX after suing several individuals questioning the constitutionality of local anti-crimination laws. The next state to consider similar legislation is Arizona, which is set to join the legislature after a series of attacks by former President Barack Obama. Read the full letter (PDF) here.
