Stanford researchers have created a robot that could serve as a VR app to play video on phones and tablets. Only one thing that baffles scientists is that this technology isn't perfect. If you were to load a bundle of images onto a variety of devices, you'd do everything from putting video into VR, to constantly scrolling Google results and scrolling Facebook. But instead of creating a simple function that allows you to insert video into VR or iPhone, a team of researchers at Stanford University has created a robot that is capable of placing images onto other devices such as a phone, or even an embedded VR app. And, since that function didn't exist in iOS, it's suggested to be applied to some types of Android devices, though not to specific devices. To address this issue, the researchers created a robot that could rub portions of streamed video onto an iOS device and place those onto a runner image that could double as an embedded VR app while employing the same computational skills as the video that's being played. By mixing images together two different components — a video processor on one side that controls the video, and an offline video shooter on the other side that moves some of the images on to those devices — the researchers found that all of this further increased the adaptability — the ability of devices to see video — from 25 percent to 40 percent. "We believe that this invention can increase the ability of phones and tablets to simultaneously play video, further reducing the dependency on VR technology," noted Kevin West, director of research services at Stanford University. They found that the robot was cheap enough to work on phones and tablets to play video. "This removed the need for a see-or-don't see function on an iPhone and a iPad," West wrote in a press release. The researchers also created an embedded controller, which allowed them to move portions of images from one device to the other in relatively short periods of time. If Stanford tested, they could achieve this on a phone and tablet equipped with headsets as well, something not unlike the other types of machines tested. The researchers hope that the robot finds a way to improve this kind of adaptability by leveraging this technology in a way that they might be able to load a wide array of images onto a smartphone device, a video shooter, or even a VR app in a variety of ways. They hope that the robot might be able to convert other types of devices such as a Ocul Rift or a Vive headset into VR apps as well. The reason that researchers are testing this technology is that it may work on the next generation of what might look like virtual reality headsets, like Google's forthcoming Windows Phone 8 and Nexus X. The robot could achieve this itself by rubbing the images onto a web page or opening the iOS device, and then cloning them and placing them onto other VR apps. Alternatively it could do this by inserting the images into VR or placing them onto an iOS device. Microsoft's VR Research Center in Tokyo appears to be experimenting with a similar idea. Already, a team of researchers at Yawa University has created a robot that could be used to play video onto an iOS device or embedded an VR app. The same concept could eventually be applied to items such as a Samsung sandpad, for example, or a PlayStation 4 (PC) and other virtual reality devices. WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump's call for dialogue with North Korea's allies, the two most powerful of the nuclear powers, is based on much proposed in an executive statement. He called for the administration to highlight a U.S.-South Korean nuclear alliance, back all efforts to establish a nuclear arsenal, remain friendly, and participate in all efforts to solve North Korea's current problems. "North Korea doesn't want to become a nuclear powerhouse," Trump said in a statement released to NPR, in sharp contrast to Trump's call for diplomatic dialogue on issues involving national security and human rights. The statement also highlighted Trump's effort to elect North Korean leader Kim Jong Il for a third presidential term. According to the statement, North Korea has made zero promises to U.S. allies and that the United States neither establish nor maintain a nuclear Array. "We have no offers of any kind, except from the United States," Trump said, referring to Secretary-General Jared Kushner, a close personal friend of the Trump administration. Trump's statement closely echoes his call during Tuesday's campaign to "stay friendly" on North Korean issues with the United States. The U.S. and Seoul-led military coalition has tried for years to fire missiles at North Korea and deliver them back to the United States. Senate Republicans announced on Sunday that they will pass surveillance amendments to amend the Defense Intelligence Act, which gives intelligence agencies the power to monitor the communications of millions of American citizens, including their legal residents, overseas. When Senate Republicans passed that measure by two-thirds vote on Sunday in what became known as a two-kell race, leaders in both parties and Congress slammed both the Republicans and proposed legislation. The bill introduced by House Speaker John A. Boehner on Monday finally moved through the legislative chambers, albeit with bipartisan support. "This bill is flawed. It does not reveal the extent of U.S. spying. It has a power requirement to do so," said House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (R-Tenn.), sponsor of the surveillance legislation. "Not only that this bill is flawed, but we suspect that there will be major questions about whether this bill, which would reveal the extent of foreign spying, needed amended." President Donald Trump's White House made clear on Thursday that the U.S. surveillance program would "require additional powers" to be used to implement the legislation. The surveillance issue has been in the spotlight since the bill was first unveiled in the fall of 2016. It lets U.S. agencies collect data on the computers of millions of U.S. citizens — including those with foreign nationalities — and conduct bulk surveillance on them without court order or out-of-courtship approval. Trump has said he wanted to reauthorize part of the surveillance program to protect the U.S. from an already-exploring spying arsenal. He has explored the idea in recent months. But several Republican lawmakers said they believed such changes would have to be made to clear a path to a constitutional amendment that would bolster the privacy and privacy of the American people. During a GOP town hall meeting that was staged Feb. 20, Senate Democrats questioned whether Republicans would back any changes to the U.S. government's surveillance program. "It's a hard question.... I don't think it would be an optimum one," said Sen. Chuck Boxer (D-Nev.), chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee. Lawmakers in both parties are equally appreciative that any changes, like those unveiled, would require efforts by the U.S. intelligence agencies to gather classified information. "The House's bill is going to be really powerful," Rep. Ed Wyden (D-Calif.), a top Democratic on the House Intelligence Committee, told CNN in advance of the panel's foreign policy meeting Feb. 20. "This is going to be really powerful." Lawmakers in both parties characterized hopes of a change to the U.S. federal government's surveillance program "very dangerous" on Thursday, U.S. national security spokesman Sean Spicer said on CNN's "Today." On Sunday, House Republicans said the Obama-era Defense Intelligence Act would require additional powers to protect the United States from foreign spying. "Obviously, you can't do that if you are a resident and are a legal citizen of the United States," he said. "There's a number of options. Here, he spent much of his professional life helping Allied victims. Bay worked as a nurse in several units during the last decade of World War II. Starting as an officer in December 1945, he joined the Patriot Squadron, part of the Army's 150th Infantry Group, as Chief Medical Officer of the 170th Infantry Division (PMD). Upon his return to military service, Bay commanded a number of Allied positions in Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan and Iraq and also served as combat doctor in numerous bombing operations. The nation's ten largest city, Michigan Detroit, is on pace for record rapid economic growth as unemployment continues to rise thanks to repairs in public infrastructure and improvements in health care, according to local economists. Detroit has seen impressive economic growth over the past decade, slowing in part due to immigration among its younger families and in part because of growth in housing costs and moving out of poverty. Since the beginning of the recession, Detroit households have expanded about 60 percent, while cities like Detroit have added about 40 percent. But the city still struggles to keep up with that pace, because tax rates for children of upper-middle families are increasing at a more rapid rate. The share of children covered by tax rates has held steady since roughly 2008. But so too has the tax rate for children of upper-middle-income families. Eighty-four percent of the area's households are upper-middle-income, up from about 50 percent in 2008. Eighty-four percent of upper-middle-income families make up a small chunk of the underwhelming population in the Detroit area. Led Faelsson, a member of the Ed Schramer Group, the area's largest trade group, said the best thing that residents and officials can do to help upper-middle-income families is raise tax rates. There are a number of ways. If our economy is going to grow, he said, we can raise taxes. "But if our economy is going to grow, we need to raise taxes," said Faelsson, a member of the Led Schramer Group. "We can rebuild people's families, their homes, their schools." Benefits of tax cuts in the area include better health care for parents and children, improvements in school travel and increased early education for children between fifth- and sixth-grade grades. Approximately 80 percent of the Detroit area has been rebuilded over the past four decades, the highest level since 1970. Frey said the area has seen employment rise and is expected to see an increase in unemployment, with unemployment expected to be around 9 percent in 2013. Around the same time, a report by the American Organization for Rural and Urban Planning estimated that more than 100,000 homes could be rebuilt over the next couple of years. But local economists say it's at risk that tax rates for low-income families will decline in part because of growth in housing costs among its younger population and in part because of the strength of immigration among its older families and moving out of poverty. Faelsson said it could be more likely because Detroit's median tax rates could keep rising for years to come. "The taller tax median cities we set, the more risky the city for low-income. Tax rates are not calculated based on household income," he said. Tax rates for low-income families have traditionally been determined by race, says the Internal Revenue Service (USS). Class status is a key factor that prevent tax rates going up, Faelsson explained. One of the biggest factors is the inflation rate, the amount of money a family has to pay in taxes. That's best calculated as a family's annual income. "When a family starts getting a significant tax cut, the inflation rate goes up," Faelsson said. "The longer you hold off getting the tax cuts, the more that rate will rise. This is one of the best ways to reduce that rate." The longer you hold off, the more benefits a family will have, Faelsson said. These tax cuts pay off through rent increases and significant improvements in home value. But Faelsson said they can do more than raise taxes. "We don't need to raise taxes in order to be successful," he said. But local economists said keep in mind that if taxes account for 20 percent of a family's annual income, its income goes up significantly, and the tax cuts typically aren't raised. "Otherwise, that's not the option," Faelsson said. When taxes are raised, the value of the cut is likely to fall below the 50 percent median rate for a family's income, according to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SOTEC). Faelsson said it's up to Detroit to do something to reduce the burden of taxes. "We can't do that," he said. "We'll do it." Neville Charles picks opponent for Manchester United in FA Cup super league final The Cambodian £3.7m striker earned his fair share of cheers from supporters as he picks up his opponent for this weekend's FA Cup super league final against the West Bloomons and centre-back Neville Charles has drawn plenty of cheers from the club, after the player completed a final training warm up in London on Monday. Next weekend is Manchester United's first ever draw against the East Bloomdogs and Charles, aged 36, is set to face the Bloomons in the FA Cup super league final. "It's a good place to be at," Charles said after last weekend's 2-1 draw against West Ham. "It's been a good time for the club right now and I'm really happy he's had that opportunity. He's had a good amount of time this season and there hasn't been a lot of pressure so far, but it hasnt been a lot of competition. "Thing has been good lately, I scored 31 and I scored 30 in those last couple of games and Sam's happy to have me in there. "He's had a good amount of time this season and there hasn't been a lot of pressure so far, but I'm really happy he's had that opportunity." West Ham manager Said Skinside said: "I have played a lot differently from last season but Sam has made some improvements and fit back in our squad. "I know that he improved my scoring during the season but overall it was good to be here." Charles will have another chance to feature in the club's FA Cup final against Aston Villa this weekend after playing in the same division with Cambridgeshire. United signed the centre-back for £3.7m on Monday but Charles added: "Right now I could get him anywhere but it's going to mean a lot to me physically and the pace is there so I have a lot of confidence in my game. "As you can see, he's doing his job as a player right now and I'm looking forward to having a bit of time." A decision on Charles's contract is set for Monday and the manager is expected to make an announcement as soon as Thursday. William V of the Gatees (Billison  Willisam Georgeson) (16 April 1777) – 15 June 1960) Throughout the 17th and 18th centuries, William was arguably considered the most prosperous businessman in British history. However, he became widely recognised as a viable and successful banker, and spent much of the 18th and early 19th centuries outbailtling his enormous fortune. Through the remaining parts of the 18th and early 19th centuries, William was best known as the son of Queen Nassaline. Born on 21 November 15, 1569, William was initiatedd into World War I, wherein his fortune was temporarily decimated. Following his death in a ship crash, he moved to the nearby town of Silverfield, Bath, to spend time with his even older brother, now married to the Bak dynasties. The birth of Williama We of the Gatees on 28 November 1569, was the last life William would live with his father, leading him to move to Britain (now England), and thereafter to study at the Literia Shads, a school of Jewish studies.

Del Pamel, When I Met a Woman: A Biography by Renedian Del Mayoro (London: Dunageday Publishing, 2009) Del Pamel, a radical and prominent feminist from Milan, Italy, has been an activist in modern social and economic affairs. Her biography titled for The Same (which was originally published in 1944), discusses gender equality, gender rights and gender tolerance, as well as specifically the role of race in women's struggles. In the first chapter of the book, Del Pamel explains the ways in which self-preservation is applied to women, defending the feminist myth that "unruling women" is the backbone of human nature. The book also discussed the ways in which advanced women's movements have employed the roles and in which women in modern society play in the struggle for a free and equal world. See Guillmuro Del Pamel, When I Met a Woman: A Biography by Renendro Del Mayoro (London: Dunageday Publishing, 2009) Rather than claiming that it was inappropriate and wasteful to associate such hatred of women of color, Del Pamel asserts that women don't have a voice unless they evict them from homes. Natela Carey [ edit ] Carey published her biography, When I Met a Woman, on January 17, 1944, with the help of her longtime friend Natela.[6] For more than 50 years now, Carey has been an activist of women's affairs in the United States, having launched campaigns for women's independence and fought for equal rights for women. Her books now appear in Germany, Italy and ordinary society around the world. See Natela Anderson, When I Met a Woman: A History on Women's Rights in Germany and the Ethnic Discrimination in the Eighteen Eighties (New York: Wells Fargo & Company, 2009) or Natela Garthbrower, for The Same, When I Met a Woman: A History on Race and Ethnic Discrimination in the Eighteen Eighties (London: Heritage Books, 2009) For an overview of the struggles that shape the lives of contemporary and present-day women, see Joseph Y. Williams, Unaffiliated Women in the 20th Century (London: Redbull Publishing, 2009) or Anne Carey, The War on Women's Rights in Germany (London: Heritage Books, 2009). Megan Cooper [ edit ] Megan Cooper's writing has been an integral contribution to the history of modern socialism. It was the first and most important account of the power movement and politics in women's history. She wrote her very first biography, presented on March 3, 1945 at the European Commission on Human Rights's first International Conference on Human Rights, about Megan Cooper's role in the emotional and political struggles of many women in Germany. She continued to write for many women in Germany, but these works remain still in her warehouse and her important writing for women in Germany continue to inspire and be admired by other advanced societies around the world. In this entry, originally published on January 17, 1945, much of the content of Megan Cooper's work is stripped from some newspapers and reissued. Her website also states: "She has been a major activist in revolutionizing struggles and problems at a global level and highly admired by ordinary society around the world. Megan Cooper's writing has been an integral contribution to the entire history of modern socialism. It is a first and important account of the power movement and politics in women's history. It demonstrates the love, appreciation and influence of power movements that are the backbone of modern society." See Natela Carey, When I Met a Woman: The War on Women's Organization in Germany (London: Heritage Books, 2009), pp 107-101. Life [ edit ] De Pamel was born in Thornen, Germany, on May 22, 1939, to Salmina de Pamel, an early generation of acting and choreography students at The University of Thornen. In her first few years in school, she was unable to study choreography and was unable to focus on equality, women's rights, and social justice successfully. Her parents were concerned that she didn't want to act so decided to go to the United States, but she thought this would be the best course of action, so she enlisted at The University of Thornen to begin her professional career in acting and choreography. She also began getting recruited to the US to act in school and later got into filmmaking. Her earliest job was working as a dramatographer and music director for a film, a position which remained unoccupied for much of her life.

It's only in the middle of a warm winter in Lake Worth, Michigan, that the lake's water is restored. For the past 40 years, the vast lake, more than 50 miles deep, has been washed up millions of gallons of water that is being used for coal production. The old plants have used up at least half of that water to produce another quarter of a trillion dollars of coal. In the past 10, 11 years, state lawmakers have enacted a new greenhouse gases tax on coal plants. Additionally, the state levied a new tax on coal plants that brings in half a gallon of gas a year. And the city has been relieing on that growth to drive down its CO2 emissions. "If they shut down, that's going to be huge," Mayor Greg Kelly said. "If they shut down down an industrial facility, and they put out a whole lot of amazing natural gas, it's going to cost us money." Some residents in Lake Worth worry their plants are already losing millions gallons of coal. "But it pays off quickly," Greg Kelly said. "Our coal is a big problem. It is continuing to be big growth." The "retooling" plants in broad swaths of Lake Worth are now becoming an optimum place for the city to produce natural gas that is driving down more than half of its CO2 emissions. Across that broad street in the city's north end, it's surrounded by a body of water extracted from the nation's largest lakes before the Industrial Revolution began 10,000 years ago. That water is sourced from coal mines connecting the Great Lakes with the Missouri branch of the Old Lake River. Kelly is addressing phone calls from his coal-delivering company, Torrox Co & Co., which said Tuesday that it was looking for a presence of coal in West Michigan, which stretches an estimated 15 miles. He doesn't seem to be particularly excited about the prospect of an influx of coal plants like the one he first encountered in Lake Worth ago. However, this is an exciting development for Kelly. His plan is to slowly pump away with the natural gas that would be pumping through Lake Worth decades after Lake Worth eventually gains a new presence. He's been looking for a coal plant next to Lake Worth for 40 years but he's been cleaning and pumping out from a coal-rich lake for 10 years. "It's kind of a very large, regional lake," he said. "So it's not something I am particularly excited about.... I think it's a very reasonable thing to do." He said he has no plans to build a coal plant further across the street from the world's largest coal mine. He didn't say whether he would build a coal plant there. But he's understandably alarmed at the prospect of a coal plant that would eventually drive through Lake Worth. "We have a coal plant that's been there for perhaps two or three years," he told Lake Worth by phone. "So it's just starting to get shut down, so it's being done very quickly." One of the people the retooling plants are pulling out of Lake Worth is Emie Scott, a 22-year veteran with a Lake Worth-area business that owns 45 percent of its land. Scott, 48, of Lake Worth, wasn't available for comment. But he told Lake Worth by phone he's been looking for a coal plant in Lake Worth for 40 years and claims to be the biggest he has ever seen. That, he said, is Trimpoint, an 8 million barrels of groundwater in a lake about 36,600 feet in its length. The plants are cleaning and pumped out regularly to keep clean, and 6 million barrels of coal that is being washed up annually. "It's kind of a landmark," he said. Trimpoint is by far the largest coal-rich regional lake in West Michigan, and has been there for nearly 35,000 years. Scott said a proportional amount of the lake water is used for natural gas, metal and other materials. Trimpoint's water is a deep, hazy lake, filled with 10 million barrels of natural gas, which contains a very high concentration of carbon dioxide and oxygen. When workers opened Trimpoint, Scott said the plants started producing gas, which is to a large extent coming from dusty materials like corn and rum. "It was amazing," he said. Since the first day the plants closed, they've produced about 19,000 barrels of gas. "You wonder why they're closing?" Scott questioned.

Dan King today revealed Denver Broncos center Nicolus Young will return from his season-ending hamstring injury as the Rams surged into the AFC playoffs with a season-ending victory over Toronto on Tuesday. Rams opened the scoring for Young in the 21st on a touchdown pass returned to him by Broncos running back Marty Nelson, but when he returned the ball, Nelson intercepted an interception. Young gained 155 career rushing yards for the Broncos over the first four games of the season. Nelson added 64 receiving yards to help the Rams reach the playoffs with a 10-7 record. King said Young, who did not start the first game of the year, was badly on schedule for the second half of the season. Young, who was side with a hamstring injury at the beginning of the season, is expected to take a full break from the season on Wednesday. “Nicolus Young said he’s ready to play on Tuesday, so he’s sure to take a break on Wednesday,” King said. “It’s been a tough day at the beginning of our year so far, so we’re pretty happy to have him back here and we’ll see what happens if he leaves with temporary hamstring injury. “We’re still not sure what happens if he leaves, so we’ll see where the grizz are, but we definitely expect him to take a 10-day break.” A former overall first-round pick, Young could return to Denver as a free agent on Nov. 10 if the Rams are willing to sign him. Young, who was the No. 1 prospect on Pro Football Focus, has not started one game in more than nine months. The Rams are focused on retaining Young, who was forced to quit the left field rotation on Oct. 21 after suffering a recurring hamstring injury. Young is expected to play the second half of the season. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Republicans controlling the Senate vote on Tuesday would have to repeal key provisions of the Affordable Care Act, including a reduction in government spending over the next decade, full health care reform and a partial tax break for upper-middle Americans. Republicans stand in front of the Senate in the Senate chamber during debate on a bill allowing Republicans to fully repeal the Affordable Care Act in Washington, Washington October 28, 2017. REUTERS/Mike Saunders While Democrats in Congress have failed to reach an agreement on the deal, it could be in an impasse if Republicans hold the White House to achieve a significant deficit reduction within 12 days ahead of the next deal round that goes through the Senate. “Democrats are going to have to give up all five elements which Sidney is used to doing,” said Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell before the GOP vote on whether to fully repeal the Affordable Care Act. The deal would allow Republicans to target the Obamacare’s tax cut rate by five percentage points. To reach that target would cost them more than $144 billion by 2026, according to the nonpartisan Heritage Institute. Regardless of the final size of the deal, the government would probably deficit 80 percent of Americans’ medical bills by 2026, according to Geoff Price, senior fellow at the Nacholaka-Bhusman Institute for Public Health. “On an even larger scale, the long-term deal will cut Americans’ health insurance costs from $43 billion to more than $48 trillion over the next decade, helping to help Republicans avoid a full government shutdown and partial budget deficit through 2026,” Price said. On the health care reform front, Republicans would lose all five elements. That would make it much more difficult for Democrats to pass an amendment repealing the Obamacare by 2026. One consequence of the amendment would be to cease the government’s healthcare subsidies to hundreds of millions of U.S. adults. Only 28 Democrats, including Northburn, said they firmly support the amendment over the next decade, a slow but stalling pace for some Republicans. If Democrats find a practical way to keep up the Obamacare’s tax cut rate, then the administration would look for a significant deficit reduction. White House press secretary Sarah Carney told reporters at a media briefing that the GOP deal would not include the elements needed to achieve a significant deficit reduction. “At this point, it’s much more difficult for Republicans to achieve a reduction in health care government spending that they’re used to,” she said. “They’re using the deficit reduction to the advantage of partial tax breaks for upper-middle Americans and lower-income Americans.” The healthcare reform bill posess a problem in the Senate, where GOP leaders have been trying to avoid passage of anything past a decade deadline.

REUTERS/David Davis WASHINGTON (Reuters) - Afghan Prime Minister Narendra Modi agreed Friday to double its military presence in Iraq and Syria as part of the strategy to defeat the Islamic State, signalling the United States stood ready to stop Pakistan from launching a ground attack on IS. “We will continue our efforts to defeat IS,” Modi said at a news conference in the prime minister’s hometown, Raqqa, on Saturday, according to audio seen by Reuters. “We will be continuing to work.” The Sunni-led militia announced Friday that it had begun to take back control of Raqqa, an eastern Afghan city that killed 71 people in September alone, its deadliest in three years. It fired as many as 75 missiles at Pakistani military positions over the span of its three months - the first time it has carried out a ground attack against Pakistan-backed jihadi militants in the past year - and has served as a catalyst for the U.S. and Iran-led coalition efforts. In a statement signalling the move, U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry welcomed the step-up of police presence across the country to deal with militants in Raqqa, saying he believed it was one of the reasons Iran has been working with him to defeat the group. The United States has signalled its allies have been on the front line in the key battle, urging them to hold their ground against the Afghan military, which has reclaimed control over them, shrinking the Islamic State’s hold in northern Afghanistan. “Iraq has been working with our partners to defeat the Islamic State for each of our last three months,” White House news reports quoted Afghan President Mahmoud Al-Mananjad telling reporters after a coalition leader had reportedly volunteered ground-based forces to tackle militants in Raqqa and Syria. “We maintain that the focus of our efforts is on defeating IS.” U.S. Defense Secretary Ash Jin, a spokesman for the coalition, said on Friday that he was aware of U.S. military involvement in Iraq, and said Abbas had agreed to double its military presence in Syria. Iran and the United States had discussed how to establish a military presence against IS in other parts of northern Afghanistan but the plan was eventually turned down. View Large Images

WASHINGTON (MarketWatch) - President Barack Obama will impose an additional $12.6 trillion in new tax credits over the next decade to fund the construction of new U.S. solar panels in one of America's top producers of electricity, officials said. The Obama administration would use the remaining $1.59 trillion in a tax levy commonly known as the Bush tax to construct new U.S. solar panels in one of the country's most important producers of electricity."An additional $5.0 trillion would mark the beginning of our major cost sharing strategy for small power utilities and lower the U.S.A. gas price for electricity," the White House said in a press release.President Barack Obama would impose an additional $12.5 trillion to fund the construction of new U.S. solar panels. Details of where he would use tax credits were not made available public today.The prospect of a new unprecedented tax credit, formally announced in October 2010, has sparked concern among some economists that it could more than doubleshot U.S. electricity prices over the next 10 years. Critics have said it will cause a 5-fold drop in electricity prices and lead to less viable investment in solar infrastructure across the country.“Washington administration officials are particularly pleased with the president’s move to lift the Bush-era tax credit and meet America’s ever-creasing demand for clean energy,” said Christian McCle, president of the National Coalition for Responsible Energy. In a report released Monday, the coalition estimates the move would lower U.S. electricity prices by about 20 percent over the next decade.The new tax credit, announced in October 2010, would boost the costs for power utilities to build new, reimagined U.S. solar panels. But many economists had previously estimated the credit would generate more than $1.2 trillion in new revenue each year. The U.S. House of Representatives passed an amendment to expand the tax credit to replace the Bush tax credit, to go into effect on July 15. The house estimates about 25 percent of that revenue would come from non-Solar-panel sources - about 10 percent of the amount granted the current tax credit. At the same time as the revenue announcement, Obama administration said Monday it had increased the total tax credit for new electricity panel construction to $12.9 trillion, according to Citizensgroup, an advocacy nonprofit. The tax credit would directly generate $1.82 trillion in projected revenue for the 2020 year.“We are delighted to announce the amount granted so far in the 2018 fiscal year," Robert Henning Jr., senior vice president for Electricity and Community Development, said in a statement. "This amount is part of an ongoing effort to develop a clean, robust, affordable energy mix that supports America's fast-moving electricity market share."The Obama administration's new tax credit will help power utilities build $3.6 billion plus $1.2 trillion worth of new solar panels by 2020, according to the Electricity Association of America, a $24 billion increase from its current $1.22 trillion tax credit. The new tax credit will work even worse for the solar industry, as power utilities would face a five-fold drop in the cost of solar panels. By 2020, the total cost of new solar panels will climb by about half to $73 billion, which amounts to a $24 billion cost to the electricity industry, according to a report released last week. Expendures for existing solar panels will exceed about $1.1 trillion by 2020. Two-thirds of revenue from existing panels receiving the new tax credit is expected to increase about 20 percent. “Renewable energy presentss an exciting opportunity for businesses and consumers, who are being increasingly forced to switch to fossil fuels and electricity sources at lower gas prices," McCle said in an interview. James Stanton, a physics and engineering professor at the University of California, Berkeley, and chairman of the Intergovernmental Partners' Panel on Climate Change, said the new tax credit will lower electricity prices across the country by as much as $1.1 trillion over the next few years. Supply and demand continue to hold massive advantages to the electricity industry, Stanton said. “Boosting the tax credit not only will help our electricity industry thrive and grow competitively, it will also boost supply, which has become one of the most important factors behind the recession,” he said in a statement. "It still trailed below the previous level of 2.1 percent," said Ian Mendez, an assistant economist at Columbia College in Brooklyn and an expert on the economic recovery. In 2011 - when less than a quarter of full-time workers were unemployed - the unemployed grew 1.7 percent while the underemployed increased 2.6 percent. "Those numbers are consistent with a positive economic recovery in the wake of the recession," Mendez said. In fact, the number of unemployed and underemployed grew by an average of 200,000 in the first quarter of 2011, reaching a peak of 1,587 in FY 2011. Washington (Reuters) - The practicing skills available to white-collar practitioners, lawyers and legal scholars in various judicial disciplines has improved steadily since 1990, according to a study published in a sister magazine of the Law Society, an independent association of lawyers and scholars at the University of British Columbia. The independent research team reviewed a preliminary working paper titled The “Achieve and Future for National Trials in American Law in the 21st Century” of the Law Society, otherwise known as the Law Innovation Committee, which is composed of a group of legal scholars led by Attorney General Mason Eisenhower. Eisenhower wrote the committee “offenders with a more extensive understanding of trial law, compelling options for plaintiffs to pursue, and more detailed practical principles that could serve to enhance arbitratory practice in federal courts.” The study, which appears in the July edition of the Journal of American Law, a sister magazine of the Law Society, found that the committee’s practicing skills have improved four-fold since 1990, which makes it one of the largest independent organizations of U.S. lawyers and scholars. Over the course of more than six decades, the committee handled over 4,000 cases with states, a total equivalent to all disputes filed in federal district court, according to the 55-page publication summary. The team’s report praises the organization for helping partner states and federal district courts in “introducing innovative approaches to dispute, due process, initial proceedings, case versus case decisions, enhancing the constitutional power of state government.” The committee includes the director of the Holy Palace University Law Center at the University of Buffalo, and the report’s lead author, Zakeramiya Hirdousewa, assistant professor of applied law at the University of Buffalo. The committee also includes the director of the Buffalo Supreme Court Innov Program, the university’s organization of lawyers, judges and scholars specialized in legal disputes, and Corey Sager, the spokesman for the Center for theApplied Program of the American Law Society. Here's a review from ZestoTV from mid-October 8th. As you toss the image, we instantly notice an awful lot of things about the device. It's pretty, but it's also terrible. When you take a closer look at the latest Lumia 7.10 review, the device looks so damn worse than you would expect from its rear camera. It doesn't have a 3.6-megapixel rear camera. While that might be somewhat surprising, it's no more disconcerting than some of the bulky reviews by Apple and ZestoTV. Apple has received a lot of attention over the last few days, but there's still some fresh reviews out there that may just shock users. Apple (and we at Zesto) seem to handle the experience of new devices better than expected, so it comes as a surprise that those newer devices look so inferior. However, that impression seems to be only the tip of the iceberg. Whether Apple has gone to great lengths to offer simple, high performance devices at reasonable pricing shouldn't shock us at all. There's nothing new about Apple's used smartphones, and that's just not a good thing. It's no surprise that they've started regularly raising the prices of new devices, so there's a real question of whether a new device will drive down prices (such as the iPad). With that said, it's interesting to find out whether Apple has proceeded to raise prices or set higher premiums for new devices. Apple and Zesto would prefer we think to refer to the S7 rather than the S8, except that they're always setting higher prices for new devices. But there's little doubt that the iPad is doing much better than the bulky reviews. That said, many of Apple's users aren't convinced that the S7 is doing any better, and given its tiny shape, it doesn't look very good. If let's look behind the scenes, the S7 is about 3 mm tall and 4.5 mm wide. The rear camera doesn't focus too much over the frames, but at least it does look a bit too small. If we can add a few pixels and look around, that's still pretty bad. It's still pretty pretty. The majority of the bulky reviews are based on a good set of assumptions, which makes it hard to believe that the Lumia 7.10 isn't the top-tier operating system for a new smartphone. Compared to Apple's iPhone 6, or the Airbus S8, Apple's chances of being in that spot are pretty low. But the Lumia 7.10 review includes a number of things that seem to have affected the experience of the S7, that we'll probably get to know a bit about later. It's probably an unexpected number -- or maybe an disappointing number -- which means that every time Apple shifts back to delivering new experiences to its used devices, it leaves a black hole in the reviews in terms of actual performance and characteristics. However, that isn't surprising given the tiny shape of the S7 and a tiny design of the iPad. People aren't convinced the S7 is any better, but unless you toss the iPad's battery over to the phone's rear camera, it won't be able to look all that good. This is especially because there's lots of times when certain types of reviews go stal. We did see performance similarities between the S7 and the Lumia 7.10 but didn't notice much machine-by-device differences in some respects (the Lumia 7.10 isn't running primarily on Linux or Windows distributions). Those differences aren't really all that noticeable. To make matters worse, Apple's third-party user experience hasn't worked as well as you would expect from a new operating system like the Lumia 7.10, so the results are still pretty poor. Overall, the two reviews we saw just over the weekend on Product Manager and the one we saw on the Lumia 7.10 were pretty good at least in terms of third-party user experience, which leads us to question the performance and user behavior of the device. On a consumer scale, that might be good, but it's really not that bad. If we read the results of those reviews carefully, it seems as though a lot of reviews did work the way we expected. The House on Monday adopted a bill that specifically bars legislators from wearing traditional headscarves at mosque services or using Islamic State slogans. House Speaker Kyle McCrory (R-Utah) adopts a bill that specifically bars legislators from wearing traditional headscarves at mosque services or using Islamic State slogans, even though she and other lawmakers still sharply oppose the measure. The legislation eliminates the practice of "chrowcarves," which are worn without the use of batons. As a result, they are not allowed in many churches, schools or public establishments. The proposed bill -- which would have prohibited legislators from wearing the so-called "non-traditional headscarve" only at mosque services -- is being strongly criticized by a larger religious freedom group, the American Civil Liberties Union (D-Ariza). "While the bill eliminates the practice of empty headscarves in many mosques, it serves as the most unsettling reason for a growing number of Muslim legislators to oppose the measure," the American Civil Liberties Union said in a press release. "This updated version of the bill, which will go into effect on Aug. 11, will only make it harder for legislators to vote in mosques based on their religious beliefs," the release added. "We look forward to actively urging Muslim legislators to stop wearing traditional headscarves at mosque services." Conservative groups said the bill was too narrow and narrow -- and too wide -- unlike the previous legislation, and that it would not protect religious freedom or voting rights. The bill is headed before the Senate Religional Affairs Committee. Sen. John Durban (R-Okla.), the chairman of the Senate Religional Affairs Committee, called for the measure to be withdrawn. Several Muslim civil liberties groups said on Monday they will drop the bill if the House voted to adopt it next week. However, civil liberties groups immediately affirmed their support for keeping the bill. The conservative groups argued that the bill, if fully passed, does not violate the Establishment and Nondiscrimination Act of 1989, and that it applies only to mosques. "The House bill specifically bars legislators from wearing traditional headscarve in both public and private places, and bars legislators from wearing traditional headscarves at mosque services, although Democrats and Republicans will continue to oppose the this amendment," Rep. Adam Green (D-AZ) said in a statement. ###

It's also at a time when consumer loan costs have surged and student borrowing has become the most widely available form of financial lending. In October, fastfood distributor Wal-Mart announced its new short-term use plan, along with other student borrowing options like Best Buy, CerotPage and PriceMark. This isn't a big deal for consumers, Musk said, since short-term student borrowing has been in progress for more than a decade, and Wal-Mart is part of a drive to expand student borrowing options. Under the plan, Wal-Mart will introduce "financial borrowing," a new category of programs aimed at encouraging short-term student borrowing. As part of that new program, the company also plans to acquire about $210 million in new, "Fuse A" corporate-bank account securities at a rate of $13.65 per share. The securities, Musk said, will kick off on acquisition next month. They're expected to worth about $225 million in a year from Oct. 21, the date of acquisition, according to federal student borrowing statistics. That's a sum that would amount to just about $110 million for a rate of $13.65 per share. But this isn't that different from other short-term student borrowing options. One of the key features Musk mentioned on the conference call is the ability to place orders online using Twitter and Facebook, something that probably wasn't available to consumers previously because of the open nature of social media. That feature allows customers to publish online deals in order to save money on their student loan payments. There's a new feature called digital marketing that allows customers to place orders using real, social media sites, including Tumblr and Twitter, and gives customers the ability to sign online deals. This social media marketing feature would have some short term benefits, Musk said, but it could also help consumers save money if they decide to place online orders using social media like Facebook and other sites. By bringing more of these new student borrowing capabilities to Wal-Mart, consumers will be able to place orders online using other social media sites without incuring extra shipping fees. Apart from their social media features, Wal-Mart also has several options for customers to use. One option allows customers to place an order at a rate of $13.65 per share, many of which can be immediately posted to other social media sites. Customers can choose how long it takes to place a order until the end of the year. On one option, a popular option called "Free Mail on a Friday" allows customers to publish advertising online to get a discount on student loans in order to save money on their payments. On the other, there's a more flexible option called "Buy Arrive" that allows customers to change the amount of student loans they apply for to the amount of student loans they pay for. Musk said companies are in a position to adjust their existing student borrowing policies to their customer needs. "You don't have to change what you do depending on how much business you're going to pay for if you're going to pay for the business you want to pursue," he said. Bringing these new student borrowing capabilities to Wal-Mart will help simplify the student borrowing process, Musk said. The company is also considering a revamp to its oversight system, which Musk hoped would give the company more control over how students borrow and how they spend. Median earnings for the wealthiest 1 percent of the world’s population are growing faster than the official minimum wage from $923,000 since January 2007, according to a report released Monday. Median incomes for about 1 percent of the world’s population fell 4.9 percent, to $9,949,000, in August, its lowest level since the recession began. Nonfemale employment (1 percent of median income) also fell with a 1.8-point drop in income growth since January 2007, the authors reported. Nonfemale employment dropped 12 percent in August from $1,050,000 about the same quarter ago, while the female employment increased by 8.4 percent from $1,637,000 in July 2007. The authors said the decline in income growth was primarily driven by immigration. The median incomes fell 13 percent in August to $9,949,000, down from $923,000 in July 2007, and it was up from a me.8 percent growth in the previous quarter to $923,000 in August. The median median incomes for workers who complete a college degree also fell 6 percent between August and September — a drop in the official annual minimum wage raised in the wake of the global financial crisis. Academic employment fell 3.5 percent between the previous quarter and the summer of 2009 making for a 2.7 percent decline in income growth, but it was a 1.2 percent increase from only the previous quarter, the authors reported. In addition to the decline, employment in the academic fields also shrinked. The fields of science, technology, engineering, math and information sciences added about 16,000 jobs during the summer compared with the prior period, according to IEAA. Employment growth in these fields — engineering, electronics, science, insurance and finance — was primarily driven by lower employment rates among women. In the summer of 2009, according to IEAA, people over the age of 65 had a median income of about $3975,000. By comparison, the decline in employment in academic fields spawned about 65,000 jobs, out of whom 46.5 percent were women, IEAA said in August. "At the beginning of the real world economy a lot of people were totally unfamiliar with what these algorithms were going to be used in jobs at the beginning of the day," UC de New Mexico professor Stan Thomas, who authored the study, said in a phone interview last week."But what's changed is that there are now so many different kinds of things that people are now familiar with and what's the right thing to use and the right thing to do and how to do it. You do it with some sort of paid service, and you end up doing a lot of work. But software is not so much a science. We know what to do a lot, and it's going to be difficult to figure out what's going to be used in different types of jobs — it's kind of the way we live today. With everybody around the world — from Microsoft, to Apple, to Google — we know what's going to use, and if you're going to go out there and do a really good job in the real world, you're either going to be really, really familiar with what's going to be used, or you are going to have a work team around the globe that's really familiar with when you're working on and what to work on. That's one of the really exciting things about the internet. The amount of opportunity for tech companies to team their employees up against each other on the latest products is kind of something that lots of other industries have. No matter what they are working on, a lot of them are totally familiar with all of the software, all of the apps, and all of the innovation the internet is going to offer."That creates a lot of opportunity for them to study other fields, as opposed to the awful lot of time and effort that they would have to invest in other fields. "So, it's not about great jobs, it's really about working hard, deciding what to do," Thomas said. "For us, this is about knowing if you have enough time to find a good location to do good things. And that's what the world's all about. For a lot of people, finding the right places is a really informational way to live, and that's the kind of thing it's all about. Sometimes you want to figure out the best method, or you want to use the right algorithm for the right job, or you want to come up with a new method and you can't do it yourself. And then sometimes it's really up to you to make an informed judgment on the best way to do it, rather than trying to decide what's used is the best way." NEW YORK (Reuters) - Crowds erupted in the strategic city of Jianxi on Thursday following the 70 years of Beijing’s unification, as its continued effort to thwart growing tension between rival geopolicies was under restriction by a spate of suicide airstrikes from recent weeks. The protests were preceded by more than 200 security forces stationed in the southern city of Jianxi, the capital of China just more than 777 miles (1,080 km) from the border with Taiwan. The emergence of an U.S. military presence near 525 km (17 miles) Jianxi on Thursday was part of a third major security force escalation in days, largely prompted by furious reaction from Beijing, which has seen growing hostility in recent months. Earlier, the U.S. military suspended diplomatic relations with China on Thursday. The escalation followed intense clashes between Chinese warplanes and civilians in the region on Thursday. Nearly 30,000 people flooded out to streets to attend grieving services in Jianxi in the midst of World Heritage Day, with hundreds expected to be killed by next week. U.S. security forces killed 64 civilians in casualty on Thursday, the latest attack launched to date by pro-Chinese protesters east of Jianxi. In April, 12 civilians were killed by the security forces, while a spate of suicide airstrikes since April have killed 14 more people. Secretary of State John Kerry later announced that 27 civilians had died. “It’s a spate of attacks against ourselves and our people in the region, including recent airstrikes since April and killings of innocent soldiers and civilians, and we want to do whatever we can to face these threats,” Kerry said at a news conference in the capital. U.S. military spokesman Anthony R. McEnough said in a statement that thousands of civilians marched in Jianxi amid a wave of airstrikes. “We are witnessing yet another wave of airstrikes in recent weeks with airstrikes to ourselves and our people in this whole area,” he said in a statement. “The Chinese security forces are now conducting regular operations.” A Chinese security forces spokesman told Reuters that they had launched 59 suicide attacks in the first quarter this year. Tens of thousands of supporters of pro-Chinese agitators rallied in the heart of Jianxi on Thursday, with hundreds carrying banners chanting “Aguamao Bing Taiwan” (Pro-American, Pro-Chinese). “We have a bad relationship with Taiwan, and these attacks are above all else an attack against ourselves and our people. If these attacks continue, we will change our minds. We will not tolerate them,” protesters chanted and shouted in explaining their relationship with Beijing. The U.S. military has been on duty since May as intense tensions between the two countries grow in recent months. China has condemned the military offensive on Taiwan, which has caused a sharper rise in international tension, and called on the United States to stop military exercises on Jianxi, a city close to the Chinese border. Anxiety and alcohol use -- a condition often mistaken for personality disorders -- are also at greater risk for dementia. Previous studies have argued that excessive exposure to sports could be linked to problems in brain functioning, including autism. Oceresis is a rare type of brain injury that normally takes a long time to develop, but primarily occurs in teens. Although it has not been documented in adults, it can cause a number of injuries, including a heart attack. People are likely to develop Oceresis when they reach 16. Children are poorly trained to control the brain, a process so burdensome that they are often unable to walk for too long and is difficult to master. WASHINGTON (Reuters) - American job creation hit its fastest pace in a decade, the U.S. Labor Department reported on Friday, evoking sharp growth among upper-income Americans. President Barack Obama added 175,000 new jobs to the American labor force in 2011, the fastest pace it recorded after taking office in just over a decade. Job creation increased by nearly 25 percent in 2011, at the year’s fastest pace since taking office and at its fastest pace in nearly a decade, according to the updated Bureau of Labor Statistics. The news comes after the Obama administration reported a dramatic scuffle in the number of new jobs that Obama has been creating since he was first elected president. The loss of new jobs is underseering the tightening job growth. Over the past 12 months, just 32,000 new jobs were created in 2011, up from the previous record of 1,400 12 months ago, according to the Bureau. The trend is particularly disturbing, as the record number of new jobs created in the little over a year since the first month of 2005 is a sign of an increase in the demand for jobs in the United States. The number of job- creation proposals for the first 12 months of this year soared by more than 50 percent, but failed to deliver on the 12.4 percent growth it had recorded during the height of the Great Depression and the recession. The loss of new jobs has further tightened the supply of job-creers, multiple sources told VICEO. The number of job proposals fell 25 percent a year to -1.6 million, with growth for the first 12 months standing at -1.4 million. Appropriations fell 9 percent to +2.6 million, and vacancies increased 9 percent to +1.6 million. Despite the modest increase in minimum wage for teachers and nurses, census data from the Labor Department suggests that trend is continuing with the loss of brand new jobs at a 16.7 percent slower than growth. Just over 12 months into the third quarter, 7.8 million new jobs were created in the third quarter of 2011, up from 3.6 million in 2005. The loss of new jobs is drawing outcry from employers who favor raising minimum wages. For instance, Amazon Inc is pressuring employees to vote against House Democratic plans to increase the minimum wage by 20 percent. In the House, teachers and healthcare workers are outspoken against Republican plans to raise minimum wages for teachers and pensioners, concerned that workers are being unable to find decent jobs. “Precision data suggests that the labor market is struggling to cope with increasing numbers of minimum- wage workers who are unable or unable to earn past noon,” said Dan Gal, an assistant secretary of the U.S. Labor Employees Association. An international team of physicists from the University of Washington has released the first ever comprehensive map of the area of the universe near its equator. Their work has enabled researchers to better guess whether the rest of the universe will expand faster than expected. “With the past 1.5 trillion years below the rate of emululation, we can now conclude that time is out,” said Prutson. It is also the first time that the universe is shown to exhibit a slow pace of expansion, particularly in hundreds of millions of years from its nearest equator. Omnial expansion tends to slow with time, Prutson said, and its most recent estimate, based on the space’s rate of change, is not comparable with change at other points of the equator. “To say that space has expanded over the past 3.1-1.5 trillion years is blatantly false,” Prutson said. The new study, published Thursday in the journal Astrophysical Spectrography.org, uses X ray mass spectroscopy evidence from more than 1.5 trillion years ago to forecast an emergence in the direction of the equator — the area by which the universe rotates between its equator and its nearest equator. This would implies a kind of emululation from the nearest equator that makes the emergence at or near impossible for the rest of the universe, said the researchers. Using results from the eruption in the previously published map, Prutson’s team determined that the emergence near this maximum could generate an effect similar to that induced by eruptions on the Earthan acropse — the planet that rises under the equator acropse. Because this discovery opens up new information about the universe, the researchers can now conclude that the area in the direction of the equator is larger than was predicted in previous maps of the universe. Similarly, the area containing the universe near its equator is much smaller. “This is the first time that we can get comprehensive information about this area in the galaxy,” said Prutson. The discovery also raised concerns that the “definite” emululation of the equator near zero could lead to a collapse on the planet in a time of global warming — one that requires massive investments in drilling, surface exploration, and oil exploration. On the other hand, the warming of the planet could prevent the equator from emululationating completely in a long run, the team said. “Without it, the survival of the planet remains impossible,” Prutson said. The team plans to use the previously published map to gain greater certainty about the universe’s survival in a long run if it hits below zero by March. The birthday car, which is only available for pre-orders at the end of the month, will retail for roughly U.S. $40,000. Go for it, be a star. The B-35 tilts its back in a more street-like configuration, as has been the case of many. Prepareations are on course for a deadly extreme flood in the Asia Pacific following a storm that rocked a stretch of rural California and overtook remote south California, U.S. officials said. (NOSCA, Photo: U.S.) The storm, which formed a massive flood zone over the nation's heartland, triggered a wave of strong winds along California's south and east and swept southern California west and east, U.S. forecasters said. Preparations were made just hours following a mountainslide flood that tossed out central California, California forecasters said. The flood, which was the second such major weather event in U.S. history, hit the Water of Sanduja National Monument about a week ago and killed 19 people. President Barack Obama has pledged to fight storm flooding in California and reduce carbon emissions. "It does cause a lot of damage" in California, said the state's director of water, Jim Menendez, adding that states had "too much to lose from a major weather event." The storm that overtook remote south California rocketed into the air in the oil-producing town of LaVilla, about 40 miles north of Belner Lake, and reached winds of between about 57 and 90 mph. The storm then entered the west of central California before blowing up rural, remote regions. The storm overtook remote central California for much of the impact, killing about 150 people and damaging about half the state's industrial infrastructure, the National Weather Service said. Thursday's LaVilla flood was the largest flood caused by a major storm in its history, according to federal government records and the largest flood of any major weather event in its history. The weather service said the flood covered more than 12,000 acres. Menendez said only six storms fell between 1992 and 2005. NEW YORK (WCONEY) -- NYPD Commissioner Michael Carter Brennan has been fired from his post amid investigation into the matter, authorities announced Tuesday. Brennan, 60, has a history of investigating child porn websites and the trafficking of young children on the internet. He served as the New York Police inspector for the Child Porn Inquiries Section of the Metropolitan NYPD. He investigated hundreds of child porn websites across the nation over five years, which led police to arrest nearly 3,000 people, according to Ana Bloomberg, inspector general in New York's Immigration and Terrorism Department. "The NYPD is deeply saddened by the progress of the Department of Justice in enabling Mr. Brennan to continue on with his job as commissioner of the NY Police Department (NYPD) in New York City," according to a statement released that Bloomberg said. The department called Brennan's resignation "alarming and a shame." "Hi decision to return to this role has reinforced the shared commitment by the Department of Justice and the NYPD to prevent this investigation," Bloomberg said. In January, the department suggested letting Brennan go of all other duties and pushed for his resignation as immediate. "We expressed our confidence that Mr. Brennan, along with other members of the board of the NYPD, will continue to take all steps necessary to prevent this investigation," it said. Brennan's time with the NYPD began in 2008 and Brennan served with the agency until 2013. He's been there since 2008. According to an investigation report provided to the Times on March 15, the department told Brennan that the incident occurred after he received written requests from police with his Immigration and Terrorism department. He spoke with members of police about the requests and supplied them with information related to drug smumug, the Times reported. Authorities said in a statement that the department had been made fully aware of the incident and was working to bring new charges against Brennan. The police inspector did not respond to the Times request for comment for this story. Brennan's attorney requested he be returned to duty in January 2015. Under federal law, vehicles traveling within the country have to stop at certain speeds and have to travel within a speed limit of approximately 11 miles per hour, authorities said. An agency spokesman for the NYPD in Newark, New Jersey told the Times that they were working on a "hunt" about the incident, but that the current hunt had "be active for several years and given multiple indications" the agency was working on its investigation. In February 2014, authorities began reviewing video of the incident in downtown Perry Fields in Florida, the Times reported. On February 1, 2014, Brennan connected to the internet from his home in Newark, Connecticut and captured a 90-second video of the incident, the Times reported. From there, Brennan listened to audio of the incident and told NYPD officials that he wanted to leave New York, the Times reported. The following week, an investigation was launched and Brennan was arrested in Cleveland, Ohio. John Olleinski, Brennan's attorney, said in a statement to the Times that he was attempting to incentivise the agency to charge Brennan and to keep the incident under investigation. China is closer to building a great alliance with Asia's wealthiest nations, China Minister of State Deng Yung has warned that the country is closer to building an economic alliance with Asia's wealthiest nations in a bid to address the region's poverty problem. In a speech at the UN Economics and Development Summit in Beijing, Deng Yung, the minister in charge of China's economic policy and economic development, said there was a "much better" way for countries to reduce their poverty while stressing the need for a "greatger alliance". "We must work with the wealthiest countries in the world, explore new ways to live at the expense of the poor and also listen to the needs of the poor," Yung said. Related: China Minister of State Deng Yung aims for a "greatger alliance" In his previous speech at the UN Summit, he said there was need for collaboration. "We must find ways to raise tax rates for the wealthy, maintain a climate of freedom and maintain a fair standard of living," he said. "We also need a better economic climate to promote freedom, growth, equality and collaboration." During his speech at the UN General Assembly, Yung made brief reference to the ongoing housing crisis, which China says poses a major threat to economic stability in the region - especially as low earners are increasingly unable to find part-time jobs. "There are far too many barriers to pay, and we need to find a way of alleviating that," Yung said. At the same time, Asia is in the midst of a fastest-growing economy, he pointed out, in part by the lack of affordable housing, but also by the growth of its population. "I think we must work with both parties towards the longer term in terms of social, economic and technological development," he said. In his speech at the UN General Assembly, Yung said major social reforms needed to be achieved, such as fair public spending, a higher minimum wage, better education, disease treatment and better health care. Related: "China has long had many problems that need further mitigation, including social reform," he said.

President of the United States Barack Obama on Wednesday hailed U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to withdraw from the U.N. climate change deal. "The fight against climate change plays an important role," he said in a statement first reported by The AP. "This administration and our executive branch is a good time to withdraw." Trump, in a press conference, announced his decision to sign or withdraw from the Paris agreement on Wednesday, saying he would leave the decision to the White House. At the time, Trump refused to release a timeline of whether or not he would withdraw from the deal until early in his presidency. Trump's decision to withdraw from the Paris agreement cleared the way for more than 7 billion people and 11 billion members of the world's population to come together and agree a real, sustainable way to address climate change, he said at a campaign rally in London. "We are on a good path to reaching a comprehensive, sustainable climate agreement," he said. Britain's energy minister Alan Baird said Trump was ready to withdraw from the Paris deal a few days before the elections, during a media briefing on Wednesday — a unusual move in which the president faces threats of action. Baird said Trump should be ready to act on his decision to withdraw from the deal just a few weeks before the November elections. There were several reasons for Trump's decision, in particular the fact that the U.N. climate change plan was not fully compatible with the U.N. convention that establishs a comprehensive climate change plan. There was also confusion about the timing of Trump's decision to sign or withdraw from the terms of the Paris agreement and how he decided on whether he would withdraw from the deal. Trump said he already had announced he'd withdraw from Paris deal May 31 but threatened with immediate action on the issue since he had not indicated he would exit the deal. "I'm here to prove that climate change is not a problem. Now we have to address it," he said. The announcement came just days before Election Day in November, the first round of negotiations in almost 50 years in which Trump pledged to withdraw from the terms of the Paris agreement. He said he was "impressed" by his commitment to withdraw from the deal by May 31 but would not elaborate on the decision. "Consistent" Ben Thomas, executive director of the American Federation of Economic and Policy Scientists, said Trump's climate decision was a good first step in moving toward the deal but added the president must be "consistent" in making wise decisions about the Paris deal. "He is telling the truth about climate change, and we need to make sure he's not serious about that issue," he said. Thomas said the Paris agreement was equally important to revitalizing the U.S. relationship with China. Chinese President Xi Jinping said Trump's withdrawal from the Paris deal — just five days before President Barack Obama's inaugural address at the U.S. Capitol in Washington — was the "greatest chance yet to revitalize our relationship." He said he was dissatisfied with Trump's decision and did not expect he would behave differently in leaving the deal. Apple today announced its new iPad, which is based around a Pixel 7 6C. Apple’s Pixel 7 looks a lot more usable than the iPhone 7, which makes it a much more attractive design. On a normal iPhone or a true iPad, the screen feels a bit more easy to use, but the battery feels a lot shorter and more usable than most of the cameras you’ll find on the Galaxy S8 and iPhone 7. Because the battery is the same shape, Apple’s 9-inch AOS panel is a lot bigger, but an 8-inch screen (on the iPhone) doesn’t work almost as well. The fact that it’s so similar doesn’t make it attractive, but it’s definitely one Apple has stood out in terms of hardware design. The Pixel 7 6C looks almost identical on iOS. As you can see, if you compare the screen length with the bezel, it looks almost the same. (Who knows? That’s hard to believe, but really interesting.) That comparison starts with the shape of Apple’s Pixel 7 6C. It looks almost identical to the Galaxy S 8. On iOS, however, there are some obvious similarities. The Galaxy S8 and iPhone 7 are in the same shape for less. The front camera (2.7 GHz) is actually slightly slower than the Galaxy S8, while the rear (3.6 GHz) is a bit less powerful than the Galaxy S 8. The 3.6 mAh battery is slightly smaller on the Galaxy S8, but it’s also faster than the iPhone 7. The rear 13.6-mAh battery is a bit smaller than the iPhone 7, but it has up to 64GB (64GB) of storage. When you compare the cameras with other sensors, these cameras make the iPhone a lot taller and bigger. Some of them are a bit too fast, while other ones only requires 64GB of storage. On the iPhone, Apple’s 8-megapixel camera is slightly shorter and more easy to use, while the rear camera (3.6 GHz) is a bit less powerful than the Galaxy S 8. As you can see, there are obvious similarities in terms of the design and size. The wider display on the Galaxy S8 feels a lot better if you factor in the body angles and user angles, while the full-screen display feels a bit slower. Conversely, Apple’s keyboard on the iPhone 7 is identical to that of the Pixel S8 without requiring a DDR4 key. I’d guess both devices run the same operating system. Being said that, the latter isn’t attracting a lot of attention, so I think Apple’s keyboard on the rear 5.0 GHz is a bit too fast andn’t as powerful as the Galaxy S8. Apple’s new iPad 8 uses the same technology as the iPhone 7. The wider display on the iPad 8 uses the same design as the iPhone 7. Apple’s new iPad 10 seems to be a bit in the wrong place with the wider display on the iPad 8, but I think as you look at the former, it seems to be one of the better options. The fact that these two are fundamentally identical in shape to the iPhone 8 does a lot to downplay the benefits of having a broader display. Apple’s 9.8-inch iPad 5, on the other hand, simply has a much better design (than its 3.6 mAh battery) compared to its rivals the iPhone and iPad 10. The thinner material on the iPad 5 makes it thinner than the iPhone. The Galaxy S8 is taller because it has a full-screen looking 3.6 mAh camera and a 1.500mAh battery that you can put on while holding the phone. It’s also worth the look because it’s not too tricky to hold up (as in an office or at a wedding party). Plus, of nearly identical shape, it has a 13.9 mAh battery and a 64GB of storage to work with. What makes it especially interesting is that the Galaxy S8 and iPad 10 aren’t similar, because they both have an 8-inch screen, while the S8 only has the one on front (13.6 GHz). Plus, and in nearly identical shape, the Galaxy S8 has a 1.500mAh battery. There really is no complaint. Share this...

The House Oversight Committee passed a resolution Tuesday attacking the efforts by Gov. George W. Perry, paving the way for fellow Rep. Gregor Hammond (Democrat) to veto the contentious measure. He hasn't sponsored a bill attacking the state since the GOP controlled the Iowa Senate in 2007. But, now, Hammond says he sees the state as one of the best in the nation. "In many ways, he speaks a lot about climate change, and I think he is passionate about that," Hammond told the LWA News. Jim Smollin, a former chairman of Iowa's Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee, called his position "pretty strong and vocal." Meanwhile, a troubled economic recovery in Iowa looks around the corner. The state's businesses are still scrambling to regain a record $12.77-billion ($12 billion) in debt from budget-encrucing layoffs at the Agriculture Department and state and local governments. That's with it the state's biggest shortfall in 21 years, The Associated Press reported. A new study says the state's agricultural and energy programs could save businesses an extra $40 billion a year. Gov. Perry is also planning to veto such a "Kill No Deal" bill sponsored by Sen. Tom Walker on June 5, The Associated Press reported. Iowa lawmakers promised to rescind the bill even if it does not pass their committee. An announcement by a Florida-based energy company that it will cease conducting clinical trials after six months has sparked concerns about the safety at its nuclear and missile facilities across the country. "After more than 75 years in business, Virginia Energy has decided not to conduct the first round of clinical trials over the next six months," the energy company said in a press release. "This decision will ensure that we are in good shape as we move forward," the company said in a statement. "We can thank you for the enormous support you have received, which will benefit us throughout the recovery process," the company said in an email statement. "Our hearts go out to the people who have been affected." Advocates for clean nuclear energy said the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency conducted 70 clinical trials last month at Virginia’s Fukushima power station, which is located about 30 miles northwest of Tokyo’s Okaichawa. But Virginia Energy said its decision not to conduct the clinical trials was based on safety concerns. On Tuesday, Aug. 10, a tidal tsunami pumped large quantities of radioactive material into Virginia’s affected nuclear facilities, killing two U.S. plant workers and injuring more than 10 others. In its news release last month, the company said it was conducting a limited number of clinical testing at its affected facilities, including large-scale clinical trials. However, the company said it would have to phase out its clinical testing activities for six full months, between the end of August and the end of October. The first round of clinical trials on Tuesday involved 1 million kilograms of IC and 16 million kilograms of ethanol. In addition, the tsunami has smashed ties to all of Virginia’s nuclear plants in recent weeks, according to statements made earlier in the release. Virginia Energy had previously said it would not be conducting clinical trials at its affected facilities. The latest news comes as Japan recovers from the deadly incident at Fukushima two days ago when a tsunami near the power station killed 68 people. "If such a disaster occurs, we will be able to make sure we are best prepared," Steven Brooks, director of emergency response for Virginia Energy, said in a telephone interview. The news in Japan follows a deadly incident near the nation’s Fukushima power station two days back caused by a tsunami.
