CLOSE Trump appeals to Senate conservatives to push to remove the EPA from federal budget By Mkuri Masaeou Masomaka For the past few days, President Donald Trump has publicly urged Senate conservatives to remove the EPA from the federal budget. But it did the exact opposite on Monday. In the end, every Republican in the Senate voted to keep the EPA. This set off a showdown between opposing Republicans and the GOP Congress over passage of a long-contested bill that would establish the EPA as a governing agency. Most Republicans in that Congress agreed with the bill, leading all Democrats to vote no. Forty-seven Republicans in the Senate worked hours toassemble an amendment to the bill before it was ever passed. And, like last week, it’s sinking under them. They only just announced the outcome a few hours after their votes were cast. Now a Republican president has made a more confluent comment about the EPA as a budget he intends to take home. Speaking from his golf course in Charlottesville, Vt., Trump responded to a question at a White House press conference, where he said he felt very “interested” about deciding whether to keep the EPA as part of his budget. “I think it would be great for myself to be able to bring in someone who is just a bit better than me,” he said. “Anybody but someone who is better than me should be able to resign or move on with their job.” “I like to think that I’m going to get fired, and I’m going to try to get a little more involved,” Trump continued. “But now instead of slogging taxpayer dollars into the government, I just have to make a hell of a push to keep EPA. I think this is a time when someone has to get fired. I think this is really a time where the sky ticks.” Trump did not provide an explanation, but his remarks would serve as a significant catalyst in his efforts to pull off the 2016 election, in which he had what he considered the best chances of winning. The House also approved a bill Friday allowing employers to defer retirement benefits unless they receive over $25,000 in annual earnings. And the Senate version of the plan said would open the door to mandatory retirement benefits for employees who work for more than four years or unpaid leave until age 75. A review of the plan, published Monday in the Journal of Economic Policymaking, named 13 states where the number of workers who retire has fallen by more than half. Retirement benefit deferments have risen to a rate of 55 percent in 36 states. Meanwhile, an assessment by the US Department of Labor found that retired workers are the fastest growing source of annual earnings. "Mleanage growth in America is progressing at an incredibly slow pace, and problems are starting to take center stage," the IRS report said. "Therefore, with many states either slowing down, with economies shutting down or slowing down, the real cause is yet to be identified." Arizona, New Hampshire, Washington and Wisconsin saw the highest overall rates of wage growth over the last decade, representing increases of 1.6 percent and 1.5 percent, a review of the plan said. By contrast, Texas and Kansas have rounded out the list of states where wage growth fell from 1.6 percent to 1.5 percent. Eight states, including Louisiana and Arizona have recently passed legislation to set minimum wages too high to provide some economic protection for workers, while North Carolina and Oregon have topped those areas in the top five. "This plan does not target states that have higher-than-average rates of workers receiving a reasonable amount of retirement benefits they are eligible for," said Steve Corkin, executive director of the Labor Policy Center, an economic research group for the ACLU's Office of Economic Policy & Budget. "retisted workers are expected to benefit from higher hourly productivity and employment rates, pay higher 90-hours rates with less sales tax, and therefore are more likely to be paid significantly above the mandatory minimum wage." Other states, like North Carolina and South Dakota -- the fastest-growing states in the country -- appear less likely to tax inflation, or introduce a form of sales tax, the report said. Middle class states have also recently passed legislation to set higher wages on full-time workers earning a federal minimum wage of $146 an hour. Lawmakers said they're concerned about the impact of the legislation on the working-class economy. "What this plan does is give extremely high-paying workers significant economic protection by making them eligible to pay unusually higher wages in the largest segment of the middle class," said Steve Harwood, executive director of the Labor Policy Center, a conservative advocacy group for corporate policymakers in New Hampshire and Washington states. James Diamond, whose technology firm resides in Edinburgh, has ignored a unanimous call for a trial after the firm stopped collecting its customer data, a move the investor described as “stupidious”. In an interview with the Guardian on Tuesday evening, the Guardian reported that Mr Diamond’s work was thwarted when the chairman of the firm, John Richard Stone, asked during the hearing ahead of the trial why he didn’t have a policy that firms could obtain customer data from their internal databases. Mr Stone also asked whether he had a policy that firms should be careful when they were using customer data. In an interview following the hearing, Mr Diamond said: “It’s like always leaving the ball in the sand – that’s not true. “I think consumers have to be realistic when it comes to wanting to work at another firm. “They will have to pull back when the trial begins and then try to figure out why they want to work at another firm. “He doesn’t want to be coerce to look over his shoulders and say, ‘Hey, that’s a problem for a prosperous business’.” Records obtained by the Guardian revealed that the firm had pledged to ensure that the business of Mr Diamond and his partners upheld “the highest standards in data collection, privacy, and financial services”. The records includes a list of variables familiar to businesses and consumers, and revealed that Mr Diamond had collected £1.4 million in customer data from five and a half firms over the period between July 2009 and March 2010. The firm registered 96 variables that appear to be closely related to a customer’s data, such as account numbers such as birth address, distance, phone numbers, and email addresses. The policy makes offenders punishable with fines of up to 10 months in jail. A trial for Mr Diamond and Mr Stone, both allegedly charged in that incident, is expected to begin on Monday, with their final verdict on Thursday. WASHINGTON -- Taking advantage of Treasury's GDP spending prediction this week drove the U.S. closer to its goal of growing 4 percent in 2026 than in 2015 for the first-time in two decades. This year, the Administration is forecast the economy hits a new growth rate of 12.6 percent against the 2015 rate of 16.4 percent. National average GDP growth of 5.7 percent over the next four years falls behind the economy's forecast growth rate of 16.8 percent to 27.6 percent. National average spending per capita is projected to decline by 3.6 percent over the next five years against the final figures released by the Department of the Treasury late Thursday, a proportional fall to the Administration's 2015 prediction of 1.6 percent growth. That figure is the updated version of a forecast outlined by Treasury Secretary Paul Kelly. Kelly said the forecast was if the economy hits a new rate of 3.6 percent or grows 1.8 percent at a steady pace by the end of February later this month. The economy is projecting a linear decline about to its 2015 target of 3.6 percent. Kelly said that decline occurs around February or March when the final figures will come into effect before the forecast is Feb. 31. During the coming year, the forecast will change annually from January to November, but as with the forecast for 2013, the Administration expects the economy to grow by 3.6 percent in 2012 and 4 percent in 2013. The economy could be at risk of falling back to a five-year target of 3.6 percent in 2013. It would also lead to a budget deficit triggered by budget deficits. "If you're getting only 3.6 percent of GDP growth, a 11.6 percent budget deficit or a 14.9 percent budget deficit, that basically means we're going to be at risk of a budget deficit over the next seven years," said Patrick Reynsmann, assistant director of economics for the Brookings Institute Group. "This year, we're at greater risk of a budget deficit than a budget deficit," Reynsmann said. Looking ahead to the next year, 2013 will see GDP spending reaching a seven-year low of 1.8 percent, but officials say that could put price pressure on imports and boost exports — both trade patterns that could help slow foreign goods production and boost competition from oil and gas markets. Administration officials said it's "relatively early" for the U.S. to enact a "blacklist" of actions to allow for further tax cuts. And as the amount that would go up, the resulting increase in spending would be at least as great as, if not greater than, a total tax cut. "It's not like we look back at the next year and start to turn a blind eye to it and say, What will happen next? It will take three to five years before we start looking at this picture," an Administration official said. Ordinarily, policy analysts say a total tax cut would cost about $18 trillion in states that phase out a federal tax rate that happens to be 1 percent of national income. That's more than half the cost in the states of Oklahoma, Oklahoma, North Carolina and Louisiana. "This is one of the minimum spending increases we need in order for a sustainable total tax cut," Reynsmann said. It's based on an analysis by the National Institute for Economic Research and Policy Analysis at Newton & Webster University in Raleigh, NM.C.C. Policymakers said it would be easier to prevent a further tax cut effect in 2013 than to prepare for further tax cuts in 2014. However, they said the Administration's concerns about upcoming 2026 actions only create opportunities for U.S. natural resource firms to escape tax taxes. "In most economies where oil prices go down or production slows, firms are more likely to be prepared to benefit from further tax cuts," said Hannah Wilson, head of the economic policy program at Thomas F. Kennedy Law School in Boston, Mass. "The more opportunities they see to escape, the more likely to come to the finishing board and say, 'Oh, we've got to start tax cuts in 2026.' " One of the few options considered by policymakers is the Administration's new Economic Growth Plan, which is a 1996 effort to promote economic growth and lays out a plan for greater economic growth. The Administration's projected tax cuts would initially slash capital and utilities spending to 70 or 72 percent of annual GDP, and policymakers say that could rise to 73 percent or 75 percent of annual GDP by 2025. Between 72 and 74 percent would face a national budget deficit worth $1.47 trillion. In 2013, the Administration would reduce a five-year budget deficit from 2 percent of annual GDP to 4 percent over the next five years.

Apparently, when it comes to Republican presidential candidates, Donald Trump's refusal to accept blame for the Paris terror attacks was just the opposite. That was a point made Wednesday by CNN's Howard Jeansdale and CNN's Chris Christie, both of whom sought to put a patch of irony on a Trump-related editorial released after a campaign that was widely criticised by progressive editors in the New York Times and Oklahoma Republican. The paper accused Trump of "smolstorming" black people with guns after the GOP candidate questioned him at a anti-war rally in Tacoma, Oklahoma. The Washington Post cited an Oklahoma Republican report saying Trump was asked by advisers about going to the city when he faced intense gunfire. In the report, Jeansdale wrote, "Trump has been to the city multiple times, and has gone there as a last-minute excuse." In a rare city hall speech on Wednesday, the Republican presidential candidate took the opportunity to reiterate his criticism of neo-liberalism. When asked in an interview by one of his advisers why he would never call a white supremacist or a phenomenon of any kind that hurts black people or of any colour, Trump insisted that that is what he had to say. "In fact," Trump said, "we can debate what it is, whether it is a restaurant attack or a school attack, whether it's a terrorist attack." The president at first reiterated the notion that racists originated as a society-building phenomenon rather than as mindless criminals of the modern era. "The right thing I am saying about this white supremacist," he said, "is that racists were behind the worst violence in our nation, especially in human history. That looks like we're not racists anymore, and if you look at the violence that happened in Paris, I may not be as concerned as I am about the racists that happened there, I would certainly like to reiterate that in my view, the people of our nation today — overwhelmingly black people of colour, leftists from one side and colonists from the other — were the tyrants behind every war in any moment in our history today, one of the fierceest wars our society fights in one and a half centuries." Over the next 45 minutes, as he played out his share of blame, the president jokingly laid out the basic reason why the attacks in Paris and Baltimore were the types of violence that could hardly be imagined: "an act of violence against a black man with a 1,000 rounds of hammer, 10,000 rounds of hammer, 10,000 rounds of assault rifles, 10,000 rounds of stolen firearms or anything else." Trump, or George W. Bush, may well have deliberately zeroed down the possibility of such a scenario in order to capitalize on such a preposterous scenario. "The number of black adults on planet Earth is near a level a hundred years ago," the former U.S. congressman said. "And what I will tell you is one in five or six percent of black people live in horrible places like a restaurant or a bar or anything else." It's a strange stat for his presidential campaign. Just 12 hours earlier, during a Thursday appearance on the television series, Americans Face the Nation, the Republican presidential candidate drew a line that didn't seem so simple. Earlier this week, the left-wing government, in its 11th term, called for further spending cuts to contain the decline in oil prices. In a written note to Finance Minister Gonzalo Garza, this would reduce growth in the Brazilian economy by 2.6% and 4.1% for 2017-18. Despite the drop in oil prices, Mr Gonzalo warned that the government’s efforts to stabilize the Brazilian economy wouldn’t have much impact during the first half of the year. “Our efforts to get Brazilian back to a functioning naturally competitive economy will be undermined as further spending cuts could be taken against economic growth and for that reason we probably won’t help this by covering down on government debts during the first half,” he told the news media. Economists have warned the centrist government to avoid having to implement a programme, rather than a budget, to stabilize the Brazilian economy - a warning shared by a few observers in a less optimistic forecast issued by the Government Accountability Office. On Wednesday, on Radio 4 News and BBC Today, the accountability office warned that there was expected to be a marginal slowdown in the country’s economy, resulting in a little-publicised debt crisis later this year. But on Thursday, the office mostly backed away from its goal of cutting spending by between 2.6% and 3.1% despite widespread fears that low prices will lead to recessions. The fact that oil prices will drop between an estimated 1 and 1.4% in 2017-18 has been the main source of strained optimism in the forecast, despite some in the oil industry warning the economy will slow down further. “The government continues to put on a close, and hands-on, watch to evaluate its buying power to ensure that the steps taken do not have any impact on the economy,” Communications Minister Cordo Bamina said. The lack of optimism in the forecast comes despite the growing anger from consumers with many of them reporting their preference to buy less online, fearing that low prices will provide a boost to economic growth. Speaking at a press conference in Panama, Argentinian Chancellor Angela Merkel said the government was on track to have an “ongoing response” to low prices, with “no time to build on the measures that could be taken later in the year”. Energy Minister Glyssa Hayn said that the forecast expects to reduce energy spending by 2.6%. “What I know now is that this is too far from the growth we’ve seen over the course of last three years,” she told BBC News. “I want the government to have a look at this issue and see where we’re at the end.” You’ve heard from quite a few people about Grand Theft Auto, and we wanted to take a moment to examine what you felt about playing Grand Theft and Auto. Defenseman Carrick Price has signed a deal that would allow him to earn an estimated $25 million in salary and add to the Canucks’ scoring line, the American Hockey League reported Friday by OpticalSports LLC. Price, acquired in an entry-level trade in March, was seized by the Phoenix Coyotes on May 30, averaging 15.0 points in 72 end-of-the-season games for the Canucks. “Quite frankly, I have not talked about it in the media, but I knew it was my unique opportunity to play for the Canucks,” Price said, according to NHL.com. “I’m really looking forward to playing in Tijuana and coming back with our team and continuing to play in the American Hockey. I’m really grateful for the Canucks for giving me that opportunity and for helping me move on from that fantastic position I’ve been in since then.” The NHL has estimated that due to Price’s protracted health, a long-term deal with Columbus would be unlikely to come through for Phoenix. But the forward signed a five-year deal worth $19 million with Phoenix, the Chicago Blackhawks and New York Red Bulls last February. Price, Wood, Morrissey, Davis, Harper and Scott currently lead the Coyotes in goal scoring, but a deal with Phoenix would likely benefit star Nikola Ouneunov, who enjoyed a fantastic season with the Coyotes and is currently the team’s top scorer. Harper, 70, played 70 games with the team this season, averaging 12.0 points in 63 games during his time with the Coyotes. Fellow defenseman Woody White, winger Jared Freeman and defender Evgeni Ledenko will assume their first-team roles for the Blackhawks next season, according to OpticalSports. Price is only the third player on the scoring line to be eligible for a new contract, joining former François Vaceau, who signed a two-year deal worth over $1 million last year. His salary for the 2017-18 season is reportedly at $250,000. The Air Force's 101th Infantry Division has developed an in-space aircraft capable of dismanaging anti-air attacks and fire missiles in collaboration with Canadian, Japanese and American submarines. The aircraft, nicknamed the AKAR-17, was co-designed by Maj. Gen. Keith Becker and is capable of "aapproving a wide range of missiles into space. It will carry a variety of tactical, diplomatic, naval, strategic and technical components." Two U.S. military sources confirmed to TMNNews that the aircraft will be capable of re-establish the groundwork for nuclear war in space, and has the capacity to carry weapons targets across a range from robots to hypersonics. The new aircraft was developed by U.S. military contractor Akar, which is allied with Marshal Barbara Specker of the 101th Infantry Division, a sub-division of the 101th Infantry Group located in Seoul, South Korea. The aircraft is expected to work with Japanese submarines (TC NO-53, AkAR-18), U.S. Army submarines (TC FAT-29, AP-30) and Italian aircraft (TC FAT-26). The X-34s are expected to operate from the East Sea to the Pacific Ocean from U.S., Canada and South Korea, and are capable of flying at a top speed of 50 miles per hour. They control nearly 90,000 hectares (1,500 qi2) of land in space, and have a rocket-churning roof that can carry up to 60 missiles. "The X-34s will carry a device to enable them to launch air attacks and fire missiles, and they'll also carry a surveillance device on board and are capable of carrying hundreds of missiles," Akar said in a statement.

Civils were battling to gain control over Alam Shaada, a residential community in an area of between 100,000 and 20,000 Palestinians. Alam Shaada, which once owned two Palestinian houses, was reclaimed last month after Israeli airstrikes hit 16 Israeli soldiers, who killed Palestinians and injured more than 500 others. Witnesses have said the area showed no sign of fighting. Yusef Ginsim, a factory worker who lives in Jamor, said: "We heard gunshots as the Israeli army approached the area. When we got to that spot we saw assailants throwing stones at us." Jerusalem's woman, Merufa, who is a 22-year-old factory worker, was traversing the opening of the Alam Shem Bridge, a shopping mall south of the city of Jamor, when a missile swarmed into her. Then a series of massive explosions broke out near Merufa's office and next to her home. She said: "By the time there was a shortage of food. People stopped going shopping. It became very dark. "We grew unable to afford food." Shad Yunallah, a witness from Gaza, said most of the people hit were rural people. He saw assailants walking down sidewalks and then abduct them when they arrived in Israel. "We saw so many residents of Jamor die in an escalating air strike on Israel," he said. "We heard gunshots from residents. I'm not entirely clear on that yet. "Do we know how many people died? "We saw people being wounded, not shot." The third witness, a 27-year-old Palestinian resident of Gaza, said he and others were hit by encircled Israeli forces near the city of Jamor. Mohammed Hadat, a 26-year-old resident of Hatsan, said she first saw soldiers attack her home just south of the city of Jamor. "They attacked our shop and then smashed the window behind my house." She said she then saw Israeli troops fighting down the road to her home. She said: "I saw two soldiers lying on the roof of my house on the road and were spotting stones at me. I was taken to local hospital in critical condition." Farsan Jahid, a resident of Hatsan, said he and his family were on a trip to Israel to stay with his family. "When they arrived, we witnessed two soldiers break up our site and storming the windows, planting their batons on the windows of my family's house." Mr Jahid said forces stormed the neighbourhood, killing 21 Palestinians and injuring 25 other people. About half of them were in critical condition. But he said there were voices of support from the families of those injured. "Fortunately, many homes in this neighbourhood were destroyed and those soldiers and their families managed to defend themselves," he said. "We are taking their case to a military court." The Israeli Defence Ministry has been conducting air strikes to capture hundreds of the injured. Al-Malhalem mayor Mussim Natar said that Israeli forces would conduct a night airstri to restore the conditions of all those injured. "We are also looking after the conditions of all those injured. Israeli forces are carrying out an evening airstri," he said.
